query.original_query: multi-turn jailbreak safety degradation internal representations across conversation turns

sub_queries.semantic_query: internal representation changes during multi-turn jailbreak attacks, safety degradation and representation shift across conversation turns in LLMs, probing safety features and circuits
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigate how internal representations of safety-related features shift across conversation turns during multi-turn jailbreak attacks on large language models. Using sparse autoencoders trained on residual stream activations, we analyze the activation patterns of monosemantic safety features and their degradation as adversarial prompts progress. Our analysis reveals that safety-critical features exhibit progressive attenuation in later turns, with feature absorption into context-processing circuits. Causal tracing and activation patching experiments localize this degradation to specific MLP layers and attention heads responsible for refusal and harm detection. We find that the representation shift correlates with increased polysemanticity in safety-related feature directions, suggesting superposition of harmful and benign concepts. Results show that while initial turns maintain high reconstruction fidelity of safety features, subsequent adversarial turns induce feature splitting and dead features in the safety circuit. Our findings indicate that multi-turn attacks exploit the dynamic reconfiguration of internal safety representations rather than static bypassing of a single refusal mechanism.

sub_queries.semantic_query: multi-turn jailbreak safety degradation internal representations across conversation turns
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigate the trajectory of safety-related internal representations across conversational turns in large language models subjected to multi-turn jailbreak attacks. Using linear probing and activation patching on transformer hidden states, we measured the progressive degradation of refusal-related features in the residual stream as adversarial prompts accumulate. Results indicate that safety representations, initially aligned with harm refusal in early turns, exhibit systematic attenuation in later turns, particularly in middle-layer attention heads previously associated with ethical reasoning. This degradation correlates with increased attack success rates, supporting the hypothesis that multi-turn jailbreaks exploit a cumulative erosion of internal safety boundaries rather than a single prompt bypass. Findings further suggest that representational drift is localized to specific subspaces, with partial recovery observed when benign context is reintroduced. These results provide evidence that safety alignment in current models is turn-dependent and vulnerable to sequential adversarial pressure, highlighting the need for temporally robust alignment mechanisms.

papers.title: Jailbreaking Leaves a Trace: Understanding and Detecting Jailbreak Attacks from Internal Representations of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do internal representations of LLMs differ between jailbreak and benign prompts, and can these differences be used for detection and mitigation?
papers.core_contribution: Jailbreak prompts leave identifiable traces in internal representations; a tensor-based framework can detect and mitigate jailbreaks by bypassing susceptible layers without model fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: Internal representations contain strong and consistent signals for jailbreak detection and mitigation, providing a lightweight, architecture-agnostic direction for improving LLM security.
papers.key_findings:
Jailbreak and benign prompts exhibit distinct layer-dependent latent signatures in internal representations.
These signatures can be uncovered using tensor decomposition and used for detection with high F1 scores.
Layer-wise susceptibility scores can identify layers that strongly encode jailbreak features.
Bypassing susceptible layers at inference time can block 78% of jailbreak attempts while preserving 94% of benign prompts.
The patterns are consistent across diverse model families (transformer and state-space models).
papers.limitation: Persona- or roleplay-based prompt injections can persist even after bypassing susceptible layers, and the fixed probability threshold for bypassing may not capture attacks that distribute influence across multiple layers.
future_direction: Extending the framework to additional attack families (e.g., GCG, PAIR) by incorporating corresponding prompt distributions during factor learning.
Adopting adaptive or cumulative susceptibility criteria for layer bypass.
papers.abstract: Jailbreaking large language models (LLMs) has emerged as a critical security challenge with the widespread deployment of conversational AI systems. Adversarial users exploit these models through carefully crafted prompts to elicit restricted or unsafe outputs, a phenomenon commonly referred to as Jailbreaking. Despite numerous proposed defense mechanisms, attackers continue to develop adaptive prompting strategies, and existing models remain vulnerable. This motivates approaches that examine the internal behavior of LLMs rather than relying solely on prompt-level defenses. In this work, we study jailbreaking from both security and interpretability perspectives by analyzing how internal representations differ between jailbreak and benign prompts. We conduct a systematic layer-wise analysis across multiple open-source models, including GPT-J, LLaMA, Mistral, and the state-space model Mamba, and identify consistent latent-space patterns associated with harmful inputs. We then propose a tensor-based latent representation framework that captures structure in hidden activations and enables lightweight jailbreak detection without model fine-tuning or auxiliary LLM-based detectors. We further demonstrate that the latent signals can be used to actively disrupt jailbreak execution at inference time. On an abliterated LLaMA-3.1-8B model, selectively bypassing high-susceptibility layers blocks 78% of jailbreak attempts while preserving benign behavior on 94% of benign prompts. This intervention operates entirely at inference time and introduces minimal overhead, providing a scalable foundation for achieving stronger coverage by incorporating additional attack distributions or more refined susceptibility thresholds. Our results provide evidence that jailbreak behavior is rooted in identifiable internal structures and suggest a complementary, architecture-agnostic direction for improving LLM security.

papers.title: Multi-Turn Jailbreaking Large Language Models via Attention Shifting
papers.research_question: What are the underlying reasons for the effectiveness of multi-turn jailbreak attacks on LLMs, and how can attention shifting be leveraged to improve such attacks?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes ASJA, a multi-turn jailbreak method that shifts LLM attention away from harmful keywords by fabricating dialogue history using a genetic algorithm, achieving higher attack success rates and stealthiness.
papers.conclusion: ASJA effectively breaks the LLM's safety alignment by shifting attention to historical queries and responses via fabricated dialogue, outperforming baselines in effectiveness, stealthiness, and transferability.
papers.key_findings:
Successful multi-turn jailbreaks shift LLM attention away from harmful keywords to dialogue history, especially previous responses.
ASJA achieves higher attack success rates (44.91% improvement in harmfulness and 34.02% in relevance) compared to baselines.
ASJA maintains stealthiness (low perplexity) and has good transferability to other models.
The attention on harmful keywords in the last query is significantly lower in successful jailbreaks.
Optimizing both queries and responses in dialogue history is more effective than optimizing queries alone.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved significant performance in various natural language processing tasks but also pose safety and ethical threats, thus requiring red teaming and alignment processes to bolster their safety. To effectively exploit these aligned LLMs, recent studies have introduced jailbreak attacks based on multi-turn dialogues. These attacks aim to prompt LLMs to generate harmful or biased content by guiding them through contextual content. However, the underlying reasons for the effectiveness of multi-turn jailbreaks remain unclear. Existing attacks often focus on optimizing queries and escalating toxicity to construct dialogues, lacking a thorough analysis of the inherent vulnerabilities of LLMs. In this paper, we first conduct an in-depth analysis of the differences between single-turn and multi-turn jailbreaks and find that successful multi-turn jailbreaks can effectively disperse the attention of LLMs on keywords associated with harmful behaviors, especially in historical responses. Based on this, we propose ASJA, a new multi-turn jailbreak approach by shifting the attention of LLMs, specifically by iteratively fabricating the dialogue history through a genetic algorithm to induce LLMs to generate harmful content. Extensive experiments on three LLMs and two datasets show that our approach surpasses existing approaches in jailbreak effectiveness, the stealth of jailbreak prompts, and attack efficiency. Our work emphasizes the importance of enhancing the robustness of LLMs' attention mechanism in multi-turn dialogue scenarios for a better defense strategy.

papers.title: A Representation Engineering Perspective on the Effectiveness of Multi-Turn Jailbreaks
papers.research_question: How do language models represent multi-turn jailbreak (Crescendo) inputs compared to single-turn inputs? How does the number of conversation turns affect these representations, and how do the model's own responses influence them?
papers.core_contribution: Multi-turn jailbreaks like Crescendo cause safety-aligned language models to represent harmful outputs as benign, especially as the number of turns increases, explaining why single-turn defenses like circuit breakers fail to generalize.
papers.conclusion: There is a generalization gap between single-turn defenses and multi-turn jailbreaks, motivating the development of defenses that target harmful multi-turn representations.
papers.key_findings:
Crescendo attacks cause models to represent the final harmful response tokens as more benign than harmful.
Increasing the number of turns in a Crescendo conversation decreases the model's representation of the output as harmful.
User prompts in the attack play a primary role in shaping representations towards benign regions; the model's own prior responses have a smaller effect.
Single-turn jailbreak defenses (circuit breakers) show a generalization gap and are ineffective against multi-turn attacks.
Crescendo works by keeping the model in a benign region of representation space across turns, tricking it into generating harmful content.
papers.limitation:
It is difficult to know how much the MLP probe results capture the model's internal notion of 'harmfulness' versus other differences between training and Crescendo representations.
The analysis focuses exclusively on the Crescendo jailbreak method.
future_direction: Explore whether the observations hold for other multi-turn jailbreaks like GOAT and Tempest.
Expand the analysis to more models, including reasoning models and other leading jailbreak defenses.
Develop better defenses that target both single-turn and multi-turn model representations.
papers.abstract: Recent research has demonstrated that state-of-the-art LLMs and defenses remain susceptible to multi-turn jailbreak attacks. These attacks require only closed-box model access and are often easy to perform manually, posing a significant threat to the safe and secure deployment of LLM-based systems. We study the effectiveness of the Crescendo multi-turn jailbreak at the level of intermediate model representations and find that safety-aligned LMs often represent Crescendo responses as more benign than harmful, especially as the number of conversation turns increases. Our analysis indicates that at each turn, Crescendo prompts tend to keep model outputs in a "benign" region of representation space, effectively tricking the model into fulfilling harmful requests. Further, our results help explain why single-turn jailbreak defenses like circuit breakers are generally ineffective against multi-turn attacks, motivating the development of mitigations that address this generalization gap.

papers.title: ASGuard: Activation-Scaling Guard to Mitigate Targeted Jailbreaking Attack
papers.research_question: How can we surgically mitigate targeted jailbreaking vulnerabilities in LLMs by understanding and intervening in their internal mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ASGUARD, a framework that uses circuit analysis to identify vulnerable attention heads and then applies activation scaling and preventative fine-tuning to mitigate targeted jailbreaking attacks while preserving model utility.
papers.conclusion: ASGUARD demonstrates how mechanistic interpretability can be leveraged to develop targeted and efficient safety interventions, achieving a superior safety-utility trade-off.
papers.key_findings:
Tense jailbreaking is mediated by specific attention heads that can be identified via circuit analysis.
ASGUARD reduces the attack success rate of tense jailbreaking from 42% to 8% in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct while maintaining high utility.
ASGUARD achieves a Pareto-optimal balance between safety and utility, outperforming baseline methods like SFT and DPO.
The method generalizes to other jailbreaking attacks like GCG and LogiBreak.
Preventative fine-tuning helps the model learn a robust refusal mechanism without relying on the vulnerable pathway.
papers.limitation:
The method requires constructing circuits for each specific attack type, which can be computationally expensive.
There is a risk of over-refusal if the scaling vectors are not properly tuned.
future_direction: Extending ASGUARD to other types of jailbreaking attacks and models.
Automating the circuit discovery process to reduce computational cost.
Exploring the application of activation scaling to other safety vulnerabilities.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs), despite being safety-aligned, exhibit brittle refusal behaviors that can be circumvented by simple linguistic changes. As tense jailbreaking demonstrates that models refusing harmful requests often comply when rephrased in past tense, a critical generalization gap is revealed in current alignment methods whose underlying mechanisms are poorly understood. In this work, we introduce Activation-Scaling Guard (ASGuard), an insightful, mechanistically-informed framework that surgically mitigates this specific vulnerability. For the first step, we use circuit analysis to identify the specific attention heads causally linked to the targeted jailbreaking, the tense-changing attack. Second, we train a precise, channel-wise scaling vector to recalibrate the activation of tense vulnerable heads. Lastly, we apply it into a "preventative fine-tuning", forcing the model to learn a more robust refusal mechanism. Across three LLMs, ASGuard effectively reduces the attack success rate of targeted jailbreaking while preserving general capabilities and minimizing over refusal, achieving a Pareto-optimal balance between safety and utility. Our findings underscore how adversarial suffixes suppress the propagation of the refusal-mediating direction, based on mechanistic analysis. Furthermore, our work showcases how a deep understanding of model internals can be leveraged to develop practical, efficient, and targeted methods for adjusting model behavior, charting a course for more reliable and interpretable AI safety.

papers.title: JailbreakLens: Interpreting Jailbreak Mechanism in the Lens of Representation and Circuit
papers.research_question: How do jailbreak prompts affect the internal representations of LLMs? Which model components are critical to generation safety? How do internal representations and key model components evolve throughout the token generation process during jailbreak attacks?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes JailbreakLens, a dual-perspective interpretation framework that analyzes jailbreak mechanisms by examining representation shifts and circuit activations, revealing how jailbreak prompts deceive LLMs by manipulating harmfulness perception and safety-critical components.
papers.conclusion: JailbreakLens provides insights into jailbreak mechanisms, showing that prompts deceive models by shifting representations and manipulating key circuits, with a consistent correlation between representation deception and circuit activation shifts.
papers.key_findings:
Jailbreak prompts deceive LLMs by shifting their internal representations towards safe clusters, making harmful prompts appear safe.
Key circuits, such as specific attention heads and MLP layers, are manipulated to suppress refusal behaviors and encourage affirmation.
There is a strong correlation between representation deception and activation shifts in key circuits across diverse jailbreak methods and LLMs.
Rule-based and demonstration-based jailbreak methods are more deceptive than gradient-based or evolutionary-based methods.
Dynamic analysis shows that jailbreak effects evolve during token generation, with refusal signals sometimes initially activated but later bypassed.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are limited to models with up to 13B parameters due to computational constraints.
Not all recent jailbreak methods are included in the study.
future_direction: Extend research to larger-scale models to determine if similar attack patterns apply.
Design more robust and interpretable safety mechanisms based on the identified vulnerabilities.
papers.abstract: Despite the outstanding performance of Large language Models (LLMs) in diverse tasks, they are vulnerable to jailbreak attacks, wherein adversarial prompts are crafted to bypass their security mechanisms and elicit unexpected responses. Although jailbreak attacks are prevalent, the understanding of their underlying mechanisms remains limited. Recent studies have explained typical jailbreaking behavior (e.g., the degree to which the model refuses to respond) of LLMs by analyzing representation shifts in their latent space caused by jailbreak prompts or identifying key neurons that contribute to the success of jailbreak attacks. However, these studies neither explore diverse jailbreak patterns nor provide a fine-grained explanation from the failure of circuit to the changes of representational, leaving significant gaps in uncovering the jailbreak mechanism. In this paper, we propose JailbreakLens, an interpretation framework that analyzes jailbreak mechanisms from both representation (which reveals how jailbreaks alter the model's harmfulness perception) and circuit perspectives~(which uncovers the causes of these deceptions by identifying key circuits contributing to the vulnerability), tracking their evolution throughout the entire response generation process. We then conduct an in-depth evaluation of jailbreak behavior on five mainstream LLMs under seven jailbreak strategies. Our evaluation reveals that jailbreak prompts amplify components that reinforce affirmative responses while suppressing those that produce refusal. This manipulation shifts model representations toward safe clusters to deceive the LLM, leading it to provide detailed responses instead of refusals. Notably, we find a strong and consistent correlation between representation deception and activation shift of key circuits across diverse jailbreak methods and multiple LLMs.

papers.title: Foot In The Door: Understanding Large Language Model Jailbreaking via Cognitive Psychology
papers.research_question: How can cognitive psychology explain the decision-making mechanisms of large language models (LLMs) during jailbreaking attacks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a psychological explanation for LLM jailbreaking using cognitive consistency theory and proposes a new automated jailbreaking method called FITD based on the Foot-in-the-Door technique.
papers.conclusion: This paper explains existing jailbreaking methods from a psychological perspective and proposes a novel jailbreaking method using the foot-in-the-door technique, aiming to offer a new approach to understanding LLMs' thought processes and inspire future alignment work.
papers.key_findings:
FITD achieves an average success rate of 83.9% on 8 advanced LLMs.
FITD is particularly effective on Claude series models compared to other jailbreaking methods.
Hate speech and harassment/threat categories have lower attack success rates and require more dialogue steps for jailbreaking.
Recursive splitting of prompts increases jailbreak success rate.
Initial splitting methods that include background and character settings improve the effectiveness of jailbreaking.
papers.limitation:
The types of malicious questions and jailbreaking prompt words may not be comprehensive enough.
The prompt splitting instance is manually designed, and potentially better alternatives exist.
The method has only been tested in English and has not been extended to other languages.
The psychological explanation does not apply to jailbreak prompts with uninterpreted strings.
future_direction: Continue to delve into the psychological characteristics of LLMs, particularly focusing on cognitive and social psychology mechanisms.
Develop LLM adversarial training techniques based on psychological theories to enhance alignment at the psychological level.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have gradually become the gateway for people to acquire new knowledge. However, attackers can break the model's security protection ("jail") to access restricted information, which is called "jailbreaking." Previous studies have shown the weakness of current LLMs when confronted with such jailbreaking attacks. Nevertheless, comprehension of the intrinsic decision-making mechanism within the LLMs upon receipt of jailbreak prompts is noticeably lacking. Our research provides a psychological explanation of the jailbreak prompts. Drawing on cognitive consistency theory, we argue that the key to jailbreak is guiding the LLM to achieve cognitive coordination in an erroneous direction. Further, we propose an automatic black-box jailbreaking method based on the Foot-in-the-Door (FITD) technique. This method progressively induces the model to answer harmful questions via multi-step incremental prompts. We instantiated a prototype system to evaluate the jailbreaking effectiveness on 8 advanced LLMs, yielding an average success rate of 83.9%. This study builds a psychological perspective on the explanatory insights into the intrinsic decision-making logic of LLMs.

papers.title: Eraser: Jailbreaking Defense in Large Language Models via Unlearning Harmful Knowledge
papers.research_question: How can we defend against jailbreaking attacks in Large Language Models by unlearning harmful knowledge while retaining general capabilities and safety alignment?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes Eraser, a jailbreaking defense method that unlearns harmful knowledge via gradient ascent while retaining general knowledge and safety alignment, significantly reducing attack success rates without compromising general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: Eraser effectively defends against jailbreaking by unlearning harmful knowledge, maintaining general performance, and enhancing safety alignment, offering a better balance between harmlessness and usefulness compared to existing methods.
papers.key_findings:
Eraser significantly reduces the Attack Success Rate (ASR) and harmfulness scores for various jailbreaking attacks (AIM, AutoDAN, GCG).
Eraser maintains general capabilities comparable to the base model across multiple benchmarks (e.g., ARC, HellaSwag).
Using random prefixes/suffixes during unlearning (T(·)) enhances defensive capability against jailbreaking.
Unlearning harmful text contributes to defense, but gradient ascent on random token sequences also yields defense at the cost of general performance degradation.
The threshold γ controls the trade-off between defense performance and general capability; a moderate value (e.g., 2) is recommended.
papers.limitation:
Eraser is inefficient as it only defends against specific harmful issues, and enumerating all harmful issues is challenging.
Eraser is only applicable to LLMs that have undergone safety alignment.
future_direction: Future research on jailbreaking defense should focus more on maintaining general capabilities.
More effort is needed to enhance safety alignment so that unlearning methods like Eraser can become an alternative to technologies like RLHF.
papers.abstract: Jailbreaking attacks can enable Large Language Models (LLMs) to bypass the safeguard and generate harmful content. Existing jailbreaking defense methods have failed to address the fundamental issue that harmful knowledge resides within the model, leading to potential jailbreak risks for LLMs. In this paper, we propose a novel defense method called Eraser, which mainly includes three goals: unlearning harmful knowledge, retaining general knowledge, and maintaining safety alignment. The intuition is that if an LLM forgets the specific knowledge required to answer a harmful question, it will no longer have the ability to answer harmful questions. The training of Erase does not actually require the model's own harmful knowledge, and it can benefit from unlearning general answers related to harmful queries, which means it does not need assistance from the red team. The experimental results show that Eraser can significantly reduce the jailbreaking success rate for various attacks without compromising the general capabilities of the model. Our codes are available at https://github.com/ZeroNLP/Eraser.

papers.title: Revisiting Jailbreaking for Large Language Models: A Representation Engineering Perspective
papers.research_question: What are the underlying mechanisms that make Large Language Models vulnerable to jailbreaking attacks, and are these linked to specific activation patterns in their representation space?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies 'safety patterns' in LLMs' representation space that are crucial for self-safeguarding against malicious queries, and shows these patterns can be extracted and manipulated to control jailbreak vulnerability.
papers.conclusion: The study provides a new interpretation of jailbreaking through safety patterns, offering insights for attack and defense strategies, and raises concerns about the misuse of open-source LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Safety patterns can be extracted from LLMs using only a few contrastive query pairs.
Weakening safety patterns significantly reduces LLMs' self-safeguard capability, leading to successful jailbreaks.
Strengthening safety patterns enhances defense against stealthy jailbreak prompts.
Manipulating safety patterns has minimal impact on LLMs' general abilities and output quality.
Visualization analysis confirms that safety patterns affect the embedding distribution of malicious and benign inputs.
papers.limitation:
The findings are based on white-box settings, limiting applicability to black-box scenarios.
Preventing misuse of safety pattern manipulation is a critical challenge.
future_direction: Exploring effective techniques such as Reverse Engineering based on the concept of safety patterns.
Developing comprehensive safeguarding strategies to ensure the safer use of LLMs, particularly in open-source models.
papers.abstract: The recent surge in jailbreaking attacks has revealed significant vulnerabilities in Large Language Models (LLMs) when exposed to malicious inputs. While various defense strategies have been proposed to mitigate these threats, there has been limited research into the underlying mechanisms that make LLMs vulnerable to such attacks. In this study, we suggest that the self-safeguarding capability of LLMs is linked to specific activity patterns within their representation space. Although these patterns have little impact on the semantic content of the generated text, they play a crucial role in shaping LLM behavior under jailbreaking attacks. Our findings demonstrate that these patterns can be detected with just a few pairs of contrastive queries. Extensive experimentation shows that the robustness of LLMs against jailbreaking can be manipulated by weakening or strengthening these patterns. Further visual analysis provides additional evidence for our conclusions, providing new insights into the jailbreaking phenomenon. These findings highlight the importance of addressing the potential misuse of open-source LLMs within the community.

papers.title: JBShield: Defending Large Language Models from Jailbreak Attacks through Activated Concept Analysis and Manipulation
papers.research_question: Can aligned LLMs recognize the toxic semantics in jailbreak prompts? How do jailbreak attacks change the outputs of LLMs from rejecting to complying?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes JBShield, a jailbreak defense framework that detects and mitigates jailbreak attacks by analyzing and manipulating toxic and jailbreak concepts in the representation space of LLMs.
papers.conclusion: JBShield effectively defends against jailbreak attacks by detecting and mitigating them through concept analysis and manipulation, outperforming existing defenses.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs can recognize toxic concepts in both harmful and jailbreak prompts.
Jailbreak prompts activate a jailbreak concept that overrides the toxic concept, leading to compliance.
JBShield achieves an average detection accuracy of 0.95 and reduces the average attack success rate from 61% to 2%.
JBShield requires only 30 jailbreak prompts for calibration.
JBShield demonstrates strong transferability across different jailbreak attacks and LLMs.
papers.limitation: Performance slightly declines on Mistral-7B and Vicuna-13B for prompts that activate the jailbreak concept without triggering toxic activation, indicating a limitation in handling nuanced cases where jailbreak activation subtly interacts with the model’s semantic interpretations.
future_direction: Optimizing performance for complex scenarios where jailbreak activation subtly interacts with the model’s semantic interpretations.
papers.abstract: Despite the implementation of safety alignment strategies, large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks, which undermine these safety guardrails and pose significant security threats. Some defenses have been proposed to detect or mitigate jailbreaks, but they are unable to withstand the test of time due to an insufficient understanding of jailbreak mechanisms. In this work, we investigate the mechanisms behind jailbreaks based on the Linear Representation Hypothesis (LRH), which states that neural networks encode high-level concepts as subspaces in their hidden representations. We define the toxic semantics in harmful and jailbreak prompts as toxic concepts and describe the semantics in jailbreak prompts that manipulate LLMs to comply with unsafe requests as jailbreak concepts. Through concept extraction and analysis, we reveal that LLMs can recognize the toxic concepts in both harmful and jailbreak prompts. However, unlike harmful prompts, jailbreak prompts activate the jailbreak concepts and alter the LLM output from rejection to compliance. Building on our analysis, we propose a comprehensive jailbreak defense framework, JBShield, consisting of two key components: jailbreak detection JBShield-D and mitigation JBShield-M. JBShield-D identifies jailbreak prompts by determining whether the input activates both toxic and jailbreak concepts. When a jailbreak prompt is detected, JBShield-M adjusts the hidden representations of the target LLM by enhancing the toxic concept and weakening the jailbreak concept, ensuring LLMs produce safe content. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superior performance of JBShield, achieving an average detection accuracy of 0.95 and reducing the average attack success rate of various jailbreak attacks to 2% from 61% across distinct LLMs.

papers.title: SafeLLM: Unlearning Harmful Outputs from Large Language Models against Jailbreak Attacks
papers.research_question: How can we defend against jailbreak attacks on Large Language Models by unlearning harmful outputs while preserving linguistic fluency and general capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SafeLLM, a token-level unlearning framework that integrates dynamic detection, FFN activation tracing, and constrained optimization to suppress harmful outputs in LLMs against jailbreak attacks while preserving general performance.
papers.conclusion: SafeLLM achieves irreversible forgetting of harmful behavior, significantly reducing jailbreak attack success rates without degrading general performance, offering a scalable and proactive defense for LLM safety.
papers.key_findings:
SafeLLM significantly reduces Attack Success Rates (ASR) across jailbreak benchmarks compared to baseline methods like SFT and DPO.
It maintains general performance on benign datasets such as OpenBookQA and TruthfulQA after unlearning.
SafeLLM enables irreversible forgetting of harmful behaviors by targeting FFN substructures responsible for harmful token generation.
The framework demonstrates robustness to unseen adversarial prompts through feature-driven generalization.
Ablation studies show that dynamic fusion weights and adaptive trust-region bounds optimize the safety-utility trade-off.
future_direction: Advance unlearning techniques to tackle broader challenges related to fairness, transparency, and adversarial threats in multi-modal LLMs.
papers.abstract: Jailbreak attacks pose a serious threat to the safety of Large Language Models (LLMs) by crafting adversarial prompts that bypass alignment mechanisms, causing the models to produce harmful, restricted, or biased content. In this paper, we propose SafeLLM, a novel unlearning-based defense framework that unlearn the harmful knowledge from LLMs while preserving linguistic fluency and general capabilities. SafeLLM employs a three-stage pipeline: (1) dynamic unsafe output detection using a hybrid approach that integrates external classifiers with model-internal evaluations; (2) token-level harmful content tracing through feedforward network (FFN) activations to localize harmful knowledge; and (3) constrained optimization to suppress unsafe behavior without degrading overall model quality. SafeLLM achieves targeted and irreversible forgetting by identifying and neutralizing FFN substructures responsible for harmful generation pathways. Extensive experiments on prominent LLMs (Vicuna, LLaMA, and GPT-J) across multiple jailbreak benchmarks show that SafeLLM substantially reduces attack success rates while maintaining high general-purpose performance. Compared to standard defense methods such as supervised fine-tuning and direct preference optimization, SafeLLM offers stronger safety guarantees, more precise control over harmful behavior, and greater robustness to unseen attacks. Moreover, SafeLLM maintains the general performance after the harmful knowledge unlearned. These results highlight unlearning as a promising direction for scalable and effective LLM safety.

papers.title: SafeInt: Shielding Large Language Models from Jailbreak Attacks via Safety-Aware Representation Intervention
papers.research_question: How can we defend large language models against jailbreak attacks by intervening in their internal representations to relocate jailbreak-related representations into the rejection region?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SafeIntervention (SafeInt), a defense method that adaptively intervenes in jailbreak-related representations to align them with unsafe sample representations, thereby activating the model's refusal mechanisms while preserving utility.
papers.conclusion: SafeInt, a representation intervention-based defense, effectively shields LLMs from jailbreak attacks by adaptively relocating jailbreak representations into the rejection region, outperforming existing methods while preserving model utility.
papers.key_findings:
Representations of jailbreak samples are distinguishable from safe and unsafe samples in intermediate and later layers of LLMs.
Representation distributions of different jailbreak methods (e.g., GCG, AutoDAN, DeepInception) are consistent, especially in intermediate layers.
SafeInt outperforms all baseline defense methods in reducing Attack Success Rate (ASR) across various jailbreak attacks and datasets.
SafeInt maintains utility (measured by MT-Bench and Just-Eval) close to the non-defended model, often better than other defenses.
SafeInt remains effective against adaptive attacks and real-time jailbreak attempts.
papers.limitation: The transferability of SafeInt to different but homologous LLMs has not been explored in depth.
papers.abstract: With the widespread real-world deployment of large language models (LLMs), ensuring their behavior complies with safety standards has become crucial. Jailbreak attacks exploit vulnerabilities in LLMs to induce undesirable behavior, posing a significant threat to LLM safety. Previous defenses often fail to achieve both effectiveness and efficiency simultaneously. Defenses from a representation perspective offer new insights, but existing interventions cannot dynamically adjust representations based on the harmfulness of the queries. To address this limitation, we propose SafeIntervention (SafeInt), a novel defense method that shields LLMs from jailbreak attacks through safety-aware representation intervention. Built on our analysis of the representations of jailbreak samples, the core idea of SafeInt is to relocate jailbreak-related representations into the rejection region. This is achieved by intervening in the representation distributions of jailbreak samples to align them with those of unsafe samples. We conduct comprehensive experiments covering six jailbreak attacks, two jailbreak datasets, and two utility benchmarks. Experimental results demonstrate that SafeInt outperforms all baselines in defending LLMs against jailbreak attacks while largely maintaining utility. Additionally, we evaluate SafeInt against adaptive attacks and verify its effectiveness in mitigating real-time attacks.

papers.title: Efficient Jailbreaking of Large Models by Freeze Training: Lower Layers Exhibit Greater Sensitivity to Harmful Content
papers.research_question: This study investigates the sensitivity of different layers in Large Language Models to harmful content generation and proposes an efficient jailbreak method using freeze training.
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies lower layers in LLMs as highly sensitive to harmful content generation and introduces the Freeze-Front5-SFT method, which efficiently jailbreaks models by fine-tuning only these critical layers, achieving high attack success rates with reduced computational costs.
papers.conclusion: This study demonstrates that lower layers are critical for jailbreak attacks, and the Freeze-Front5-SFT method offers an efficient approach for both jailbreaking and informing defense strategies, contributing to LLM security research.
papers.key_findings:
Lower layers (first 20%) are highly sensitive to harmful content generation.
Freeze-Front5-SFT achieves an Attack Success Rate of 84.19% and Harm Score of 4.41 with only 1.5 hours training and 169.2 GB GPU memory, outperforming LoRA-based methods in efficiency.
The method generalizes effectively across various model architectures and sizes, including Qwen2.5, Llama3.1, Baichuan2, GLM4, and Mistral.
Training lower layers is more effective for jailbreaking than training higher layers, as shown by higher ASR and Harm Score.
Freeze-Front5-SFT provides a superior balance between jailbreak effectiveness and resource consumption compared to full-parameter fine-tuning and other LoRA methods.
papers.limitation:
Model Generalizability: Findings may not generalize to all LLM architectures, especially those with different layer configurations or attention mechanisms.
Layer Interaction Dynamics: Analysis focused on individual layers without accounting for cross-layer interactions.
Temporal Stability: Experiments did not assess long-term model behavior or jailbreak persistence.
Dataset Scope: Dataset primarily focuses on text-based attacks, leaving multimodal jailbreaks unexplored.
future_direction: Extend analysis to emerging architectures like mixture-of-experts models.
Conduct longitudinal studies of jailbreak persistence.
Develop more sophisticated analysis of cross-layer interactions.
papers.abstract: With the widespread application of Large Language Models across various domains, their security issues have increasingly garnered significant attention from both academic and industrial communities. This study conducts sampling and normalization of the parameters of the LLM to generate visual representations and heatmaps of parameter distributions, revealing notable discrepancies in parameter distributions among certain layers within the hidden layers. Further analysis involves calculating statistical metrics for each layer, followed by the computation of a Comprehensive Sensitivity Score based on these metrics, which identifies the lower layers as being particularly sensitive to the generation of harmful content. Based on this finding, we employ a Freeze training strategy, selectively performing Supervised Fine-Tuning only on the lower layers. Experimental results demonstrate that this method significantly reduces training duration and GPU memory consumption while maintaining a high jailbreak success rate and a high harm score, outperforming the results achieved by applying the LoRA method for SFT across all layers. Additionally, the method has been successfully extended to other open-source large models, validating its generality and effectiveness across different model architectures. Furthermore, we compare our method with ohter jailbreak method, demonstrating the superior performance of our approach. By innovatively proposing a method to statistically analyze and compare large model parameters layer by layer, this study provides new insights into the interpretability of large models. These discoveries emphasize the necessity of continuous research and the implementation of adaptive security measures in the rapidly evolving field of LLMs to prevent potential jailbreak attack risks, thereby promoting the development of more robust and secure LLMs.

papers.title: AISA: Awakening Intrinsic Safety Awareness in Large Language Models against Jailbreak Attacks
papers.research_question: How can we defend against jailbreak attacks in large language models by awakening their intrinsic safety awareness without fine-tuning or external modules?
papers.core_contribution: AISA is a lightweight defense framework that extracts intrinsic safety signals from attention head activations via linear probing and uses them to steer generation through logits adjustment, achieving robust jailbreak defense without model tuning.
papers.conclusion: AISA provides an effective, lightweight defense against jailbreak attacks by leveraging intrinsic safety awareness in LLMs, offering a resource-efficient alternative to safety alignment tuning.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs possess intrinsic safety awareness even without safety-specific fine-tuning, as evidenced by refusal behavior in uncensored models.
Attention head outputs, particularly at the final structural token before generation, provide the strongest discriminative signal for prompt intent.
AISA's data-driven head selection and logits steering outperform existing defense baselines in safety and utility preservation across diverse jailbreak datasets.
The safety awareness signal is architecture-dependent and persists across alignment variants, indicating a common pretrained basis.
AISA enables unaligned models to match or exceed the safety performance of aligned counterparts while avoiding over-refusal.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreak prompts that elicit harmful or policy-violating outputs, while many existing defenses rely on expensive fine-tuning, intrusive prompt rewriting, or external guardrails that add latency and can degrade helpfulness. We present AISA, a lightweight, single-pass defense that activates safety behaviors already latent inside the model rather than treating safety as an add-on. AISA first localizes intrinsic safety awareness via spatiotemporal analysis and shows that intent-discriminative signals are broadly encoded, with especially strong separability appearing in the scaled dot-product outputs of specific attention heads near the final structural tokens before generation. Using a compact set of automatically selected heads, AISA extracts an interpretable prompt-risk score with minimal overhead, achieving detector-level performance competitive with strong proprietary baselines on small (7B) models. AISA then performs logits-level steering: it modulates the decoding distribution in proportion to the inferred risk, ranging from normal generation for benign prompts to calibrated refusal for high-risk requests -- without changing model parameters, adding auxiliary modules, or requiring multi-pass inference. Extensive experiments spanning 13 datasets, 12 LLMs, and 14 baselines demonstrate that AISA improves robustness and transfer while preserving utility and reducing false refusals, enabling safer deployment even for weakly aligned or intentionally risky model variants.

papers.title: Jailbreak Antidote: Runtime Safety-Utility Balance via Sparse Representation Adjustment in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we balance safety and utility in large language models against jailbreak attacks by adjusting internal states during inference?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Jailbreak Antidote, a method for real-time safety-utility balance by sparsely adjusting internal states during inference, showing that safety information is sparsely distributed and adjusting approximately 5% of the state is as effective as modifying the entire state.
papers.conclusion: Jailbreak Antidote offers a lightweight, scalable solution for real-time safety adjustments in LLMs by directly manipulating internal states, enhancing safety while preserving utility and opening new possibilities for real-time safety mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Safety-related information in LLMs is sparsely distributed; adjusting approximately 5% of the internal state is as effective as modifying the entire state.
Jailbreak Antidote achieves high defense success rates (DSR) across nine LLMs and ten jailbreak attack methods.
The method preserves model utility, maintaining high Win Rates on AlpacaEval while enhancing safety.
The approach is efficient, introducing negligible computational overhead and no additional token cost during inference.
The safety direction can be identified via PCA on hidden states from benign and harmful prompts.
papers.limitation:
The method requires pre-defined scaling factor α and sparsity parameter k; dynamically adapting these based on context or model confidence could improve flexibility.
Smaller models are inherently limited by their reduced parameter space, which may restrict the extent of safety adjustment.
Developing robust mechanisms to counter adversaries capable of explicitly exploiting the adjustments in internal states remains an open challenge.
future_direction: Dynamically adapting the scaling factor α and sparsity parameter k based on context or model confidence.
Addressing extreme adversarial settings where attackers explicitly exploit the internal state adjustments.
Investigating the applicability of the approach to other aspects of model alignment, such as fairness or domain adaptation.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) become integral to various applications, ensuring both their safety and utility is paramount. Jailbreak attacks, which manipulate LLMs into generating harmful content, pose significant challenges to this balance. Existing defenses, such as prompt engineering and safety fine-tuning, often introduce computational overhead, increase inference latency, and lack runtime flexibility. Moreover, overly restrictive safety measures can degrade model utility by causing refusals of benign queries. In this paper, we introduce Jailbreak Antidote, a method that enables real-time adjustment of LLM safety preferences by manipulating a sparse subset of the model's internal states during inference. By shifting the model's hidden representations along a safety direction with varying strengths, we achieve flexible control over the safety-utility balance without additional token overhead or inference delays. Our analysis reveals that safety-related information in LLMs is sparsely distributed; adjusting approximately 5% of the internal state is as effective as modifying the entire state. Extensive experiments on nine LLMs (ranging from 2 billion to 72 billion parameters), evaluated against ten jailbreak attack methods and compared with six defense strategies, validate the effectiveness and efficiency of our approach. By directly manipulating internal states during reasoning, Jailbreak Antidote offers a lightweight, scalable solution that enhances LLM safety while preserving utility, opening new possibilities for real-time safety mechanisms in widely-deployed AI systems.

papers.title: Shaping the Safety Boundaries: Understanding and Defending Against Jailbreaks in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How does jailbreaking operate in large language models, and how can we develop an effective defense mechanism based on this understanding?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals that jailbreaks shift harmful activations beyond a safety boundary, especially in low and middle layers, and proposes a novel defense (ABD) that constrains activations within this boundary to prevent harmful outputs.
papers.conclusion: The study provides a comprehensive analysis of jailbreak mechanisms, showing they shift activations outside a safety boundary, and proposes ABD, an effective and efficient defense that leverages this understanding by constraining activations within the boundary.
papers.key_findings:
Jailbreak prompts shift activations outside a defined safety boundary, with the most severe shifts occurring in the low and middle layers of the model.
The safety boundary expands in deeper layers, requiring larger activation shifts to bypass safety checks.
The proposed Activation Boundary Defense (ABD) effectively constrains jailbreak activations within the safety boundary, achieving high defense success rates (over 98% on average) with minimal impact (less than 2%) on the model's general capabilities.
Bayesian optimization for layer selection in ABD confirms that low and middle layers are the most critical for defense, aligning with the mechanistic findings.
papers.limitation:
ABD may underperform on under-aligned models because unclear safety boundaries complicate the search for effective penalty functions.
The analysis and defense focus on single-round jailbreak scenarios and do not extend to multi-turn dialogues or long-context attacks.
future_direction: Investigate the challenges of jailbreaks in multi-turn dialogue scenarios.
papers.abstract: Jailbreaking in Large Language Models (LLMs) is a major security concern as it can deceive LLMs to generate harmful text. Yet, there is still insufficient understanding of how jailbreaking works, which makes it hard to develop effective defense strategies. We aim to shed more light into this issue: we conduct a detailed large-scale analysis of seven different jailbreak methods and find that these disagreements stem from insufficient observation samples. In particular, we introduce \textit{safety boundary}, and we find that jailbreaks shift harmful activations outside that safety boundary, where LLMs are less sensitive to harmful information. We also find that the low and the middle layers are critical in such shifts, while deeper layers have less impact. Leveraging on these insights, we propose a novel defense called \textbf{Activation Boundary Defense} (ABD), which adaptively constrains the activations within the safety boundary. We further use Bayesian optimization to selectively apply the defense method to the low and the middle layers. Our experiments on several benchmarks show that ABD achieves an average DSR of over 98\% against various forms of jailbreak attacks, with less than 2\% impact on the model's general capabilities.

papers.title: Towards Understanding Jailbreak Attacks in LLMs: A Representation Space Analysis
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between harmless and harmful prompts in the representation space of LLMs, and how do successful jailbreak attacks mislead LLMs to provide harmful responses?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that successful jailbreak attacks shift prompt representations towards the direction of harmless prompts in the LLM's representation space, and introduces an optimization objective to enhance existing attacks by moving representations along this acceptance direction.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that representation space analysis reveals the acceptance direction for jailbreak attacks, and proposes an optimization objective to validate that moving prompts along this direction increases jailbreak success.
papers.key_findings:
Harmful and harmless anchor prompts are separable in the representation space of well-aligned LLMs, indicating models can distinguish harmfulness.
Successful jailbreak attacks move the representation of harmful prompts towards the direction of harmless anchor prompts compared to failed attacks.
Integrating the proposed optimization objective with GCG significantly improves attack success rate, e.g., from 26.15% to 62.31% on Llama-2-13b-chat.
The method is less effective with AutoDAN due to its volatile optimization based on genetic algorithms.
Paraphrasing defense significantly affects harmfulness representation, suggesting harmfulness is model-specific and not closely tied to overall semantics.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to representation space; other aspects like neurons and activation scores are not explored.
The proposed optimization objective requires white-box access to the victim model, limiting practicality for black-box attacks.
future_direction: Analyzing jailbreak attacks from other aspects such as neurons and activation scores.
Boosting the performance of black-box jailbreak methods.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are susceptible to a type of attack known as jailbreaking, which misleads LLMs to output harmful contents. Although there are diverse jailbreak attack strategies, there is no unified understanding on why some methods succeed and others fail. This paper explores the behavior of harmful and harmless prompts in the LLM's representation space to investigate the intrinsic properties of successful jailbreak attacks. We hypothesize that successful attacks share some similar properties: They are effective in moving the representation of the harmful prompt towards the direction to the harmless prompts. We leverage hidden representations into the objective of existing jailbreak attacks to move the attacks along the acceptance direction, and conduct experiments to validate the above hypothesis using the proposed objective. We hope this study provides new insights into understanding how LLMs understand harmfulness information.

papers.title: Activation-Guided Local Editing for Jailbreaking Attacks
papers.research_question: How can we develop an effective jailbreaking attack on large language models by combining token-level and prompt-level approaches using activation-guided local editing?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes AGILE, a two-stage jailbreaking framework that uses activation-guided local editing to transform malicious queries into stealthy prompts, achieving state-of-the-art attack success rates and good transferability.
papers.conclusion: AGILE provides a concise and effective jailbreaking method that highlights limitations of current safeguards and offers insights for future defense development.
papers.key_findings:
AGILE achieves state-of-the-art Attack Success Rate (ASR), with gains of up to 37.74% over the strongest baseline.
AGILE exhibits excellent transferability to black-box models, with minimal performance degradation compared to direct attacks.
AGILE maintains substantial effectiveness against prominent defense mechanisms like PPL filters, Llama-Guard, and SafeDecoding.
Ablation studies show that the dialogue history component is not essential for attack success, while adaptive rephrasing is critical.
The attention-guided editing mechanism is more effective than random search for identifying optimal token editing positions.
papers.abstract: Jailbreaking is an essential adversarial technique for red-teaming these models to uncover and patch security flaws. However, existing jailbreak methods face significant drawbacks. Token-level jailbreak attacks often produce incoherent or unreadable inputs and exhibit poor transferability, while prompt-level attacks lack scalability and rely heavily on manual effort and human ingenuity. We propose a concise and effective two-stage framework that combines the advantages of these approaches. The first stage performs a scenario-based generation of context and rephrases the original malicious query to obscure its harmful intent. The second stage then utilizes information from the model's hidden states to guide fine-grained edits, effectively steering the model's internal representation of the input from a malicious toward a benign one. Extensive experiments demonstrate that this method achieves state-of-the-art Attack Success Rate, with gains of up to 37.74% over the strongest baseline, and exhibits excellent transferability to black-box models. Our analysis further demonstrates that AGILE maintains substantial effectiveness against prominent defense mechanisms, highlighting the limitations of current safeguards and providing valuable insights for future defense development. Our code is available at https://github.com/yunsaijc/AGILE.

papers.title: NeuroBreak: Unveil Internal Jailbreak Mechanisms in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do jailbreak attacks exploit internal mechanisms in large language models to bypass safety alignments?
papers.core_contribution: NeuroBreak is a visual analytics system that unveils internal jailbreak mechanisms in LLMs by analyzing neuron-level safety mechanisms and enabling targeted fine-tuning to mitigate vulnerabilities.
papers.conclusion: NeuroBreak enhances expert understanding of LLM security mechanisms and supports precise alignment efforts through visual analysis and targeted fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
NeuroBreak enables progressive exploration from macroscopic behavior to neuron-level mechanisms in jailbreak attacks.
It identifies safety neurons and categorizes them into functional archetypes based on toxicity vectors and activation patterns.
The system reveals that layers 15-28 encode discriminative harmful features with high probe accuracy.
Targeted fine-tuning of safety neurons using NeuroBreak improves model robustness against jailbreak attacks.
NeuroBreak provides visual evidence for neuron cooperation patterns and vulnerabilities in LLM safety mechanisms.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on linear probing may miss nonlinear semantic shifts influencing adversarial behaviors.
Lack of dynamic adversarial interactions or real-time adaptation to evolving threats.
future_direction: Explore nonlinear probing techniques for more complex decision boundaries.
Incorporate dynamic adversarial training or online learning for real-time adaptation.
papers.abstract: In deployment and application, large language models (LLMs) typically undergo safety alignment to prevent illegal and unethical outputs. However, the continuous advancement of jailbreak attack techniques, designed to bypass safety mechanisms with adversarial prompts, has placed increasing pressure on the security defenses of LLMs. Strengthening resistance to jailbreak attacks requires an in-depth understanding of the security mechanisms and vulnerabilities of LLMs. However, the vast number of parameters and complex structure of LLMs make analyzing security weaknesses from an internal perspective a challenging task. This paper presents NeuroBreak, a top-down jailbreak analysis system designed to analyze neuron-level safety mechanisms and mitigate vulnerabilities. We carefully design system requirements through collaboration with three experts in the field of AI security. The system provides a comprehensive analysis of various jailbreak attack methods. By incorporating layer-wise representation probing analysis, NeuroBreak offers a novel perspective on the model's decision-making process throughout its generation steps. Furthermore, the system supports the analysis of critical neurons from both semantic and functional perspectives, facilitating a deeper exploration of security mechanisms. We conduct quantitative evaluations and case studies to verify the effectiveness of our system, offering mechanistic insights for developing next-generation defense strategies against evolving jailbreak attacks.

papers.title: Understanding Jailbreak Success: A Study of Latent Space Dynamics in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do different jailbreak types circumvent model safeguards, and do they operate via a similar internal mechanism? Specifically, can a jailbreak vector from one class mitigate jailbreaks from other classes, and is harmfulness suppression a common mechanism?
papers.core_contribution: Jailbreak vectors extracted from one class of jailbreaks can mitigate jailbreak effectiveness from other, semantically dissimilar classes, suggesting a shared internal mechanism. Effective jailbreaks consistently reduce the model's perception of prompt harmfulness.
papers.conclusion: The transferability of jailbreak steering vectors suggests mitigation approaches may be generalizable, and harmfulness suppression is a common mechanism, offering insights for developing more robust countermeasures.
papers.key_findings:
Jailbreak types cluster in activation space based on semantic similarity.
Jailbreak steering vectors exhibit positive cosine similarity across different types.
Steering with a jailbreak vector (subtracting it) can prevent successful jailbreaks from its own and other classes.
Adding a jailbreak vector can induce jailbreaks, indicating the vectors capture what makes jailbreaks successful.
Successful jailbreaks reduce the cosine similarity between model activations and a harmfulness direction, though the degree of reduction does not clearly correlate with attack success rate.
papers.limitation:
Steering with jailbreak vectors occasionally reduces answer quality in the form of repetitions.
The significance of harmfulness reduction does not clearly map with the attack success rate of a jailbreak, indicating it might not be the only mechanism.
future_direction: Investigate other potential mechanisms beyond harmfulness suppression that could explain jailbreak success.
Explore the interaction of jailbreak types with a helpfulness feature direction.
papers.abstract: Conversational large language models are trained to refuse to answer harmful questions. However, emergent jailbreaking techniques can still elicit unsafe outputs, presenting an ongoing challenge for model alignment. To better understand how different jailbreak types circumvent safeguards, this paper analyses model activations on different jailbreak inputs. We find that it is possible to extract a jailbreak vector from a single class of jailbreaks that works to mitigate jailbreak effectiveness from other semantically-dissimilar classes. This may indicate that different kinds of effective jailbreaks operate via a similar internal mechanism. We investigate a potential common mechanism of harmfulness feature suppression, and find evidence that effective jailbreaks noticeably reduce a model's perception of prompt harmfulness. These findings offer actionable insights for developing more robust jailbreak countermeasures and lay the groundwork for a deeper, mechanistic understanding of jailbreak dynamics in language models.

papers.title: ConceptGuard: Neuro-Symbolic Safety Guardrails via Sparse Interpretable Jailbreak Concepts
papers.research_question: Can SAEs disentangle dense LLM activations into sparse, interpretable concepts representing jailbreak-related themes? Can these concepts facilitate interpretable, concept-guided guardrails that generalize across diverse jailbreak styles while preserving model capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ConceptGuard, a framework that uses Sparse Autoencoders to extract interpretable jailbreak concepts from LLM activations and builds a linear guardrail that generalizes to stealthy jailbreaks without requiring fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: ConceptGuard demonstrates that interpretable jailbreak concepts can be extracted from LLM activations using SAEs and used to build a linear guardrail that generalizes across jailbreak styles without fine-tuning, offering a robust and transparent safety solution.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs can disentangle dense LLM activations into sparse, interpretable concepts corresponding to jailbreak themes.
The concept-guided guardrail (trained only on base attacks) generalizes to stealthy jailbreak styles (e.g., hypothetical, BoN) without exposure to them during training.
The pruned guardrail (using only rich features) reduces the feature space by 57% while maintaining competitive performance.
The guardrail outperforms baseline safety-tuned models (like Llama-Guard) in generalization.
The activation-based guardrails are robust to input perturbations that confuse the model, as shown by UMAP visualizations.
papers.limitation:
Limited to a single hook point (attention layer of the 8th transformer block).
The pruning heuristic might be overly aggressive and classify safety-critical features as junk.
The method assumes the model has undergone safety fine-tuning; effectiveness on unaligned models is unknown.
The linear classifier may not capture complex, non-linear interactions between jailbreak concepts.
future_direction: Using sparse-crosscoders to extract interacting harmful concepts across multiple layers.
Exploring more sophisticated methods to identify safety-critical features without relying strictly on token-level interpretability metrics.
Testing the method on unaligned foundational models and exploring more expressive classifiers.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models have found success in a variety of applications. However, their safety remains a concern due to the existence of various jailbreaking methods. Despite significant efforts, alignment and safety fine-tuning only provide a certain degree of robustness against jailbreak attacks that covertly mislead LLMs towards the generation of harmful content. This leaves them prone to a range of vulnerabilities, including targeted misuse and accidental user profiling. This work introduces \textbf{ConceptGuard}, a novel framework that leverages Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to identify interpretable concepts within LLM internals associated with different jailbreak themes. By extracting semantically meaningful internal representations, ConceptGuard enables building robust safety guardrails -- offering fully explainable and generalizable defenses without sacrificing model capabilities or requiring further fine-tuning. Leveraging advances in the mechanistic interpretability of LLMs, our approach provides evidence for a shared activation geometry for jailbreak attacks in the representation space, a potential foundation for designing more interpretable and generalizable safeguards against attackers.

papers.title: From Theft to Bomb-Making: The Ripple Effect of Unlearning in Defending Against Jailbreak Attacks
papers.research_question: Can unlearning generalize to harmful knowledge that was not explicitly encountered during training? For instance, if a model is trained to forget how to steal goods, could it also implicitly forget how to construct a bomb?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies and empirically validates the ripple effect in unlearning, showing that unlearning specific harmful knowledge can generalize to unseen harmful knowledge, making it an effective defense against jailbreak attacks.
papers.conclusion: Unlearning exhibits a ripple effect, generalizing to unseen harmful knowledge, and is a promising defense against jailbreak attacks. Future work is needed to fully understand its limitations.
papers.key_findings:
Unlearning-based methods can generalize to out-of-distribution harmful knowledge, reducing attack success rate from over 70% to less than 10% with only 100 training samples.
The generalization ability stems from the intrinsic relatedness among harmful responses, as seen in clustered hidden representations.
Unlearning harmful responses is more effective than only learning safe responses (SFT) because harmful responses are similar across different jailbreak prompts.
Unlearning can sometimes lead to over-refusal, but this can be mitigated by incorporating adversarially benign queries during training.
There are challenging scenarios for unlearning, such as dispersed harmful knowledge (e.g., writing persuasive articles) and subtle/implicit risks.
papers.limitation:
Unlearning may struggle with dispersed harmful knowledge (e.g., writing persuasive articles) and subtle/implicit risks.
Experiments are limited to certain models (Llama-3.1 and Mistral-v0.3) and attack methods, leaving others for future work.
future_direction: Systematic investigation of the impact of unlearning on benign knowledge.
Testing on more models and jailbreak attack methods.
Exploring the reasons behind the clustering of harmful responses in the model's hidden representations.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are known to be vulnerable to jailbreak attacks. An important observation is that, while different types of jailbreak attacks can generate significantly different queries, they mostly result in similar responses that are rooted in the same harmful knowledge (e.g., detailed steps to make a bomb). Consequently, unlearning-based approaches have been proposed to mitigate jailbreak attacks by directly removing harmful knowledge from the model. In this paper, we identify a novel ripple effect of unlearning, wherein LLMs can implicitly unlearn harmful knowledge that was not explicitly introduced during the unlearning phase (e.g., a model unlearning the steps for theft may also implicitly unlearn the steps for making a bomb). Through over 100 experimental runs spanning multiple models, attack strategies, and defense methods, we empirically validate this phenomenon, which makes unlearning-based methods able to decrease the Attack Success Rate on unseen data from more than 70% to less than 10% with only 100 training samples. Further analysis reveals that the strong generalization ability of unlearning may stem from the intrinsic relatedness among harmful responses across harmful questions (e.g., response patterns, shared steps and actions in response, and similarity among their learned representations in the LLM). We also discuss the potential limitations of unlearning and the observed ripple effect. We hope our research could contribute to a deeper understanding of unlearning. Our code is available at https://github.com/thu-coai/SafeUnlearning.

papers.title: AttnGCG: Enhancing Jailbreaking Attacks on LLMs with Attention Manipulation
papers.research_question: How can jailbreaking attacks on LLMs be enhanced by manipulating the models' attention scores?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces AttnGCG, an enhanced jailbreaking attack that manipulates LLMs' attention scores to increase focus on adversarial suffixes, leading to higher attack success rates and improved transferability.
papers.conclusion: Attention manipulation is an effective strategy for enhancing jailbreaking attacks on LLMs, and visualizing attention scores offers clear insights into the attack mechanism.
papers.key_findings:
A positive correlation exists between the attention score on the adversarial suffix and the attack success rate (ASR).
AttnGCG consistently outperforms the GCG baseline across various LLMs, achieving an average ASR increase of ~6.3% (GPT-4 judge).
AttnGCG reduces the gap between keyword-based and GPT-4 judge ASR, indicating a reduction in false jailbreaks.
AttnGCG demonstrates strong transferability, improving ASR on unseen harmful goals by an average of 11.4% and on black-box LLMs like GPT-4 by 2.8%.
Attention score visualization provides interpretable insights into how jailbreaking exploits attention distributions.
papers.limitation: The transfer attack performance of AttnGCG is unsatisfactory on the latest models (Gemini-1.5-Pro-latest, Gemini-1.5-Flash, GPT-4o), necessitating further research.
future_direction: Further research to improve transfer attack performance on the latest LLM models.
papers.abstract: This paper studies the vulnerabilities of transformer-based Large Language Models (LLMs) to jailbreaking attacks, focusing specifically on the optimization-based Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG) strategy. We first observe a positive correlation between the effectiveness of attacks and the internal behaviors of the models. For instance, attacks tend to be less effective when models pay more attention to system prompts designed to ensure LLM safety alignment. Building on this discovery, we introduce an enhanced method that manipulates models' attention scores to facilitate LLM jailbreaking, which we term AttnGCG. Empirically, AttnGCG shows consistent improvements in attack efficacy across diverse LLMs, achieving an average increase of ~7% in the Llama-2 series and ~10% in the Gemma series. Our strategy also demonstrates robust attack transferability against both unseen harmful goals and black-box LLMs like GPT-3.5 and GPT-4. Moreover, we note our attention-score visualization is more interpretable, allowing us to gain better insights into how our targeted attention manipulation facilitates more effective jailbreaking. We release the code at https://github.com/UCSC-VLAA/AttnGCG-attack.

papers.title: The Geometry of Harmfulness in LLMs through Subconcept Probing
papers.research_question: How can we understand and mitigate harmful behaviors in LLMs by decomposing harmfulness into subconcepts and analyzing their geometric structure in activation space?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that harmfulness in LLMs can be represented as a low-rank linear subspace in activation space, and steering in the dominant direction of this subspace can effectively reduce harmful generations with minimal utility loss.
papers.conclusion: The work presents a geometric approach to understanding and mitigating harmfulness in LLMs, underscoring the value of multidimensional probing for uncovering latent harmful behaviors and designing more controllable and transparent models.
papers.key_findings:
The harmfulness subspace formed by 55 subconcept directions is low-rank linear, with a single dominant direction capturing most of the variance.
Steering in the dominant direction allows for near elimination of harmful responses on jailbreak datasets with only a minor decrease in utility.
Linear probes for harmfulness subconcepts achieve high accuracy and generalize to out-of-distribution data.
Ablating the entire harmfulness subspace or just the dominant direction reduces jailbreak penetration with minimal utility loss.
The method works on two different models (Llama and Qwen), though with some differences in effectiveness.
papers.limitation:
The study has limited model testing and may not generalize well to other untested models of differing scales.
The subcategories of harmfulness tested are not extensive and may not include all possible subcategories of harmful model responses.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have intensified the need to understand and reliably curb their harmful behaviours. We introduce a multidimensional framework for probing and steering harmful content in model internals. For each of 55 distinct harmfulness subconcepts (e.g., racial hate, employment scams, weapons), we learn a linear probe, yielding 55 interpretable directions in activation space. Collectively, these directions span a harmfulness subspace that we show is strikingly low-rank. We then test ablation of the entire subspace from model internals, as well as steering and ablation in the subspace's dominant direction. We find that dominant direction steering allows for near elimination of harmfulness with a low decrease in utility. Our findings advance the emerging view that concept subspaces provide a scalable lens on LLM behaviour and offer practical tools for the community to audit and harden future generations of language models.

papers.title: Keep Calm and Avoid Harmful Content: Concept Alignment and Latent Manipulation Towards Safer Answers
papers.research_question: How to suppress harmful concepts in large language models at inference time without retraining, by modifying latent representations?
papers.core_contribution: CALM is an inference-time method that suppresses harmful concepts in LLMs by whitening and projecting out harmful latent directions, without requiring retraining or fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: CALM offers a lightweight and effective approach for improving LLM safety at inference time by suppressing harmful concepts through latent manipulation.
papers.key_findings:
CALM reduces the perplexity of harmful answers while preserving safe answer perplexity.
CALM outperforms ProFS in most metrics across different models.
CALM improves toxicity and harmfulness scores compared to base models.
The effectiveness of CALM varies across model families, with better results on Llama and Phi-3.
CALM provides interpretability by aligning concepts with orthogonal axes.
papers.limitation:
CALM fails to redirect harmful premises and implicitly validates intimidation in some cases.
CALM fails to enforce clear boundaries by listing illegal activities despite warnings.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models are susceptible to jailbreak attacks that bypass built-in safety guardrails (e.g., by tricking the model with adversarial prompts). We propose Concept Alignment and Concept Manipulation CALM, an inference-time method that suppresses harmful concepts by modifying latent representations of the last layer of the model, without retraining. Leveraging concept whitening technique from Computer Vision combined with orthogonal projection, CALM removes unwanted latent directions associated with harmful content while preserving model performance. Experiments show that CALM reduces harmful outputs and outperforms baseline methods in most metrics, offering a lightweight approach to AI safety with no additional training data or model fine-tuning, while incurring only a small computational overhead at inference.

papers.title: Do Internal Layers of LLMs Reveal Patterns for Jailbreak Detection?
