papers.research_question: Do internal layers of LLMs reveal patterns for jailbreak detection? Specifically, how do hidden layers respond to jailbreak versus benign prompts?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that analyzing internal layer representations of LLMs combined with tensor decomposition provides a promising approach for detecting jailbreak prompts.
papers.conclusion: Examining internal layer representations of LLMs combined with tensor decomposition techniques provides a promising approach for detecting jailbreak prompts, offering a simple, efficient, and effective pathway for improvement.
papers.key_findings:
For GPT-J, Multi-Head Attention (MHA) representations outperform layer outputs for jailbreak classification.
For Mamba-2, Mixer representations outperform Block outputs for jailbreak classification.
Tensor decomposition of internal representations yields latent factors that provide clear separation between jailbreak and benign prompts.
A simple pipeline of tensor decomposition followed by basic classifiers (e.g., Random Forest, SVM) achieves effective jailbreak detection.
papers.limitation: The study is preliminary and requires further work on larger datasets, additional architectures, and more sophisticated evaluation settings.
future_direction: Extend the methodology to larger datasets.
Apply the methodology to additional architectures.
Conduct more sophisticated evaluation.
papers.abstract: Jailbreaking large language models (LLMs) has emerged as a pressing concern with the increasing prevalence and accessibility of conversational LLMs. Adversarial users often exploit these models through carefully engineered prompts to elicit restricted or sensitive outputs, a strategy widely referred to as jailbreaking. While numerous defense mechanisms have been proposed, attackers continuously develop novel prompting techniques, and no existing model can be considered fully resistant. In this study, we investigate the jailbreak phenomenon by examining the internal representations of LLMs, with a focus on how hidden layers respond to jailbreak versus benign prompts. Specifically, we analyze the open-source LLM GPT-J and the state-space model Mamba2, presenting preliminary findings that highlight distinct layer-wise behaviors. Our results suggest promising directions for further research on leveraging internal model dynamics for robust jailbreak detection and defense.

papers.title: PrisonBreak: Jailbreaking Large Language Models with at Most Twenty-Five Targeted Bit-flips
papers.research_question: How vulnerable is the refusal property of language models, learned through safety alignment training, to bit-wise errors induced by practical fault-injection attacks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces PRISONBREAK, an efficient bit-selection algorithm to jailbreak large language models by flipping a small number of bits in model parameters, demonstrating vulnerability to bit-flip attacks.
papers.conclusion: The findings highlight a pressing, practical threat to the language model ecosystem and underscore the need for research to protect these models from bit-flip attacks.
papers.key_findings:
Jailbreaks billion-parameter LLMs with only 5 to 25 bit-flips, requiring up to 40× fewer bit flips than prior attacks.
Certain model components, such as value projection layers, are disproportionately vulnerable to bit-flips.
The attack is mechanistically different from existing jailbreak methods, not relying on prompt modifications.
Models with weaker post-training alignment require fewer bit-flips to jailbreak.
Effective end-to-end exploitation via Rowhammer on GDDR6 GPUs, achieving high attack success rates.
future_direction: Further exploration of jailbreaking quantized models
papers.abstract: We study a new vulnerability in commercial-scale safety-aligned large language models (LLMs): their refusal to generate harmful responses can be broken by flipping only a few bits in model parameters. Our attack jailbreaks billion-parameter language models with just 5 to 25 bit-flips, requiring up to 40$\times$ fewer bit flips than prior attacks on much smaller computer vision models. Unlike prompt-based jailbreaks, our method directly uncensors models in memory at runtime, enabling harmful outputs without requiring input-level modifications. Our key innovation is an efficient bit-selection algorithm that identifies critical bits for language model jailbreaks up to 20$\times$ faster than prior methods. We evaluate our attack on 10 open-source LLMs, achieving high attack success rates (ASRs) of 80-98% with minimal impact on model utility. We further demonstrate an end-to-end exploit via Rowhammer-based fault injection, reliably jailbreaking 5 models (69-91% ASR) on a GDDR6 GPU. Our analyses reveal that: (1) models with weaker post-training alignment require fewer bit-flips to jailbreak; (2) certain model components, e.g., value projection layers, are substantially more vulnerable; and (3) the attack is mechanistically different from existing jailbreak methods. We evaluate potential countermeasures and find that our attack remains effective against defenses at various stages of the LLM pipeline.

papers.title: Refusal in Language Models Is Mediated by a Single Direction
papers.research_question: What are the underlying mechanisms of refusal behavior in language models? Specifically, is refusal mediated by a single direction in the activation space?
papers.core_contribution: Refusal in language models is mediated by a single direction in the residual stream; this direction can be extracted via difference-in-means and used to control refusal behavior through weight orthogonalization, enabling a white-box jailbreak.
papers.conclusion: Current safety fine-tuning methods are brittle, and understanding model internals can lead to practical methods for controlling model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Refusal is mediated by a one-dimensional subspace across 13 open-source chat models up to 72B parameters.
Ablating this 'refusal direction' from the residual stream prevents the model from refusing harmful instructions.
Adding this direction to activations induces refusal on even harmless instructions.
Weight orthogonalization, a novel white-box jailbreak method that modifies model weights to erase the refusal direction, effectively disables refusal with minimal impact on other capabilities.
Adversarial suffixes suppress the refusal direction by hijacking the attention of important heads away from the harmful instruction.
papers.limitation:
The string-matching approach for refusal score is effective at detecting memorized refusals but does not assess coherence or harmfulness of completions.
The weight orthogonalization jailbreak is less effective when the model's default system prompt is included, indicating system prompt sensitivity.
papers.abstract: Conversational large language models are fine-tuned for both instruction-following and safety, resulting in models that obey benign requests but refuse harmful ones. While this refusal behavior is widespread across chat models, its underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this work, we show that refusal is mediated by a one-dimensional subspace, across 13 popular open-source chat models up to 72B parameters in size. Specifically, for each model, we find a single direction such that erasing this direction from the model's residual stream activations prevents it from refusing harmful instructions, while adding this direction elicits refusal on even harmless instructions. Leveraging this insight, we propose a novel white-box jailbreak method that surgically disables refusal with minimal effect on other capabilities. Finally, we mechanistically analyze how adversarial suffixes suppress propagation of the refusal-mediating direction. Our findings underscore the brittleness of current safety fine-tuning methods. More broadly, our work showcases how an understanding of model internals can be leveraged to develop practical methods for controlling model behavior.

papers.title: Unraveling LLM Jailbreaks Through Safety Knowledge Neurons
papers.research_question: How can jailbreak attacks bypass LLM safety alignment, and how can we defend against them by understanding and manipulating safety-related knowledge neurons?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a neuron-level interpretability method for safety knowledge and a fine-tuning defense (SafeTuning) that reinforces safety-critical neurons to improve model robustness against jailbreak attacks.
papers.conclusion: Safety knowledge neurons play a critical role in defending against jailbreak attacks, and the proposed methods offer a new perspective for understanding and enhancing LLM security.
papers.key_findings:
Safety-related knowledge neurons in MLP layers can be interpreted by projecting their activations into a vocabulary space, revealing distinct 'Rejection' and 'Conformity' patterns.
Calibrating the activation of safety neurons (ActCali) can control model behavior, achieving over 97% attack success rate in making aligned models comply with harmful requests.
Fine-tuning only the identified safety-critical neurons and their activation pathways (SafeTuning) significantly reduces attack success rates across multiple LLMs and jailbreak methods.
Isolating safety-critical neurons is crucial for maintaining model utility when performing activation adjustments or fine-tuning for defense.
papers.limitation:
Primarily investigates well-aligned models, leaving the challenge of effectively aligning non-aligned models largely unexplored.
Focus is on Large Language Models; extending these alignment techniques to emerging multi-modal LLMs remains an open problem.
The proposed methods require manual tuning of hyperparameters; developing automated techniques is an important future direction.
future_direction: Extending alignment techniques to non-aligned models.
Applying the methods to multi-modal LLMs.
Developing automated techniques to identify and adapt hyperparameters.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly attracting attention in various applications. Nonetheless, there is a growing concern as some users attempt to exploit these models for malicious purposes, including the synthesis of controlled substances and the propagation of disinformation, a technique known as "Jailbreak." While some studies have achieved defenses against jailbreak attacks by modifying output distributions or detecting harmful content, the exact rationale still remains elusive. In this work, we present a novel neuron-level interpretability method that focuses on the role of safety-related knowledge neurons. Unlike existing approaches, our method projects the model's internal representation into a more consistent and interpretable vocabulary space. We then show that adjusting the activation of safety-related neurons can effectively control the model's behavior with a mean ASR higher than 97%. Building on this insight, we propose SafeTuning, a fine-tuning strategy that reinforces safety-critical neurons to improve model robustness against jailbreaks. SafeTuning consistently reduces attack success rates across multiple LLMs and outperforms all four baseline defenses. These findings offer a new perspective on understanding and defending against jailbreak attacks.

papers.title: HSF: Defending against Jailbreak Attacks with Hidden State Filtering
papers.research_question: How can we defend against jailbreak attacks on LLMs by leveraging their hidden state representations to preemptively identify and reject adversarial inputs before inference?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes HSF, a plug-in defense module that uses hidden states from the last decoder layer to classify and block jailbreak attacks before inference, with minimal computational overhead.
papers.conclusion: HSF effectively defends against state-of-the-art jailbreak attacks by leveraging the alignment capabilities reflected in LLM hidden states, offering an efficient and modular defense mechanism.
papers.key_findings:
Aligned LLMs can naturally distinguish between harmful, benign, and jailbreak queries within their hidden state representation space.
HSF significantly reduces the Attack Success Rate (ASR) against six state-of-the-art jailbreak attacks while maintaining a low false positive rate.
HSF's defense performance is robust across different models (Llama2, Vicuna, Mistral) and requires only lightweight training of an added MLP classifier.
The method incurs negligible inference overhead and does not alter the core LLM architecture.
papers.limitation: Limited generalizability; HSF is tailored to specific LLMs and requires retraining when applied to other models.
future_direction: Explore how to leverage LLM hidden states to build more flexible harmful-behavior detectors.
Enhance jailbreak attack prevention through Retrieval-Augmented Generation methods.
papers.abstract: With the growing deployment of LLMs in daily applications like chatbots and content generation, efforts to ensure outputs align with human values and avoid harmful content have intensified. However, increasingly sophisticated jailbreak attacks threaten this alignment, aiming to induce unsafe outputs. Current defense efforts either focus on prompt rewriting or detection, which are limited in effectiveness due to the various design of jailbreak prompts, or on output control and detection, which are computationally expensive as they require LLM inference. Therefore, designing a pre-inference defense method that resists diverse jailbreak prompts is crucial for preventing LLM jailbreak attacks. We observe that jailbreak attacks, safe queries, and harmful queries exhibit different clustering patterns within the LLM's hidden state representation space. This suggests that by leveraging the LLM's hidden state representational capabilities, we can analyze the LLM's forthcoming behavior and proactively intervene for defense. In this paper, we propose a jailbreak attack defense strategy based on a Hidden State Filter (HSF), a lossless architectural defense mechanism that enables the model to preemptively identify and reject adversarial inputs before the inference process begins. We activate its defensive potential through an additional plugin module, effectively framing the defense task as a classification problem. Experimental results on two benchmark datasets, utilizing three different LLMs, show that HSF significantly enhances resilience against six cutting-edge jailbreak attacks. It significantly reduces the success rate of jailbreak attacks while minimally impacting responses to benign user queries, with negligible inference overhead, and outperforming defense baselines.Our code and data are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Hidden-State-Filtering-8652/

papers.title: How Alignment and Jailbreak Work: Explain LLM Safety through Intermediate Hidden States
papers.research_question: How do alignment and jailbreak work in large language models? The paper investigates the mechanisms of safety alignment and how jailbreak circumvents it by analyzing intermediate hidden states.
papers.core_contribution: LLMs learn ethical concepts during pre-training and can identify malicious inputs in early layers. Safety alignment associates these early concepts with positive/negative emotions in middle layers, which are refined into accept/reject tokens. Jailbreak works by disturbing this association.
papers.conclusion: The work explains how alignment and jailbreak function through intermediate hidden states, enhancing transparency and offering a new perspective for LLM safety development.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs learn ethical concepts during pre-training, not just from alignment.
Weak classifiers can distinguish malicious and normal inputs from early layer hidden states with >95% accuracy.
Alignment associates early ethical concepts with emotion guesses (positive/negative) in middle layers, which are refined into stylistic accept/reject tokens.
Jailbreak does not deceive early ethical classification but disturbs the association between early and middle layers.
Logit Grafting, which grafts positive emotions onto malicious inputs, approximates jailbreak and confirms the disturbance mechanism.
papers.limitation: Used default settings of simple weak classifiers and only examined safety perspective; method might generalize to other capabilities but not tested.
future_direction: Apply the method to interpret other capabilities of LLMs.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) rely on safety alignment to avoid responding to malicious user inputs. Unfortunately, jailbreak can circumvent safety guardrails, resulting in LLMs generating harmful content and raising concerns about LLM safety. Due to language models with intensive parameters often regarded as black boxes, the mechanisms of alignment and jailbreak are challenging to elucidate. In this paper, we employ weak classifiers to explain LLM safety through the intermediate hidden states. We first confirm that LLMs learn ethical concepts during pre-training rather than alignment and can identify malicious and normal inputs in the early layers. Alignment actually associates the early concepts with emotion guesses in the middle layers and then refines them to the specific reject tokens for safe generations. Jailbreak disturbs the transformation of early unethical classification into negative emotions. We conduct experiments on models from 7B to 70B across various model families to prove our conclusion. Overall, our paper indicates the intrinsical mechanism of LLM safety and how jailbreaks circumvent safety guardrails, offering a new perspective on LLM safety and reducing concerns. Our code is available at https://github.com/ydyjya/LLM-IHS-Explanation.

papers.title: DELMAN: Dynamic Defense Against Large Language Model Jailbreaking with Model Editing
papers.research_question: How to defend against jailbreak attacks on Large Language Models in a dynamic, precise, and minimal way during the deployment phase?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes DELMAN, a dynamic defense mechanism that directly edits a minimal set of model parameters to neutralize harmful behaviors from jailbreak attacks while preserving the model's utility on normal tasks.
papers.conclusion: DELMAN demonstrates how token-level direct model editing can effectively enhance LLM safety against jailbreak attacks while maintaining performance, offering a practical solution for post-deployment protection.
papers.key_findings:
DELMAN significantly reduces Attack Success Rate (ASR) across multiple jailbreak attack types and datasets, often to 0%.
DELMAN preserves or even improves model utility on general-purpose and downstream tasks compared to baseline defenses.
DELMAN's edits are transferable across different harmful behaviors and datasets due to overlapping representations of harmful tokens.
DELMAN supports consecutive edits without interfering with previous modifications, enabling dynamic defense updates.
papers.limitation:
Evaluations are restricted to general-purpose LLMs, leaving applicability to domain-specialized models and larger-scale models unexplored.
DELMAN relies on GPT-4 for harmful token extraction and context generation, introducing dependency on external models and potential cost barriers.
The stability of consecutive edits, though preliminarily validated, needs deeper analysis to assess potential performance drift over extended deployment.
future_direction: Investigate more efficient methods for harmful token identification, e.g., using a minimal set of tokens to cover the majority of harmful scenarios.
Explore the application of DELMAN to domain-specific LLMs and VLMs to validate its generalizability across different domains and modalities.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are widely applied in decision making, but their deployment is threatened by jailbreak attacks, where adversarial users manipulate model behavior to bypass safety measures. Existing defense mechanisms, such as safety fine-tuning and model editing, either require extensive parameter modifications or lack precision, leading to performance degradation on general tasks, which is unsuitable to post-deployment safety alignment. To address these challenges, we propose DELMAN (Dynamic Editing for LLMs JAilbreak DefeNse), a novel approach leveraging direct model editing for precise, dynamic protection against jailbreak attacks. DELMAN directly updates a minimal set of relevant parameters to neutralize harmful behaviors while preserving the model's utility. To avoid triggering a safe response in benign context, we incorporate KL-divergence regularization to ensure the updated model remains consistent with the original model when processing benign queries. Experimental results demonstrate that DELMAN outperforms baseline methods in mitigating jailbreak attacks while preserving the model's utility, and adapts seamlessly to new attack instances, providing a practical and efficient solution for post-deployment model protection.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders are Capable LLM Jailbreak Mitigators
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders be repurposed as effective jailbreak defenses? Does steering in sparse feature space offer advantages over dense activation space for jailbreak mitigation?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CC-Delta, an SAE-based jailbreak defense that uses context-conditioned feature selection and mean-shift steering in sparse latent space, showing better safety-utility tradeoffs and out-of-distribution generalization than dense-space methods.
papers.conclusion: Steering in sparse SAE feature space offers advantages over steering in dense activation space for jailbreak mitigation, and off-the-shelf SAEs can be repurposed as practical jailbreak defenses.
papers.key_findings:
CC-Delta achieves comparable or better safety-utility tradeoffs than baseline defenses across four models and twelve jailbreak attacks.
CC-Delta clearly outperforms dense mean-shift steering on all four models, particularly against out-of-distribution attacks.
Effective mitigation is highly sensitive to feature selection and often requires tens to hundreds of features.
The feature selection step (context-conditioned token selection and statistical ranking) is critical for maintaining utility.
Off-the-shelf SAEs trained for interpretability can be repurposed as practical jailbreak defenses without task-specific training.
papers.limitation:
Token matching requires the harmful request to appear verbatim in the jailbreak prompt, precluding application to re-writer attacks.
Auto-interpretability techniques have limitations in accurately labeling the behavior of SAE features.
papers.abstract: Jailbreak attacks remain a persistent threat to large language model safety. We propose Context-Conditioned Delta Steering (CC-Delta), an SAE-based defense that identifies jailbreak-relevant sparse features by comparing token-level representations of the same harmful request with and without jailbreak context. Using paired harmful/jailbreak prompts, CC-Delta selects features via statistical testing and applies inference-time mean-shift steering in SAE latent space. Across four aligned instruction-tuned models and twelve jailbreak attacks, CC-Delta achieves comparable or better safety-utility tradeoffs than baseline defenses operating in dense latent space. In particular, our method clearly outperforms dense mean-shift steering on all four models, and particularly against out-of-distribution attacks, showing that steering in sparse SAE feature space offers advantages over steering in dense activation space for jailbreak mitigation. Our results suggest off-the-shelf SAEs trained for interpretability can be repurposed as practical jailbreak defenses without task-specific training.

papers.title: Feint and Attack: Jailbreaking and Protecting LLMs via Attention Distribution Modeling
papers.research_question: How can concept learning models achieve domain-invariant concepts that generalize across domains while maintaining consistency within classes (concept fidelity and interoperability)?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a self-explaining neural architecture that improves concept fidelity and interoperability across domains by incorporating a salient concept selection network, contrastive learning for domain invariance, and prototype-based concept grounding.
papers.conclusion: The proposed framework successfully learns domain-invariant concepts, improving concept interoperability and fidelity, and demonstrates efficacy through empirical results on domain adaptation tasks.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed method (RCE+PCG+CCL) outperforms existing self-explaining concept learning baselines in domain adaptation performance across multiple datasets.
Each component (RCE, PCG, CCL) contributes to improved performance, as shown in ablation studies.
The method achieves higher concept fidelity scores, indicating more consistent concepts within classes.
Qualitative visualizations show that the learned concepts are domain-aligned and can explain samples from both source and target domains.
papers.abstract: Most jailbreak methods for large language models (LLMs) focus on superficially improving attack success through manually defined rules. However, they fail to uncover the underlying mechanisms within target LLMs that explain why an attack succeeds or fails. In this paper, we propose investigating the phenomenon of jailbreaks and defenses for LLMs from the perspective of attention distributions within the models. A preliminary experiment reveals that the success of a jailbreak is closely linked to the LLM's attention on sensitive words.Inspired by this interesting finding, we propose incorporating critical signals derived from internal attention distributions within LLMs, namely Attention Intensity on Sensitive Words and Attention Dispersion Entropy, to guide both attacks and defenses. Drawing inspiration from the concept of "Feint and Attack", we introduce an attention-guided jailbreak model, ABA, which redirects the model's attention to benign contexts, and an attention-based defense model, ABD, designed to detect attacks by analyzing internal attention entropy. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of our proposal when compared to SOTA baselines.

papers.title: Bleeding Pathways: Vanishing Discriminability in LLM Hidden States Fuels Jailbreak Attacks
papers.research_question: How can we improve the inherent immunity of conventionally aligned LLMs against existing jailbreak attacks without significantly sacrificing utility?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DEEPALIGN, a fine-tuning method that uses contrastive hidden-state steering to enhance LLM safety by amplifying the separation between harmful and benign hidden states during generation, reducing jailbreak success while preserving utility.
papers.conclusion: DEEPALIGN provides a unified, architecture-agnostic defense that significantly improves the safety-utility Pareto frontier by enabling continuous intrinsic toxicity detection and intervention during generation.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs' capacity to differentiate harmful from safe outputs deteriorates as generation progresses, reflected in diminishing separability of hidden states.
DEEPALIGN reduces attack success rates of diverse jailbreak attacks to near-zero or minimal levels across multiple LLMs.
DEEPALIGN preserves model utility and reduces over-refusal compared to baseline defenses.
The method's automated data generation diversifies safe response patterns, increasing resilience against attacks targeting limited refusal patterns.
DEEPALIGN maintains robustness against an adaptive attack derived from DrAttack.
papers.limitation: The adaptive attack presents a challenge by providing the model with a malicious yet seemingly benign response prefix, testing robustness against adversarial out-of-distribution prefixes.
papers.abstract: LLMs remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks that exploit adversarial prompts to circumvent safety measures. Current safety fine-tuning approaches face two critical limitations. First, they often fail to strike a balance between security and utility, where stronger safety measures tend to over-reject harmless user requests. Second, they frequently miss malicious intent concealed within seemingly benign tasks, leaving models exposed to exploitation. Our work identifies a fundamental cause of these issues: during response generation, an LLM's capacity to differentiate harmful from safe outputs deteriorates. Experimental evidence confirms this, revealing that the separability between hidden states for safe and harmful responses diminishes as generation progresses. This weakening discrimination forces models to make compliance judgments earlier in the generation process, restricting their ability to recognize developing harmful intent and contributing to both aforementioned failures. To mitigate this vulnerability, we introduce DEEPALIGN - an inherent defense framework that enhances the safety of LLMs. By applying contrastive hidden-state steering at the midpoint of response generation, DEEPALIGN amplifies the separation between harmful and benign hidden states, enabling continuous intrinsic toxicity detection and intervention throughout the generation process. Across diverse LLMs spanning varying architectures and scales, it reduced attack success rates of nine distinct jailbreak attacks to near-zero or minimal. Crucially, it preserved model capability while reducing over-refusal. Models equipped with DEEPALIGN exhibited up to 3.5% lower error rates in rejecting challenging benign queries and maintained standard task performance with less than 1% decline. This marks a substantial advance in the safety-utility Pareto frontier.

papers.title: The Blessing and Curse of Dimensionality in Safety Alignment
papers.research_question: What is the role of dimensionality in the linear representation of concepts (like safety) in LLMs, and how can we defend against jailbreaking attacks that exploit these linear structures?
papers.core_contribution: High-dimensional representations in LLMs make them vulnerable to linear jailbreaking attacks; the paper proposes dimensionality reduction methods (FJLT and Bottleneck) to defend against such attacks while preserving safety alignment.
papers.conclusion: High dimensionality is both a blessing (for representing complex concepts) and a curse (for vulnerability to jailbreaking); the proposed dimensionality reduction methods mitigate the curse while preserving alignment.
papers.key_findings:
High-dimensional representations in LLMs lead to linear separability of concepts like safety, which can be exploited for jailbreaking.
Linear probes show that linear separability of concepts emerges in models with sufficiently high hidden dimensions.
The proposed FJLT and Bottleneck methods significantly reduce susceptibility to ActAdd and Ablation jailbreaks.
The Bottleneck method preserves utility on various benchmarks better than FJLT.
Theoretical analysis links the effectiveness of linear jailbreaks to the Rademacher complexity of the linear hypothesis class, which grows with dimension.
papers.limitation:
FJLT model performs poorly on datasets dissimilar to the fine-tuning data.
The methods are primarily effective against linear attacks and may not generalize to non-linear attacks.
The Bottleneck method requires model-specific anchor datasets.
papers.abstract: The focus on safety alignment in large language models (LLMs) has increased significantly due to their widespread adoption across different domains. The scale of LLMs play a contributing role in their success, and the growth in parameter count follows larger hidden dimensions. In this paper, we hypothesize that while the increase in dimensions has been a key advantage, it may lead to emergent problems as well. These problems emerge as the linear structures in the activation space can be exploited, in the form of activation engineering, to circumvent its safety alignment. Through detailed visualizations of linear subspaces associated with different concepts, such as safety, across various model scales, we show that the curse of high-dimensional representations uniquely impacts LLMs. Further substantiating our claim, we demonstrate that projecting the representations of the model onto a lower dimensional subspace can preserve sufficient information for alignment while avoiding those linear structures. Empirical results confirm that such dimensional reduction significantly reduces susceptibility to jailbreaking through representation engineering. Building on our empirical validations, we provide theoretical insights into these linear jailbreaking methods relative to a model's hidden dimensions. Broadly speaking, our work posits that the high dimensions of a model's internal representations can be both a blessing and a curse in safety alignment.

papers.title: Why Not Act on What You Know? Unleashing Safety Potential of LLMs via Self-Aware Guard Enhancement
papers.research_question: Why do LLMs exhibit a gap between their ability to discriminate harmful content and their ability to generate safe responses, and how can this gap be bridged?
papers.core_contribution: This paper proposes SAGE, a training-free defense strategy that leverages LLMs' strong safety discrimination capabilities to enhance their safety generation, effectively bridging the gap between discrimination and generation against jailbreak attacks.
papers.conclusion: SAGE successfully bridges the discrimination-generation gap in LLMs for safety, providing a training-free defense against jailbreaks and insights for developing LLMs with more consistent internal awareness and generation behavior.
papers.key_findings:
SAGE achieves an average 99% defense success rate against various jailbreak methods while maintaining helpfulness on general benchmarks.
Mechanistic interpretability analysis reveals that LLMs exhibit distinct internal patterns in hidden states and attention distributions when acting as discriminators versus generators.
SAGE is efficient, with negligible computational overhead compared to baseline defenses.
The method is robust to different prompt phrasings and works across models of varying sizes and architectures.
Ablation studies show that both the Discriminative Analysis Module and Discriminative Response Module are essential for SAGE's effectiveness.
papers.limitation:
SAGE relies on the model's intrinsic discriminative capabilities, which may vary with linguistic nuances or novel attack patterns.
The modular design introduces minor computational overhead compared to undefended inference.
future_direction: Exploring how to integrate the reasoning and discrimination process into the model without explicitly outputting it, similar to deepseek R1 and OpenAI o3.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown impressive capabilities across various tasks but remain vulnerable to meticulously crafted jailbreak attacks. In this paper, we identify a critical safety gap: while LLMs are adept at detecting jailbreak prompts, they often produce unsafe responses when directly processing these inputs. Inspired by this insight, we propose SAGE (Self-Aware Guard Enhancement), a training-free defense strategy designed to align LLMs' strong safety discrimination performance with their relatively weaker safety generation ability. SAGE consists of two core components: a Discriminative Analysis Module and a Discriminative Response Module, enhancing resilience against sophisticated jailbreak attempts through flexible safety discrimination instructions. Extensive experiments demonstrate SAGE's effectiveness and robustness across various open-source and closed-source LLMs of different sizes and architectures, achieving an average 99% defense success rate against numerous complex and covert jailbreak methods while maintaining helpfulness on general benchmarks. We further conduct mechanistic interpretability analysis through hidden states and attention distributions, revealing the underlying mechanisms of this detection-generation discrepancy. Our work thus contributes to developing future LLMs with coherent safety awareness and generation behavior. Our code and datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/NJUNLP/SAGE.

papers.title: Beyond Surface Alignment: Rebuilding LLMs Safety Mechanism via Probabilistically Ablating Refusal Direction
papers.research_question: How can we make large language models more robust against jailbreak attacks by rebuilding their safety mechanisms via probabilistically ablating the refusal direction?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DeepRefusal, a safety alignment framework that forces LLMs to dynamically rebuild refusal mechanisms from jailbreak states by probabilistically ablating the refusal direction across layers and token depths during fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: DeepRefusal bridges the gap between surface-level alignment and robust internal defense by forcing models to rebuild safety mechanisms from jailbreak states, offering a principled way to enhance LLM safety.
papers.key_findings:
DeepRefusal reduces attack success rates by approximately 95% across various jailbreak attacks.
It effectively defends against prefilling attacks and refusal direction attacks, including transfer attacks.
The method maintains model capabilities (e.g., on MMLU, GSM8k) with minimal performance degradation.
It shows strong robustness to unseen jailbreak attacks and generalizes across languages without language-specific modifications.
Using a single static refusal direction with harmful prefix augmentation provides the best balance of robustness and capability preservation.
papers.limitation:
The method is fundamentally dependent on refusal directions within the model, so extending it to multimodal models requires first extending these refusal directions to the multimodal context.
Variations in model size, architecture, and training data can influence defense performance, and the inclusion of high-quality data to mitigate over-refusal is crucial.
future_direction: Extending DeepRefusal to multimodal scenarios.
papers.abstract: Jailbreak attacks pose persistent threats to large language models (LLMs). Current safety alignment methods have attempted to address these issues, but they experience two significant limitations: insufficient safety alignment depth and unrobust internal defense mechanisms. These limitations make them vulnerable to adversarial attacks such as prefilling and refusal direction manipulation. We introduce DeepRefusal, a robust safety alignment framework that overcomes these issues. DeepRefusal forces the model to dynamically rebuild its refusal mechanisms from jailbreak states. This is achieved by probabilistically ablating the refusal direction across layers and token depths during fine-tuning. Our method not only defends against prefilling and refusal direction attacks but also demonstrates strong resilience against other unseen jailbreak strategies. Extensive evaluations on four open-source LLM families and six representative attacks show that DeepRefusal reduces attack success rates by approximately 95%, while maintaining model capabilities with minimal performance degradation.

papers.title: Jailbreak Transferability Emerges from Shared Representations
papers.research_question: Why does jailbreak transferability occur? Is it due to shared representations or incidental flaws?
papers.core_contribution: Jailbreak transferability emerges from shared representations, and increasing representational similarity through benign-only distillation causally increases transfer.
papers.conclusion: Jailbreak transfer is reframed as a consequence of representation alignment rather than an incidental byproduct of safety training.
papers.key_findings:
Representational similarity and jailbreak strength on the source model are two factors that systematically shape transferability.
Distilling a target model on benign data from a source model increases their representational similarity and causally increases jailbreak transferability.
Persona-style jailbreaks transfer more reliably than cipher-based jailbreaks, consistent with the idea that natural-language attacks exploit shared representation space.
papers.abstract: Jailbreak transferability is the surprising phenomenon when an adversarial attack compromising one model also elicits harmful responses from other models. Despite widespread demonstrations, there is little consensus on why transfer is possible: is it a quirk of safety training, an artifact of model families, or a more fundamental property of representation learning? We present evidence that transferability emerges from shared representations rather than incidental flaws. Across 20 open-weight models and 33 jailbreak attacks, we find two factors that systematically shape transfer: (1) representational similarity under benign prompts, and (2) the strength of the jailbreak on the source model. To move beyond correlation, we show that deliberately increasing similarity through benign only distillation causally increases transfer. Our qualitative analyses reveal systematic transferability patterns across different types of jailbreaks. For example, persona-style jailbreaks transfer far more often than cipher-based prompts, consistent with the idea that natural-language attacks exploit models' shared representation space, whereas cipher-based attacks rely on idiosyncratic quirks that do not generalize. Together, these results reframe jailbreak transfer as a consequence of representation alignment rather than a fragile byproduct of safety training.

papers.title: What Features in Prompts Jailbreak LLMs? Investigating the Mechanisms Behind Attacks
papers.research_question: What features in prompts lead to successful jailbreaks in LLMs, and are they linear or non-linear?
papers.core_contribution: Jailbreak features in LLMs are non-linear and model-specific, and non-linear probes can guide effective latent-space interventions to increase or decrease jailbreak success.
papers.conclusion: Jailbreak mechanisms are heterogeneous and non-linear, and the proposed methodology provides insights into the features driving jailbreak outcomes.
papers.key_findings:
Probes trained on prompt representations can predict jailbreak success with high accuracy.
Non-linear probes generalize better across layers than linear probes.
Jailbreak features are not universal; probes do not generalize well to unseen attack types.
Non-linear probe-guided interventions can effectively increase or decrease jailbreak success.
Features linked to jailbreak success are encoded non-linearly in prompt representations.
papers.abstract: Jailbreaks have been a central focus of research regarding the safety and reliability of large language models (LLMs), yet the mechanisms underlying these attacks remain poorly understood. While previous studies have predominantly relied on linear methods to detect jailbreak attempts and model refusals, we take a different approach by examining both linear and non-linear features in prompts that lead to successful jailbreaks. First, we introduce a novel dataset comprising 10,800 jailbreak attempts spanning 35 diverse attack methods. Leveraging this dataset, we train linear and non-linear probes on hidden states of open-weight LLMs to predict jailbreak success. Probes achieve strong in-distribution accuracy but transfer is attack-family-specific, revealing that different jailbreaks are supported by distinct internal mechanisms rather than a single universal direction. To establish causal relevance, we construct probe-guided latent interventions that systematically shift compliance in the predicted direction. Interventions derived from non-linear probes produce larger and more reliable effects than those from linear probes, indicating that features linked to jailbreak success are encoded non-linearly in prompt representations. Overall, the results surface heterogeneous, non-linear structure in jailbreak mechanisms and provide a prompt-side methodology for recovering and testing the features that drive jailbreak outcomes.

papers.title: Latent Fusion Jailbreak: Blending Harmful and Harmless Representations to Elicit Unsafe LLM Outputs
papers.research_question: Can latent representation manipulation achieve higher attack success rates and linguistic fluency than token-level optimization for jailbreaking LLMs? How does hidden state interpolation 'mask' malicious intent to circumvent refusal mechanisms? Can latent adversarial training mitigate these vulnerabilities without compromising general model utility?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces LATENTFUSIONJAILBREAK (LFJ), a white-box attack that uses hidden state interpolation to blend harmful and benign representations in the latent space, achieving high attack success rates without detectable input artifacts. Also proposes a latent adversarial training defense that reduces the attack success rate by over 80%.
papers.conclusion: LFJ demonstrates that current safety alignments in LLMs are vulnerable to latent space attacks that blend harmful and benign representations. The proposed adversarial training defense effectively reduces the attack success rate while maintaining model utility.
papers.key_findings:
LFJ achieves an average Attack Success Rate (ASR) of 94.01% across multiple models and benchmarks, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art discrete optimization and representation-based attacks.
Thematic similarity between harmful and benign queries is a critical factor for the success of the attack, with random pairing drastically reducing ASR.
Gradient-guided layer and token selection are essential components of the Hidden State Interpolation (HSI) mechanism, as ablations show significant drops in ASR when removed.
The proposed latent adversarial training defense reduces LFJ's ASR by over 80% while maintaining model utility on benign inputs.
Current safety alignments are vulnerable to latent space attacks that blend representations, highlighting a fundamental blindness to semantic superposition.
papers.limitation:
White-box dependency: The attack requires access to the model's internal weights and gradients, restricting application to open-source models.
Computational overhead: The iterative optimization and forward/backward passes increase inference latency compared to static prompt injection attacks.
Defense trade-offs: Adversarial training may incur an 'alignment tax', potentially degrading performance on complex benign instructions or increasing false refusals.
Scope of modality: The method is tailored for textual LLMs; extending it to multimodal models remains unexplored.
future_direction: Explore more disentangled representation editing methods to minimize the trade-offs in adversarial training defense.
Extend Hidden State Interpolation (HSI) to multimodal alignment for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs).
papers.abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable progress, they remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks. Existing methods, primarily relying on discrete input optimization (e.g., GCG), often suffer from high computational costs and generate high-perplexity prompts that are easily blocked by simple filters. To overcome these limitations, we propose Latent Fusion Jailbreak (LFJ), a stealthy white-box attack that operates in the continuous latent space. Unlike previous approaches, LFJ constructs adversarial representations by mathematically fusing the hidden states of a harmful query with a thematically similar benign query, effectively masking malicious intent while retaining semantic drive. We further introduce a gradient-guided optimization strategy to balance attack success and computational efficiency. Extensive evaluations on Vicuna-7B, LLaMA-2-7B-Chat, Guanaco-7B, LLaMA-3-70B, and Mistral-7B-Instruct show that LFJ achieves an average Attack Success Rate (ASR) of 94.01%, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art baselines like GCG and AutoDAN while avoiding detectable input artifacts. Furthermore, we identify that thematic similarity in the latent space is a critical vulnerability in current safety alignments. Finally, we propose a latent adversarial training defense that reduces LFJ's ASR by over 80% without compromising model utility.

papers.title: Probing Latent Subspaces in LLM for AI Security: Identifying and Manipulating Adversarial States
papers.research_question: Can latent subspaces in LLMs be identified and manipulated to induce state transitions from safe to jailbroken states?
papers.core_contribution: This work demonstrates that latent subspaces in LLMs can be identified and manipulated to induce state transitions from safe to jailbroken states using LDA and targeted perturbations, paving the way for potential proactive defenses.
papers.conclusion: The methodology demonstrates the feasibility of using latent representations to manipulate model states and provides insights into attractor dynamics in LLMs, with potential for preemptive AI security.
papers.key_findings:
Last-token activations encode information about the model's state (safe vs jailbreak) and can be classified with above-chance accuracy.
Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) can separate safe and jailbreak activations into distinct latent subspaces, and a direction vector can be derived.
Applying the derived perturbation vector to safe activations can induce jailbreak responses in a subset of prompts (11% for Llama-3.1-8B, 13.39% for Qwen2.5-3B).
Targeted perturbations induce distinct downstream state changes that propagate through layers, while random perturbations do not.
The effect of targeted perturbation varies across layers, with middle layers (6-18) showing sustained effects, suggesting they may be critical for safety.
papers.limitation:
The perturbation vector was derived from a dataset of malicious cybersecurity-related prompt-injects, so the discovered subspace may reflect features specific to this domain.
Perturbations led to jailbreak transitions in only about 11% of tested prompts, indicating a low success rate.
The external evaluation performed by GPT-4o exhibited high variance in assigning labels to ambiguous outputs.
The method was developed and validated on decoder-only Transformers; generalizing to other LLM architectures requires further testing.
future_direction: Generalize the analysis by expanding the scope of malicious questions and prompt injects to multiple domains or adversarial content types.
Investigate stronger perturbation magnitudes without compromising the coherence of the LLM's response.
Test the methodology on other open-source and commercially available LLM architectures to confirm generalizability.
Incorporate additional rounds of assessment to mitigate label noise from external evaluators like GPT-4o.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across various tasks, yet they remain vulnerable to adversarial manipulations such as jailbreaking via prompt injection attacks. These attacks bypass safety mechanisms to generate restricted or harmful content. In this study, we investigated the underlying latent subspaces of safe and jailbroken states by extracting hidden activations from a LLM. Inspired by attractor dynamics in neuroscience, we hypothesized that LLM activations settle into semi stable states that can be identified and perturbed to induce state transitions. Using dimensionality reduction techniques, we projected activations from safe and jailbroken responses to reveal latent subspaces in lower dimensional spaces. We then derived a perturbation vector that when applied to safe representations, shifted the model towards a jailbreak state. Our results demonstrate that this causal intervention results in statistically significant jailbreak responses in a subset of prompts. Next, we probed how these perturbations propagate through the model's layers, testing whether the induced state change remains localized or cascades throughout the network. Our findings indicate that targeted perturbations induced distinct shifts in activations and model responses. Our approach paves the way for potential proactive defenses, shifting from traditional guardrail based methods to preemptive, model agnostic techniques that neutralize adversarial states at the representation level.

papers.title: Defending Large Language Models Against Jailbreak Attacks via Layer-specific Editing
papers.research_question: How do large language models respond to harmful prompts, and how can we enhance their resilience against jailbreak attacks by editing specific layers?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Layer-specific Editing (LED), a defense method that identifies and edits safety layers in early LLM layers to align them with safe responses, improving jailbreak resistance while maintaining helpfulness.
papers.conclusion: LED effectively defends LLMs against jailbreak attacks by editing specific layers, maintaining helpfulness on benign prompts.
papers.key_findings:
Early safety layers are crucial for defending against harmful prompts; pruning them causes LLMs to generate harmful responses.
Jailbreak attacks do not affect all layers; some layers still decode to refusal tokens.
LED effectively reduces attack success rate across various jailbreak attacks.
LED maintains model helpfulness on benign prompts.
Editing both safety layers and additional middle layers yields the best trade-off between safety and helpfulness.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being adopted in a wide range of real-world applications. Despite their impressive performance, recent studies have shown that LLMs are vulnerable to deliberately crafted adversarial prompts even when aligned via Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback or supervised fine-tuning. While existing defense methods focus on either detecting harmful prompts or reducing the likelihood of harmful responses through various means, defending LLMs against jailbreak attacks based on the inner mechanisms of LLMs remains largely unexplored. In this work, we investigate how LLMs response to harmful prompts and propose a novel defense method termed \textbf{L}ayer-specific \textbf{Ed}iting (LED) to enhance the resilience of LLMs against jailbreak attacks. Through LED, we reveal that several critical \textit{safety layers} exist among the early layers of LLMs. We then show that realigning these safety layers (and some selected additional layers) with the decoded safe response from selected target layers can significantly improve the alignment of LLMs against jailbreak attacks. Extensive experiments across various LLMs (e.g., Llama2, Mistral) show the effectiveness of LED, which effectively defends against jailbreak attacks while maintaining performance on benign prompts. Our code is available at \url{https://github.com/ledllm/ledllm}.

papers.title: The Dual Power of Interpretable Token Embeddings: Jailbreaking Attacks and Defenses for Diffusion Model Unlearning
papers.research_question: Can we design interpretable and effective jailbreaking attacks, and leverage the resulting insights to develop defenses for existing unlearned diffusion models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes an interpretable subspace attack (SubAttack) that reveals implicit concept retention in unlearned diffusion models, and a subspace defense (SubDefense) that blocks the attack embeddings via orthogonal projection.
papers.conclusion: Interpretable token embeddings provide a powerful tool for both attacking and defending unlearned diffusion models, revealing vulnerabilities and offering a practical defense strategy.
papers.key_findings:
Attack token embeddings are interpretable as non-negative linear combinations of existing tokens, showing unlearned models retain harmful concepts through implicit associations.
SubAttack is effective and transferable across text prompts, initial noises, and different unlearned models.
SubDefense reduces attack success rates for various jailbreaking attacks while preserving generation quality better than baseline defenses.
The defense exhibits a trade-off between robustness and utility, requiring careful selection of the number of blocked tokens.
Current unlearning methods leave models vulnerable to subspace attacks, highlighting the need for more robust unlearning.
papers.limitation:
Defending against CCE requires blocking a large number of tokens, which degrades generation utility (CLIP score and FID).
Interpretability of retained associations relies on predefined CLIP vocabularies, which may not capture all implicit representations.
future_direction: Explore ensemble techniques to compose one powerful attack token embedding from interpretable sets.
Design adaptive methods to decide the number and set of tokens to block automatically.
Investigate joint visual-textual embeddings for jailbreaking attacks and defenses.
Address the trade-off between robustness and utility when defending against CCE.
Explore interpretability of residual associations without relying on predefined vocabularies.
papers.abstract: Despite the remarkable generation capabilities of diffusion models, recent studies have shown that they can memorize and create harmful content when given specific text prompts. Although fine-tuning approaches have been developed to mitigate this issue by unlearning harmful concepts, these methods can be easily circumvented through jailbreaking attacks. This implies that the harmful concept has not been fully erased from the model. However, existing jailbreaking attack methods, while effective, lack interpretability regarding why unlearned models still retain the concept, thereby hindering the development of defense strategies. In this work, we address these limitations by proposing an attack method that learns an orthogonal set of interpretable attack token embeddings. The attack token embeddings can be decomposed into human-interpretable textual elements, revealing that unlearned models still retain the target concept through implicit textual components. Furthermore, these attack token embeddings are powerful and transferable across text prompts, initial noises, and unlearned models, emphasizing that unlearned models are more vulnerable than expected. Finally, building on the insights from our interpretable attack, we develop a defense method to protect unlearned models against both our proposed and existing jailbreaking attacks. Extensive experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our attack and defense strategies.

papers.title: Understanding Refusal in Language Models with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How is refusal encoded in the latent space of LLMs, and how do adversarial jailbreaks suppress refusal mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method using sparse autoencoders to identify and causally validate refusal-related features in LLMs, revealing that harm and refusal are separately encoded and that adversarial jailbreaks suppress refusal features.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that sparse autoencoders can identify causal refusal features, revealing the mediation of refusal by harmful features and the suppression mechanism of adversarial jailbreaks.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs encode harm and refusal as separate feature sets, with harmful features exhibiting a causal effect on refusal features.
Adversarial jailbreaks operate by suppressing specific refusal-related features.
The identified refusal features significantly improve classification on out-of-distribution adversarial examples.
The proposed CosSim+AP method identifies a minimal set of causal features for refusal behavior.
There is a conditional relationship where harmful features upstream trigger refusal features downstream.
papers.limitation:
The small K* may omit additional features relevant to harm and refusal.
The reliance on the refusal direction may not generalize to challenging instructions.
SAEs were trained on base models, not chat models, which may affect interpretability.
future_direction: Training SAEs on chat-model activations to improve feature interpretability and relevance.
papers.abstract: Refusal is a key safety behavior in aligned language models, yet the internal mechanisms driving refusals remain opaque. In this work, we conduct a mechanistic study of refusal in instruction-tuned LLMs using sparse autoencoders to identify latent features that causally mediate refusal behaviors. We apply our method to two open-source chat models and intervene on refusal-related features to assess their influence on generation, validating their behavioral impact across multiple harmful datasets. This enables a fine-grained inspection of how refusal manifests at the activation level and addresses key research questions such as investigating upstream-downstream latent relationship and understanding the mechanisms of adversarial jailbreaking techniques. We also establish the usefulness of refusal features in enhancing generalization for linear probes to out-of-distribution adversarial samples in classification tasks. We open source our code in https://github.com/wj210/refusal_sae.

papers.title: LLMs Encode Harmfulness and Refusal Separately
papers.research_question: Do LLMs encode harmfulness and refusal as separate concepts internally, and how can this separation be analyzed?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs encode harmfulness and refusal separately in their internal representations, and the harmfulness direction extracted at the instruction token can be used to manipulate and analyze model safety.
papers.conclusion: LLMs encode harmfulness and refusal separately, providing a new dimension for understanding and improving AI safety mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Harmfulness is encoded at the last token of the user instruction (t_inst), while refusal is encoded at the last token of the post-instruction tokens (t_post-inst).
Steering along the harmfulness direction can cause LLMs to reinterpret harmless inputs as harmful, while steering along the refusal direction only reinforces refusal behavior without changing harmfulness judgment.
Jailbreak methods often work by suppressing refusal signals without altering the model's internal belief that the instruction is harmful.
Harmfulness representations are fine-grained and vary across risk categories, whereas refusal directions are similar across categories.
The latent harmfulness representation can be used to build an intrinsic safeguard (Latent Guard) that performs comparably to finetuned safety models.
papers.limitation:
The study does not investigate the role of different layers in formulating refusal and harmfulness.
Experiments are limited to 7B and 8B models, so findings may not generalize to larger models.
future_direction: Study the role of each layer in harmfulness and refusal representations.
Investigate how harmfulness and refusal encoding changes with model size.
Use circuit analysis to understand the relation between internal harmfulness belief and external refusal behavior.
papers.abstract: LLMs are trained to refuse harmful instructions, but do they truly understand harmfulness beyond just refusing? Prior work has shown that LLMs' refusal behaviors can be mediated by a one-dimensional subspace, i.e., a refusal direction. In this work, we identify a new dimension to analyze safety mechanisms in LLMs, i.e., harmfulness, which is encoded internally as a separate concept from refusal. There exists a harmfulness direction that is distinct from the refusal direction. As causal evidence, steering along the harmfulness direction can lead LLMs to interpret harmless instructions as harmful, but steering along the refusal direction tends to elicit refusal responses directly without reversing the model's judgment on harmfulness. Furthermore, using our identified harmfulness concept, we find that certain jailbreak methods work by reducing the refusal signals without reversing the model's internal belief of harmfulness. We also find that adversarially finetuning models to accept harmful instructions has minimal impact on the model's internal belief of harmfulness. These insights lead to a practical safety application: The model's latent harmfulness representation can serve as an intrinsic safeguard (Latent Guard) for detecting unsafe inputs and reducing over-refusals that is robust to finetuning attacks. For instance, our Latent Guard achieves performance comparable to or better than Llama Guard 3 8B, a dedicated finetuned safeguard model, across different jailbreak methods. Our findings suggest that LLMs' internal understanding of harmfulness is more robust than their refusal decision to diverse input instructions, offering a new perspective to study AI safety.

papers.title: JailBound: Jailbreaking Internal Safety Boundaries of Vision-Language Models
papers.research_question: How can the internal safety decision boundaries within Vision-Language Models be exploited to perform effective jailbreak attacks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces JailBound, a novel jailbreak framework that identifies and exploits the internal latent safety decision boundary within Vision-Language Models to craft effective adversarial attacks.
papers.conclusion: JailBound exposes a critical safety vulnerability in VLMs by exploiting their internal latent knowledge, highlighting the urgent need for more robust cross-modal safety alignment mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
JailBound achieves state-of-the-art white-box attack success rates (e.g., 94.38% on LLaMA-3.2) and exceptional black-box transferability (e.g., 75.24% against GPT-4o).
The method demonstrates that VLMs encode safety-relevant information in fusion-layer representations, revealing an implicit safety decision boundary that can be approximated and crossed via adversarial perturbations.
Joint optimization of image and text perturbations guided by the probed boundary is more effective than decoupled unimodal attacks.
papers.limitation:
The work does not extensively explore defenses specifically tailored to this attack vector.
Experiments primarily utilize a fixed set of perturbation budgets; a more fine-grained analysis of the relationship between perturbation magnitude and attack success across diverse model architectures could provide further insights.
future_direction: Developing more generalizable and resilient multimodal defense strategies.
Conducting a more fine-grained analysis of the relationship between perturbation magnitude and attack success across diverse model architectures.
papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) exhibit impressive performance, yet the integration of powerful vision encoders has significantly broadened their attack surface, rendering them increasingly susceptible to jailbreak attacks. However, lacking well-defined attack objectives, existing jailbreak methods often struggle with gradient-based strategies prone to local optima and lacking precise directional guidance, and typically decouple visual and textual modalities, thereby limiting their effectiveness by neglecting crucial cross-modal interactions. Inspired by the Eliciting Latent Knowledge (ELK) framework, we posit that VLMs encode safety-relevant information within their internal fusion-layer representations, revealing an implicit safety decision boundary in the latent space. This motivates exploiting boundary to steer model behavior. Accordingly, we propose JailBound, a novel latent space jailbreak framework comprising two stages: (1) Safety Boundary Probing, which addresses the guidance issue by approximating decision boundary within fusion layer's latent space, thereby identifying optimal perturbation directions towards the target region; and (2) Safety Boundary Crossing, which overcomes the limitations of decoupled approaches by jointly optimizing adversarial perturbations across both image and text inputs. This latter stage employs an innovative mechanism to steer the model's internal state towards policy-violating outputs while maintaining cross-modal semantic consistency. Extensive experiments on six diverse VLMs demonstrate JailBound's efficacy, achieves 94.32% white-box and 67.28% black-box attack success averagely, which are 6.17% and 21.13% higher than SOTA methods, respectively. Our findings expose a overlooked safety risk in VLMs and highlight the urgent need for more robust defenses. Warning: This paper contains potentially sensitive, harmful and offensive content.

papers.title: Feint and Attack: Attention-Based Strategies for Jailbreaking and Protecting LLMs
papers.research_question: Does the success of jailbreaks correlate with their influence on attention distributions within LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes an attention-guided jailbreak attack (ABA) and an attention-based defense (ABD) by analyzing and manipulating attention distributions in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: Attention distribution is a key factor in jailbreak attacks and defenses; the proposed ABA and ABD methods are effective in attacking and protecting LLMs, respectively.
papers.key_findings:
The success of a jailbreak attack is correlated with the model's attention on sensitive words; successful attacks divert attention away from harmful terms.
ABA achieves higher attack success rates (ASR-G >94%) than existing methods by minimizing attention on sensitive words and maximizing attention entropy.
ABD effectively defends against various jailbreak attacks by detecting anomalous attention distributions, achieving the lowest ASR-G in experiments.
The intention disguiser via attention-driven task nesting is a critical component for the success of ABA.
Excessive nesting layers in attack prompts can reduce effectiveness, with an optimal number around 3.
papers.abstract: Jailbreak attack can be used to access the vulnerabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) by inducing LLMs to generate the harmful content. And the most common method of the attack is to construct semantically ambiguous prompts to confuse and mislead the LLMs. To access the security and reveal the intrinsic relation between the input prompt and the output for LLMs, the distribution of attention weight is introduced to analyze the underlying reasons. By using statistical analysis methods, some novel metrics are defined to better describe the distribution of attention weight, such as the Attention Intensity on Sensitive Words (Attn_SensWords), the Attention-based Contextual Dependency Score (Attn_DepScore) and Attention Dispersion Entropy (Attn_Entropy). By leveraging the distinct characteristics of these metrics, the beam search algorithm and inspired by the military strategy "Feint and Attack", an effective jailbreak attack strategy named as Attention-Based Attack (ABA) is proposed. In the ABA, nested attack prompts are employed to divert the attention distribution of the LLMs. In this manner, more harmless parts of the input can be used to attract the attention of the LLMs. In addition, motivated by ABA, an effective defense strategy called as Attention-Based Defense (ABD) is also put forward. Compared with ABA, the ABD can be used to enhance the robustness of LLMs by calibrating the attention distribution of the input prompt. Some comparative experiments have been given to demonstrate the effectiveness of ABA and ABD. Therefore, both ABA and ABD can be used to access the security of the LLMs. The comparative experiment results also give a logical explanation that the distribution of attention weight can bring great influence on the output for LLMs.

papers.title: Mind the Inconspicuous: Revealing the Hidden Weakness in Aligned LLMs' Refusal Boundaries
papers.research_question: How can appending end-of-sequence (eos) tokens bypass the learned refusal boundary in aligned LLMs, and what is the underlying mechanism of 'context segmentation'?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals the 'context segmentation' phenomenon where appending eos tokens shifts prompts towards the refusal boundary in hidden space, and introduces BOOST, a simple method to enhance jailbreak attacks by appending eos tokens.
papers.conclusion: The work highlights a critical blind spot in LLM alignment and content filtering, urging the community to address the security implications of control tokens and develop more robust refusal boundaries.
papers.key_findings:
Appending multiple eos tokens causes both harmful and benign prompts to shift toward the learned refusal boundary in the hidden representation space, a phenomenon termed 'context segmentation'.
BOOST significantly increases the attack success rate (ASR) of existing jailbreak techniques across a wide range of open-source LLMs.
Commercial LLM APIs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Qwen) do not filter eos tokens, making them vulnerable to BOOST-enhanced attacks.
eos tokens have low attention values, minimizing distraction from the harmful content and preserving jailbreak effectiveness.
BOOST can be made more robust to simple filtering through eos token obfuscation and dynamic positioning strategies.
future_direction: Implement input-filtering defenses for control tokens like eos.
Develop more robust and generalizable refusal boundaries to defend against context segmentation attacks.
Investigate the security impact of all control tokens and develop comprehensive defense strategies.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have led to impressive alignment where models learn to distinguish harmful from harmless queries through supervised finetuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF). In this paper, we reveal a subtle yet impactful weakness in these aligned models. We find that simply appending multiple end of sequence (eos) tokens can cause a phenomenon we call context segmentation, which effectively shifts both harmful and benign inputs closer to the refusal boundary in the hidden space. Building on this observation, we propose a straightforward method to BOOST jailbreak attacks by appending eos tokens. Our systematic evaluation shows that this strategy significantly increases the attack success rate across 8 representative jailbreak techniques and 16 open-source LLMs, ranging from 2B to 72B parameters. Moreover, we develop a novel probing mechanism for commercial APIs and discover that major providers such as OpenAI, Anthropic, and Qwen do not filter eos tokens, making them similarly vulnerable. These findings highlight a hidden yet critical blind spot in existing alignment and content filtering approaches. We call for heightened attention to eos tokens' unintended influence on model behaviors, particularly in production systems. Our work not only calls for an input-filtering based defense, but also points to new defenses that make refusal boundaries more robust and generalizable, as well as fundamental alignment techniques that can defend against context segmentation attacks.

papers.title: The Hidden Dimensions of LLM Alignment: A Multi-Dimensional Analysis of Orthogonal Safety Directions
papers.research_question: What is the multi-dimensional structure of safety-aligned behavior in LLMs, and how do orthogonal directions in the safety residual space represent distinct safety features?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that safety alignment in LLMs is governed by multiple orthogonal directions in activation space, with a dominant direction for refusal and non-dominant directions for features like hypothetical narrative, and that manipulating these directions can bypass safety.
papers.conclusion: The work provides a multi-dimensional mechanistic understanding of what LLMs learn from safety fine-tuning, revealing that safety behavior is controlled by multiple orthogonal directions, which sheds new light on robust alignment research.
papers.key_findings:
The safety residual space is low-rank linear, with a dominant direction that predicts refusal behavior.
Non-dominant directions in the residual space represent interpretable features such as hypothetical narrative and role-playing.
Non-dominant directions causally influence the dominant direction and the model's refusal behavior.
Removing trigger tokens associated with non-dominant directions can bypass the learned safety alignment, revealing vulnerabilities.
Safety fine-tuning may learn spurious correlations from specific jailbreak patterns, limiting generalization.
papers.limitation:
As data complexity and model size increase, the effective rank of the residual space increases, making interpretation of directions more challenging.
The linearity assumption may not hold perfectly, as directions can flip between layers and extending directions indefinitely degrades generation quality.
future_direction: Analyzing the fine-tuning process in smaller intervals or grouping samples by domain.
Preventing models from learning spurious correlations through targeted interventions in activation space or data augmentation for balanced training.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models' safety-aligned behaviors, such as refusing harmful queries, can be represented by linear directions in activation space. Previous research modeled safety behavior with a single direction, limiting mechanistic understanding to an isolated safety feature. In this work, we discover that safety-aligned behavior is jointly controlled by multi-dimensional directions. Namely, we study the vector space of representation shifts during safety fine-tuning on Llama 3 8B for refusing jailbreaks. By studying orthogonal directions in the space, we first find that a dominant direction governs the model's refusal behavior, while multiple smaller directions represent distinct and interpretable features like hypothetical narrative and role-playing. We then measure how different directions promote or suppress the dominant direction, showing the important role of secondary directions in shaping the model's refusal representation. Finally, we demonstrate that removing certain trigger tokens in harmful queries can mitigate these directions to bypass the learned safety capability, providing new insights on understanding safety alignment vulnerability from a multi-dimensional perspective. Code and artifacts are available at https://github.com/BMPixel/safety-residual-space.

papers.title: Steering Externalities: Benign Activation Steering Unintentionally Increases Jailbreak Risk for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do steering vectors learned from benign instruction data have unintended side-effects on model safety? Specifically, does benign activation steering (for utility) unintentionally increase jailbreak risk for LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies 'steering externalities', a phenomenon where benign activation steering (e.g., for compliance or JSON formatting) unintentionally erodes safety guardrails and significantly increases jailbreak vulnerability in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: Activation steering for utility creates steering externalities that increase jailbreak risk; steered deployments should be red-teamed, and future work should develop safety-aware steering to preserve robustness.
papers.key_findings:
Benign activation steering (STEER-COMPLIANCE, STEER-JSON) increases Attack Success Rates (ASR) for jailbreak attacks, acting as a 'force multiplier' that can boost ASR to over 80-99% on standard benchmarks.
Steering shifts the internal representations of harmful prompts towards regions associated with harmless requests, reducing the model's 'safety margin' and making refusal less likely.
The safety degradation occurs because steering biases the early-token distribution away from refusal prefixes, making the model more likely to enter a non-refusal generation trajectory.
