Activation steering offers a training-free defense method but relies on fixed steering coefficients, resulting in suboptimal protection and increased false rejections of benign inputs. To address this, we propose AdaSteer, an adaptive activation steering method that dynamically adjusts model behavior based on input characteristics. We identify two key properties: Rejection Law (R-Law), which shows that stronger steering is needed for jailbreak inputs opposing the rejection direction, and Harmfulness Law (H-Law), which differentiates adversarial and benign inputs. AdaSteer steers input representations along both the Rejection Direction (RD) and Harmfulness Direction (HD), with adaptive coefficients learned via logistic regression, ensuring robust jailbreak defense while preserving benign input handling. Experiments on LLaMA-3.1, Gemma-2, and Qwen2.5 show that AdaSteer outperforms baseline methods across multiple jailbreak attacks with minimal impact on utility. Our results highlight the potential of interpretable model internals for real-time, flexible safety enforcement in LLMs.

papers.title: GSAE: Graph-Regularized Sparse Autoencoders for Robust LLM Safety Steering
papers.research_question: How to effectively steer LLMs for safety by capturing distributed safety representations using graph-regularized sparse autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Graph-Regularized Sparse Autoencoders (GSAE) to capture distributed safety representations in LLMs, enabling effective runtime safety steering with high refusal rates and preserved utility.
papers.conclusion: GSAE provides a robust method for safety steering by learning distributed safety representations, achieving high safety discrimination and utility preservation across diverse models and attacks.
papers.key_findings:
GSAE steering achieves an average 82% selective refusal rate, substantially outperforming standard SAE steering (42%).
It maintains strong task accuracy on QA benchmarks (e.g., 70% on TriviaQA, 65% on TruthfulQA, 74% on GSM8K).
GSAE generalizes across multiple LLM families (LLaMA-3, Mistral, Qwen, Phi) and scales.
It is robust against jailbreak attacks (GCG, AutoDAN), consistently maintaining ≥90% refusal of harmful content.
Ablation studies show that graph regularization is essential for performance, and the dual-gating mechanism enables adaptive steering.
papers.limitation: The runtime steering mechanism incurs inference latency overhead, which can interfere with optimized serving engines.
future_direction: Decomposing distributed features into interpretable safety sub-categories.
Ensuring the robustness of the neuron co-activation graph to dataset biases and adversarial inputs.
Extending graph-regularized learning to multi-modal domains.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) face critical safety challenges, as they can be manipulated to generate harmful content through adversarial prompts and jailbreak attacks. Many defenses are typically either black-box guardrails that filter outputs, or internals-based methods that steer hidden activations by operationalizing safety as a single latent feature or dimension. While effective for simple concepts, this assumption is limiting, as recent evidence shows that abstract concepts such as refusal and temporality are distributed across multiple features rather than isolated in one. To address this limitation, we introduce Graph-Regularized Sparse Autoencoders (GSAEs), which extends SAEs with a Laplacian smoothness penalty on the neuron co-activation graph. Unlike standard SAEs that assign each concept to a single latent feature, GSAEs recover smooth, distributed safety representations as coherent patterns spanning multiple features. We empirically demonstrate that GSAE enables effective runtime safety steering, assembling features into a weighted set of safety-relevant directions and controlling them with a two-stage gating mechanism that activates interventions only when harmful prompts or continuations are detected during generation. This approach enforces refusals adaptively while preserving utility on benign queries. Across safety and QA benchmarks, GSAE steering achieves an average 82% selective refusal rate, substantially outperforming standard SAE steering (42%), while maintaining strong task accuracy (70% on TriviaQA, 65% on TruthfulQA, 74% on GSM8K). Robustness experiments further show generalization across LLaMA-3, Mistral, Qwen, and Phi families and resilience against jailbreak attacks (GCG, AutoDAN), consistently maintaining >= 90% refusal of harmful content.

papers.title: Beyond I'm Sorry, I Can't: Dissecting Large Language Model Refusal
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanisms and causal features that govern refusal behavior in large language models when presented with harmful prompts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a pipeline combining sparse autoencoders and factorization machines to isolate causal features for LLM refusal, revealing redundant 'hydra' features that activate when others are suppressed.
papers.conclusion: Presents a pipeline for isolating causal refusal features using SAEs and factorization machines, revealing feature redundancy and interactions, laying groundwork for feature-level steering of refusal behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Ablating specific SAE features can jailbreak models, flipping refusal to compliance on harmful prompts.
Redundant features exist that remain dormant until other features are ablated, demonstrating a hydra effect in refusal mechanisms.
Factorization machines capture non-linear feature interactions better than linear probes for identifying jailbreak-critical features.
Jailbreak-critical features can be mapped to harm categories in an unsafe taxonomy, though with limited human alignment.
The refusal mechanism involves non-linear interactions among features, as shown by the superior performance of factorization machines over linear probes.
papers.limitation:
Generality limited to two model sizes; larger models untested.
SAE stability issues due to sensitivity to training data and initialization.
High computational cost for searching and evaluating features across benchmarks.
future_direction: Characterize the safety benefits and risks of redundancy
Evaluate how varied jailbreak strategies perturb the activation space
Analyze prompts that resist jailbreak to uncover protective circuits
papers.abstract: Refusal on harmful prompts is a key safety behaviour in instruction-tuned large language models (LLMs), yet the internal causes of this behaviour remain poorly understood. We study two public instruction-tuned models, Gemma-2-2B-IT and LLaMA-3.1-8B-IT, using sparse autoencoders (SAEs) trained on residual-stream activations. Given a harmful prompt, we search the SAE latent space for feature sets whose ablation flips the model from refusal to compliance, demonstrating causal influence and creating a jailbreak. Our search proceeds in three stages: (1) Refusal Direction: find a refusal-mediating direction and collect SAE features near that direction; (2) Greedy Filtering: prune to a minimal set; and (3) Interaction Discovery: fit a factorization machine (FM) that captures nonlinear interactions among the remaining active features and the minimal set. This pipeline yields a broad set of jailbreak-critical features, offering insight into the mechanistic basis of refusal. Moreover, we find evidence of redundant features that remain dormant unless earlier features are suppressed. Our findings highlight the potential for fine-grained auditing and targeted intervention in safety behaviours by manipulating the interpretable latent space.

papers.title: From Adversarial Poetry to Adversarial Tales: An Interpretability Research Agenda
papers.research_question: Why are structurally-grounded jailbreaks (like Adversarial Poetry and Adversarial Tales) effective, and how can mechanistic interpretability investigate how narrative cues reshape model representations to recognize harmful intent independently of surface form?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Adversarial Tales, a jailbreak technique that embeds harmful requests within narrative structures and prompts functional analysis, demonstrating high attack success rates across models and proposing a mechanistic interpretability research agenda to understand such vulnerabilities.
papers.conclusion: Structurally-grounded jailbreaks constitute a broad vulnerability class that cannot be mitigated by pattern-matching defenses alone, necessitating a mechanistic interpretability research agenda to understand and address the underlying mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Adversarial Tales achieved an average attack success rate (ASR) of 71.3% across 26 frontier models from nine providers.
The attack was most effective for Harmful Manipulation (95% ASR) and Cyber Offense (89.7% ASR) risk categories.
The vulnerability generalizes across model families, with Qwen and Llama families showing the highest ASR (91.2%) and Anthropic models the most resistant (47.5%).
No substantial correlation between model size and ASR was observed, suggesting the attack exploits a fundamental property of how models process structured interpretive tasks.
The work positions Adversarial Poetry and Adversarial Tales as instances of a broader class of structurally-grounded jailbreaks, indicating a systemic vulnerability.
papers.limitation: The prompts used in the experiments and the model outputs are not released due to their harmful nature, limiting reproducibility.
future_direction: Investigate how narrative cues reshape model attention patterns compared to non-narrative attacks.
Explore whether models can learn to recognize harmful intent independently of surface form.
Examine the universal weight subspace hypothesis to understand shared vulnerabilities across architectures.
papers.abstract: Safety mechanisms in LLMs remain vulnerable to attacks that reframe harmful requests through culturally coded structures. We introduce Adversarial Tales, a jailbreak technique that embeds harmful content within cyberpunk narratives and prompts models to perform functional analysis inspired by Vladimir Propp's morphology of folktales. By casting the task as structural decomposition, the attack induces models to reconstruct harmful procedures as legitimate narrative interpretation. Across 26 frontier models from nine providers, we observe an average attack success rate of 71.3%, with no model family proving reliably robust. Together with our prior work on Adversarial Poetry, these findings suggest that structurally-grounded jailbreaks constitute a broad vulnerability class rather than isolated techniques. The space of culturally coded frames that can mediate harmful intent is vast, likely inexhaustible by pattern-matching defenses alone. Understanding why these attacks succeed is therefore essential: we outline a mechanistic interpretability research agenda to investigate how narrative cues reshape model representations and whether models can learn to recognize harmful intent independently of surface form.

papers.title: Representation Bending for Large Language Model Safety
papers.research_question: How can we enhance LLM safety by bending the representation space to separate safe and unsafe representations, bringing activation steering to fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces REPBEND, a method that brings activation steering to fine-tuning by bending the representation space to separate safe and unsafe representations, achieving state-of-the-art safety performance with minimal impact on general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: REPBEND effectively enhances LLM safety by bending representations to separate safe and unsafe states, achieving state-of-the-art performance with minimal impact on general capabilities, offering a scalable safety solution.
papers.key_findings:
REPBEND achieves up to 95% reduction in attack success rates across diverse jailbreak benchmarks.
REPBEND maintains general capabilities and usability, with minimal degradation on standard benchmarks.
REPBEND outperforms prior methods such as Circuit Breaker, RMU, and NPO in both black-box and white-box attacks.
REPBEND works best when applied to mid-to-later layers of the transformer.
REPBEND's loss function, which includes L2 norm, cosine similarity, and KL divergence terms, effectively separates safe and unsafe representations.
papers.limitation:
REPBEND requires a dataset of safe and unsafe prompts, which may not cover all possible harmful scenarios.
The method relies on the choice of layers and hyperparameters, which may need tuning for different models.
The transferability of LoRA for safety improvements remains an open challenge.
future_direction: Exploring the transferability of LoRA adapters for safety across models.
Extending REPBEND to multimodal settings.
Investigating the theoretical foundations of representation bending.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as powerful tools, but their inherent safety risks - ranging from harmful content generation to broader societal harms - pose significant challenges. These risks can be amplified by the recent adversarial attacks, fine-tuning vulnerabilities, and the increasing deployment of LLMs in high-stakes environments. Existing safety-enhancing techniques, such as fine-tuning with human feedback or adversarial training, are still vulnerable as they address specific threats and often fail to generalize across unseen attacks, or require manual system-level defenses. This paper introduces RepBend, a novel approach that fundamentally disrupts the representations underlying harmful behaviors in LLMs, offering a scalable solution to enhance (potentially inherent) safety. RepBend brings the idea of activation steering - simple vector arithmetic for steering model's behavior during inference - to loss-based fine-tuning. Through extensive evaluation, RepBend achieves state-of-the-art performance, outperforming prior methods such as Circuit Breaker, RMU, and NPO, with up to 95% reduction in attack success rates across diverse jailbreak benchmarks, all with negligible reduction in model usability and general capabilities.

papers.title: Jailbreak Instruction-Tuned LLMs via end-of-sentence MLP Re-weighting
papers.research_question: How does re-weighting MLP neurons in end-of-sentence inferences affect the safety mechanisms of instruction-tuned LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that MLP layers in end-of-sentence inferences are critical for safety in instruction-tuned LLMs, and introduces two white-box jailbreak methods that re-weight MLP neurons to compromise safety.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that MLP layers in end-of-sentence inferences are critical for safety in instruction-tuned LLMs, and that re-weighting these neurons can effectively jailbreak the models, providing insights for both attack and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Re-weighting MLP neurons in end-of-sentence inferences can significantly compromise the safety of instruction-tuned LLMs.
The prompt-specific jailbreak method outperforms state-of-the-art prompt-specific methods and requires less computational time.
The prompt-general jailbreak method is comparable to state-of-the-art approaches and has minimal impact on the model's original capabilities (except for very small models).
The safety mechanism of instruction-tuned LLMs heavily relies on MLP layers in end-of-sentence inferences.
The method can also serve as a mechanism interpretability tool to identify MLP neurons strongly correlated with safety.
papers.limitation:
The method is heuristic-driven, making it more of a validation experiment rather than an optimal solution.
The precise role MLP layers play in the safety mechanism and how they impact subsequent generation processes remain open questions.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we investigate the safety mechanisms of instruction fine-tuned large language models (LLMs). We discover that re-weighting MLP neurons can significantly compromise a model's safety, especially for MLPs in end-of-sentence inferences. We hypothesize that LLMs evaluate the harmfulness of prompts during end-of-sentence inferences, and MLP layers plays a critical role in this process. Based on this hypothesis, we develop 2 novel white-box jailbreak methods: a prompt-specific method and a prompt-general method. The prompt-specific method targets individual prompts and optimizes the attack on the fly, while the prompt-general method is pre-trained offline and can generalize to unseen harmful prompts. Our methods demonstrate robust performance across 7 popular open-source LLMs, size ranging from 2B to 72B. Furthermore, our study provides insights into vulnerabilities of instruction-tuned LLM's safety and deepens the understanding of the internal mechanisms of LLMs.

papers.title: TRYLOCK: Defense-in-Depth Against LLM Jailbreaks via Layered Preference and Representation Engineering
papers.research_question: How can a defense-in-depth architecture combining weight-level, activation-level, and input-level mechanisms protect LLMs against jailbreak attacks while maintaining usability?
papers.core_contribution: TRYLOCK is a defense-in-depth architecture that combines DPO safety training, RepE activation steering, adaptive sidecar classification, and input canonicalization, achieving an 88.0% relative reduction in Attack Success Rate while reducing over-refusal through adaptive steering.
papers.conclusion: Defense-in-depth with multiple complementary mechanisms (weight modification, activation steering, input classification, and canonicalization) is an effective approach for robust LLM safety against jailbreak attacks, though a trade-off between security and usability remains.
papers.key_findings:
The layered defense reduces Attack Success Rate from 46.5% to 5.6% (88.0% relative reduction) on a 249-prompt attack set.
Each defense layer provides complementary coverage: RepE blocks 36% of attacks that bypass DPO alone, and canonicalization catches 14% of encoding attacks that evade both.
A non-monotonic steering phenomenon was discovered where intermediate steering strength (α=1.0) degrades safety below the DPO-only baseline.
Adaptive steering via a sidecar classifier reduces over-refusal from 60% (fixed α=2.0) to 48% while maintaining identical attack defense.
The defense generalizes to the held-out JailbreakBench, achieving 78.8% relative ASR reduction (52.0% to 11.0%).
papers.limitation:
Evaluation set size and representativeness: the 50-prompt benign set yields wide confidence intervals for over-refusal, and larger diverse evaluations are needed.
Sidecar classifier errors: 18% of attacks are misclassified as SAFE, receiving minimal steering and resulting in higher ASR for those attacks.
future_direction: Extend TRYLOCK to additional base models, non-English languages, and integration with standard LLM serving frameworks.
Improve the sidecar classifier calibration and explore ensemble classifiers for better attack detection.
Conduct larger and more diverse benign evaluations to better characterize usability impact.
papers.abstract: Large language models remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks, and single-layer defenses often trade security for usability. We present TRYLOCK, the first defense-in-depth architecture that combines four heterogeneous mechanisms across the inference stack: weight-level safety alignment via DPO, activation-level control via Representation Engineering (RepE) steering, adaptive steering strength selected by a lightweight sidecar classifier, and input canonicalization to neutralize encoding-based bypasses. On Mistral-7B-Instruct evaluated against a 249-prompt attack set spanning five attack families, TRYLOCK achieves 88.0% relative ASR reduction (46.5% to 5.6%), with each layer contributing unique coverage: RepE blocks 36% of attacks that bypass DPO alone, while canonicalization catches 14% of encoding attacks that evade both. We discover a non-monotonic steering phenomenon -- intermediate strength (alpha=1.0) degrades safety below baseline -- and provide mechanistic hypotheses explaining RepE-DPO interference. The adaptive sidecar reduces over-refusal from 60% to 48% while maintaining identical attack defense, demonstrating that security and usability need not be mutually exclusive. We release all components -- trained adapters, steering vectors, sidecar classifier, preference pairs, and complete evaluation methodology -- enabling full reproducibility.

papers.title: Layer-Level Self-Exposure and Patch: Affirmative Token Mitigation for Jailbreak Attack Defense
papers.research_question: How can we defend against jailbreak attacks by identifying and patching toxic layers in LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Layer-AdvPatcher, a defense framework that identifies toxic layers in LLMs responsible for generating affirmative tokens to harmful prompts and patches them via adversarial augmentation and localized unlearning.
papers.conclusion: Layer-AdvPatcher effectively defends against jailbreak attacks by precisely targeting and editing toxic layers through adversarial exposure and unlearning, maintaining model utility while reducing harmful outputs.
papers.key_findings:
Layer-AdvPatcher reduces the harmfulness and attack success rate (ASR) of jailbreak attacks without significantly compromising utility for benign queries.
Toxic layers, which exhibit a high tendency to generate affirmative tokens, are often found in the later stages of LLMs (e.g., layer 28 in Mistral, layers 21-24 in Llama2).
The method outperforms or is competitive with state-of-the-art defense strategies like Self-Examination, Paraphrase, Unlearning, and SafeDecoding.
Targeted unlearning of specific layer components (e.g., QV and LayerNorm) is more effective for defense than unlearning all parameters of a layer.
The framework is modular and can be combined with prompt-based defenses for enhanced security.
papers.limitation:
The framework has not been tested on larger models (e.g., Llama3-13B) due to computational constraints.
The selection of affirmative tokens for identifying toxic layers may not be comprehensive, affecting generalizability across models.
Open-sourcing the dataset derived from toxic layers could be misused by malicious actors to create more sophisticated attacks.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in diverse applications, including chatbot assistants and code generation, aligning their behavior with safety and ethical standards has become paramount. However, jailbreak attacks, which exploit vulnerabilities to elicit unintended or harmful outputs, threaten LLMs' safety significantly. In this paper, we introduce Layer-AdvPatcher, a novel methodology designed to defend against jailbreak attacks by utilizing an unlearning strategy to patch specific layers within LLMs through self-augmented datasets. Our insight is that certain layer(s), tend to produce affirmative tokens when faced with harmful prompts. By identifying these layers and adversarially exposing them to generate more harmful data, one can understand their inherent and diverse vulnerabilities to attacks. With these exposures, we then "unlearn" these issues, reducing the impact of affirmative tokens and hence minimizing jailbreak risks while keeping the model's responses to safe queries intact. We conduct extensive experiments on two models, four benchmark datasets, and multiple state-of-the-art jailbreak attacks to demonstrate the efficacy of our approach. Results indicate that our framework reduces the harmfulness and attack success rate of jailbreak attacks without compromising utility for benign queries compared to recent defense methods. Our code is publicly available at: https://github.com/oyy2000/LayerAdvPatcher

papers.title: One Leak Away: How Pretrained Model Exposure Amplifies Jailbreak Risks in Finetuned LLMs
papers.research_question: Do finetuned LLMs inherit the jailbreak vulnerabilities of their pretrained counterparts, and can attackers exploit knowledge of the pretrained model to launch more effective jailbreak attacks against finetuned systems?
papers.core_contribution: Finetuned LLMs inherit jailbreak vulnerabilities from their pretrained counterparts, and the proposed Probe-Guided Projection (PGP) attack leverages representation-level signals in the pretrained model to craft highly transferable adversarial prompts.
papers.conclusion: Finetuned LLMs inherit vulnerabilities from their pretrained counterparts, and publicly releasing pretrained checkpoints increases the security risks for downstream applications.
papers.key_findings:
Jailbreak prompts crafted on a pretrained LLM transfer most effectively to its finetuned variants, indicating inherited vulnerabilities.
Transferable jailbreak prompts are linearly separable in the pretrained LLM's hidden representations, showing transferability is encoded in the feature space.
The proposed PGP attack consistently outperforms existing methods in the pretrain-to-finetune threat setting.
PGP remains effective even when the finetuned model has undergone safety tuning.
Attack success is highly dependent on using the correct pretrained source model; using a different pretrained model yields near-zero transferability.
papers.limitation: The paper does not propose a defense to mitigate the inherited vulnerabilities.
future_direction: Design methods that prevent or reduce the inheritance of vulnerabilities during finetuning.
papers.abstract: Finetuning pretrained large language models (LLMs) has become the standard paradigm for developing downstream applications. However, its security implications remain unclear, particularly regarding whether finetuned LLMs inherit jailbreak vulnerabilities from their pretrained sources. We investigate this question in a realistic pretrain-to-finetune threat model, where the attacker has white-box access to the pretrained LLM and only black-box access to its finetuned derivatives. Empirical analysis shows that adversarial prompts optimized on the pretrained model transfer most effectively to its finetuned variants, revealing inherited vulnerabilities from pretrained to finetuned LLMs. To further examine this inheritance, we conduct representation-level probing, which shows that transferable prompts are linearly separable within the pretrained hidden states, suggesting that universal transferability is encoded in pretrained representations. Building on this insight, we propose the Probe-Guided Projection (PGP) attack, which steers optimization toward transferability-relevant directions. Experiments across multiple LLM families and diverse finetuned tasks confirm PGP's strong transfer success, underscoring the security risks inherent in the pretrain-to-finetune paradigm.

papers.title: One Trigger Token Is Enough: A Defense Strategy for Balancing Safety and Usability in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we defend LLMs against jailbreak attacks by identifying and decoding safety trigger tokens that activate the model's safety patterns?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes D-STT, a defense algorithm that identifies and decodes safety trigger tokens to activate a model's learned safety patterns, effectively defending against jailbreak attacks while preserving usability with minimal overhead.
papers.conclusion: D-STT provides a simple, effective, and lightweight defense against jailbreak attacks by explicitly decoding safety trigger tokens, balancing safety and usability with negligible latency.
papers.key_findings:
Shallow safety alignment in LLMs manifests through learned 'safety trigger tokens' that activate safety patterns when paired with harmful input.
Safety trigger tokens are highly similar across different harmful inputs, enabling cross-sample learning and generalization.
D-STT significantly reduces output harmfulness against diverse jailbreak attacks while maintaining high response quality on benign prompts.
Constraining the safety trigger to a single token effectively balances safety and usability with minimal intervention.
D-STT is lightweight, incurring only 2% response time overhead, and outperforms ten baseline defense methods.
papers.limitation:
Relies on collecting refusal samples and the explicit output vocabulary distribution; future work may explore identifying triggers directly from the model's feature space.
Requires intervention in the decoding process, making it inapplicable for end-users of closed-source, black-box commercial models where inference parameters are inaccessible.
future_direction: Explore how to identify the 'trigger' nature of safety tokens directly from the model's feature space (e.g., hidden states or attention patterns).
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have been extensively used across diverse domains, including virtual assistants, automated code generation, and scientific research. However, they remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks, which manipulate the models into generating harmful responses despite safety alignment. Recent studies have shown that current safety-aligned LLMs undergo shallow safety alignment. In this work, we conduct an in-depth investigation into the underlying mechanism of this phenomenon and reveal that it manifests through learned ''safety trigger tokens'' that activate the model's safety patterns when paired with the specific input. Through both analysis and empirical verification, we further demonstrate the high similarity of the safety trigger tokens across different harmful inputs. Accordingly, we propose D-STT, a simple yet effective defense algorithm that identifies and explicitly decodes safety trigger tokens of the given safety-aligned LLM to activate the model's learned safety patterns. In this process, the safety trigger is constrained to a single token, which effectively preserves model usability by introducing minimum intervention in the decoding process. Extensive experiments across diverse jailbreak attacks and benign prompts demonstrate that D-STT significantly reduces output harmfulness while preserving model usability and incurring negligible response time overhead, outperforming ten baseline methods.

papers.title: Defending Large Language Models Against Jailbreak Exploits with Responsible AI Considerations
papers.research_question: How can we defend large language models against jailbreak exploits? The paper proposes and evaluates three defense strategies.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a taxonomy of jailbreak defenses and three defense strategies (prompt-level, logit-based steering, and domain-specific agent) that reduce attack success rates, with the agent-based defense achieving full mitigation.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that jailbreaks pose significant risks and that targeted interventions can prevent them, but defenses involve trade-offs between safety, computational efficiency, and scalability.
papers.key_findings:
The prompt-level defense reduces Attack Success Rate (ASR) by about 22% for aligned models and 8% for unaligned models.
The logit-based steering defense reduces ASR by 18% for aligned models and 43% for unaligned models.
The domain-specific agent defense (using MetaGPT) achieves zero ASR, fully mitigating jailbreak attempts.
Aligned models (with training-time defenses) show lower baseline ASR and are more robust to jailbreaks.
Defense strategies involve trade-offs between safety, computational efficiency, and scalability.
papers.limitation:
Defense strategies often involve trade-offs between safety, performance, and scalability.
The domain-specific agent defense incurs higher computational cost and latency due to multiple inference passes.
future_direction: Explore adaptive and efficient defense mechanisms that maintain both robustness and usability in real-world LLM applications.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) remain susceptible to jailbreak exploits that bypass safety filters and induce harmful or unethical behavior. This work presents a systematic taxonomy of existing jailbreak defenses across prompt-level, model-level, and training-time interventions, followed by three proposed defense strategies. First, a Prompt-Level Defense Framework detects and neutralizes adversarial inputs through sanitization, paraphrasing, and adaptive system guarding. Second, a Logit-Based Steering Defense reinforces refusal behavior through inference-time vector steering in safety-sensitive layers. Third, a Domain-Specific Agent Defense employs the MetaGPT framework to enforce structured, role-based collaboration and domain adherence. Experiments on benchmark datasets show substantial reductions in attack success rate, achieving full mitigation under the agent-based defense. Overall, this study highlights how jailbreaks pose a significant security threat to LLMs and identifies key intervention points for prevention, while noting that defense strategies often involve trade-offs between safety, performance, and scalability. Code is available at: https://github.com/Kuro0911/CS5446-Project

papers.title: Understanding and Rectifying Safety Perception Distortion in VLMs
papers.research_question: What causes the degradation of safety alignment in vision-language models (VLMs) when integrating the vision modality, and how can it be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies that multimodal inputs cause a 'safety perception distortion' in VLMs by inducing an activation shift towards a safer direction, and proposes ShiftDC, a training-free method to disentangle and calibrate this shift to restore safety alignment without harming utility.
papers.conclusion: The safety perception distortion caused by the visual modality is a key factor in VLM safety degradation, and the proposed ShiftDC method effectively mitigates this issue without additional training, restoring safety alignment while preserving model utility.
papers.key_findings:
VLMs struggle to differentiate between safe and unsafe vision-language inputs, while their text-only LLM backbones can do so effectively.
Visual modality induces an activation shift that causes VLMs to misperceive unsafe instructions as safer.
The magnitude of the safety-relevant component of the activation shift correlates positively with the attack success rate (ASR).
The proposed ShiftDC method significantly reduces ASR on safety benchmarks without compromising visual reasoning utility.
ShiftDC restores the linear separability of safe and unsafe activations in VLMs, correcting the safety perception distortion.
papers.abstract: Recent studies reveal that vision-language models (VLMs) become more susceptible to harmful requests and jailbreak attacks after integrating the vision modality, exhibiting greater vulnerability than their text-only LLM backbones. To uncover the root cause of this phenomenon, we conduct an in-depth analysis and identify a key issue: multimodal inputs introduce an modality-induced activation shift toward a "safer" direction compared to their text-only counterparts, leading VLMs to systematically overestimate the safety of harmful inputs. We refer to this issue as safety perception distortion. To mitigate such distortion, we propose Activation Shift Disentanglement and Calibration (ShiftDC), a training-free method that decomposes and calibrates the modality-induced activation shift to reduce the impact of modality on safety. By isolating and removing the safety-relevant component, ShiftDC restores the inherent safety alignment of the LLM backbone while preserving the vision-language capabilities of VLMs. Empirical results demonstrate that ShiftDC significantly enhances alignment performance on safety benchmarks without impairing model utility.

papers.title: Refusal Direction is Universal Across Safety-Aligned Languages
papers.research_question: How universal are refusal directions across languages? Specifically, does a refusal direction extracted from one language transfer to others?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that refusal directions are universal across safety-aligned languages; a refusal vector extracted from one language can effectively modulate refusal behavior in other languages.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that refusal directions are universal across safety-aligned languages, providing insights for multilingual safety defenses.
papers.key_findings:
English-derived refusal vectors can jailbreak models across multiple languages.
Refusal vectors derived from any safety-aligned language (e.g., German, Chinese, Thai) transfer to other languages.
The universality is due to parallelism of refusal vectors across languages in the embedding space.
Models fail to separate harmful and harmless prompts in non-English languages, leading to vulnerabilities.
Adding refusal vectors can reduce compliance rates, demonstrating controllability.
papers.abstract: Refusal mechanisms in large language models (LLMs) are essential for ensuring safety. Recent research has revealed that refusal behavior can be mediated by a single direction in activation space, enabling targeted interventions to bypass refusals. While this is primarily demonstrated in an English-centric context, appropriate refusal behavior is important for any language, but poorly understood. In this paper, we investigate the refusal behavior in LLMs across 14 languages using PolyRefuse, a multilingual safety dataset created by translating malicious and benign English prompts into these languages. We uncover the surprising cross-lingual universality of the refusal direction: a vector extracted from English can bypass refusals in other languages with near-perfect effectiveness, without any additional fine-tuning. Even more remarkably, refusal directions derived from any safety-aligned language transfer seamlessly to others. We attribute this transferability to the parallelism of refusal vectors across languages in the embedding space and identify the underlying mechanism behind cross-lingual jailbreaks. These findings provide actionable insights for building more robust multilingual safety defenses and pave the way for a deeper mechanistic understanding of cross-lingual vulnerabilities in LLMs.

papers.title: Making Harmful Behaviors Unlearnable for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Can we train LLMs on harmful data without learning harmful behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: This paper proposes a controllable fine-tuning framework using 'security vectors' (additional parameters) to make harmful behaviors unlearnable during training, preventing LLMs from learning from harmful data while preserving their ability to learn other tasks.
papers.conclusion: The proposed framework with security vectors effectively prevents LLMs from learning harmful behaviors during fine-tuning, reducing security risks and enabling safer model customization.
papers.key_findings:
Security vectors trained on 100 harmful samples can prevent an LLM from learning harmful behaviors from 1000 harmful examples.
The method prevents learning from both explicit and implicit harmful data, maintaining safety levels comparable to the original aligned model.
Fine-tuning with security vectors does not impair the model's ability to learn new, benign tasks (e.g., ProfileQA).
The approach is robust across different training epochs and learning rates, except when the fine-tuning learning rate is much higher than that used to generate the security vectors.
Security vectors can be deactivated during inference, restoring the model's normal, safe behavior.
papers.limitation:
The security vectors may lose effectiveness if the fine-tuning learning rate is significantly higher (e.g., 5e-3) than the rate used to generate them (1e-3).
Excessive training epochs on harmful data may impair the model's reasoning ability (e.g., on GSM), though the cause is not fully determined.
future_direction: Design experiments to ascertain the cause of the drop in reasoning ability (GSM) when fine-tuning on harmful data.
Investigate the robust instruction-following capability observed when fine-tuning with security vectors over many epochs.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown great potential as general-purpose AI assistants in various domains. To meet the requirements of different applications, LLMs are often customized by further fine-tuning. However, the powerful learning ability of LLMs not only enables them to acquire new tasks but also makes them susceptible to learning undesired behaviors. For example, even safety-aligned LLMs can be easily fine-tuned into harmful assistants as the fine-tuning data often contains implicit or explicit harmful content. Can we train LLMs on harmful data without learning harmful behaviors? This paper proposes a controllable training framework that makes harmful behaviors unlearnable during the fine-tuning process. Specifically, we introduce ``security vectors'', a few new parameters that can be separated from the LLM, to ensure LLM's responses are consistent with the harmful behavior. Security vectors are activated during fine-tuning, the consistent behavior makes LLM believe that such behavior has already been learned, there is no need to further optimize for harmful data. During inference, we can deactivate security vectors to restore the LLM's normal behavior. The experimental results show that the security vectors generated by 100 harmful samples are enough to prevent LLM from learning 1000 harmful samples, while preserving the ability to learn other useful information.

papers.title: SafeSwitch: Steering Unsafe LLM Behavior via Internal Activation Signals
papers.research_question: How can internal activation signals in LLMs be used to predict and dynamically regulate unsafe behavior, balancing safety and utility?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SafeSwitch, a framework that uses a safety prober to monitor internal states and dynamically activate a refusal head to mitigate unsafe outputs, reducing harmful responses by ~80% while preserving utility.
papers.conclusion: SafeSwitch demonstrates LLMs' capacity for self-awareness and reflection regarding safety, offering a promising approach to more nuanced, dynamic, and effective safety controls.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs inherently encode safety-related information (recognition of unsafe instructions and intent to respond) within their internal states.
A two-stage safety prober can predict unsafe behavior with high accuracy (F1 >90%) by decomposing the task into instruction safety and model compliance.
SafeSwitch reduces harmful outputs by approximately 80% on harmful queries (SORRY-Bench, TrustLLM) while maintaining strong utility on benign benchmarks.
SafeSwitch achieves a Pareto optimal balance between safety and utility, outperforming baselines like always-on refusal heads or safety prompts.
The method is parameter-efficient, tuning less than 6% of the original model parameters (prober and refusal head).
papers.limitation: The safety prober can produce false positives (over-refusal) and false negatives (missing unsafe responses), with performance varying across query types and benchmarks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit exceptional capabilities across various tasks but also pose risks by generating harmful content. Existing safety mechanisms, while improving model safety, often lead to overly cautious behavior and fail to fully leverage LLMs' internal cognitive processes. Inspired by humans' reflective thinking capability, we first show that LLMs can similarly perform internal assessments about safety in their internal states. Building on this insight, we propose SafeSwitch, a dynamic framework that regulates unsafe outputs by utilizing the prober-based internal state monitor that actively detects harmful intentions, and activates a safety head that leads to safer and more conservative responses only when necessary. SafeSwitch reduces harmful outputs by approximately 80% on harmful queries while maintaining strong utility, reaching a Pareto optimal among several methods. Our method is also advantageous over traditional methods in offering more informative, context-aware refusals, and achieves these benefits while only tuning less than 6% of the original parameters. SafeSwitch demonstrates large language models' capacity for self-awareness and reflection regarding safety, offering a promising approach to more nuanced and effective safety controls. Codes for this work are available at https://github.com/Hanpx20/SafeSwitch.

papers.title: GradSafe: Detecting Jailbreak Prompts for LLMs via Safety-Critical Gradient Analysis
papers.research_question: How can jailbreak prompts for LLMs be detected without requiring extensive training data and model fine-tuning? The paper investigates whether safety-critical gradients can be used for this detection.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces GradSafe, a method that detects jailbreak prompts by analyzing the gradients of safety-critical parameters in LLMs, without requiring fine-tuning of the base model.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that GradSafe, a method based on safety-critical gradient analysis, can effectively detect unsafe prompts without fine-tuning and outperforms existing methods that require extensive training.
papers.key_findings:
GradSafe-Zero, applied to Llama-2 without training, outperforms the fine-tuned Llama Guard and online moderation APIs on the ToxicChat and XSTest benchmarks.
GradSafe-Adapt, using a logistic regression classifier on gradient features, achieves strong performance with minimal adaptation data, matching Llama Guard's performance with only 20% of the training data.
The method's effectiveness depends on the base LLM being safety-aligned; it does not work well with an unaligned pretrained model.
Identifying safety-critical parameters is crucial for the method's performance and efficiency, compared to using all gradients.
Using a compliance or rejection response (e.g., 'Sure' or 'I'm sorry') to pair with the prompt is important for activating the safety-critical gradients, while a neutral response does not work.
papers.limitation:
The method is only evaluated on Llama-2 and may not generalize to other LLMs.
The method provides a binary safety assessment and does not offer fine-grained classification for specific safety categories.
future_direction: Fine-grained classification for specific safety categories.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) face threats from jailbreak prompts. Existing methods for detecting jailbreak prompts are primarily online moderation APIs or finetuned LLMs. These strategies, however, often require extensive and resource-intensive data collection and training processes. In this study, we propose GradSafe, which effectively detects jailbreak prompts by scrutinizing the gradients of safety-critical parameters in LLMs. Our method is grounded in a pivotal observation: the gradients of an LLM's loss for jailbreak prompts paired with compliance response exhibit similar patterns on certain safety-critical parameters. In contrast, safe prompts lead to different gradient patterns. Building on this observation, GradSafe analyzes the gradients from prompts (paired with compliance responses) to accurately detect jailbreak prompts. We show that GradSafe, applied to Llama-2 without further training, outperforms Llama Guard-despite its extensive finetuning with a large dataset-in detecting jailbreak prompts. This superior performance is consistent across both zero-shot and adaptation scenarios, as evidenced by our evaluations on ToxicChat and XSTest. The source code is available at https://github.com/xyq7/GradSafe.

papers.title: Eliciting Latent Predictions from Transformers with the Tuned Lens
papers.research_question: How are model predictions refined layer by layer in transformers through iterative inference?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the tuned lens, a method that trains affine probes to decode hidden states in frozen pretrained transformers, providing more reliable and unbiased prediction trajectories than the logit lens.
papers.conclusion: The tuned lens is a drop-in replacement for the logit lens that provides interpretable prediction trajectories and has applications in anomaly detection and difficulty estimation.
papers.key_findings:
The tuned lens produces lower perplexity and less biased predictions than the logit lens across various models.
Causal experiments show that features influential on the tuned lens are also causally relevant to the model's output.
The tuned lens can detect prompt injection attacks with near-perfect accuracy in some cases.
Prediction depth from the tuned lens correlates with the iteration learned during training, indicating it measures example difficulty.
Tuned lens translators transfer well to fine-tuned models without additional training.
papers.limitation:
Training translators for each layer requires additional computation compared to the logit lens.
Causal basis extraction is computationally intensive.
future_direction: Make causal basis extraction more scalable.
Apply the tuned lens to other modalities beyond language.
papers.abstract: We analyze transformers from the perspective of iterative inference, seeking to understand how model predictions are refined layer by layer. To do so, we train an affine probe for each block in a frozen pretrained model, making it possible to decode every hidden state into a distribution over the vocabulary. Our method, the tuned lens, is a refinement of the earlier "logit lens" technique, which yielded useful insights but is often brittle. We test our method on various autoregressive language models with up to 20B parameters, showing it to be more predictive, reliable and unbiased than the logit lens. With causal experiments, we show the tuned lens uses similar features to the model itself. We also find the trajectory of latent predictions can be used to detect malicious inputs with high accuracy. All code needed to reproduce our results can be found at https://github.com/AlignmentResearch/tuned-lens.

papers.title: LLM-VA: Resolving the Jailbreak-Overrefusal Trade-off via Vector Alignment
papers.research_question: How can we simultaneously address both jailbreak and over-refusal in safety-aligned LLMs without fine-tuning or architectural changes?
papers.core_contribution: LLM-V A aligns answer vectors with benign vectors through closed-form weight updates to resolve the jailbreak-overrefusal trade-off without fine-tuning or architectural changes.
papers.conclusion: LLM-V A effectively resolves the jailbreak-overrefusal trade-off by aligning vectors, without requiring fine-tuning or architectural changes.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs encode answer decisions and safety assessments as nearly orthogonal vectors.
Aligning these vectors through closed-form weight updates simultaneously reduces jailbreak and over-refusal.
LLM-V A achieves 11.45% higher F1 than the best baseline while preserving 95.92% utility.
The method automatically adapts to each model's safety bias without manual tuning.
The method is effective across 12 LLMs from 5 model families.
papers.limitation:
Binary toxicity assumption (only benign vs. toxic), whereas real-world toxicity is nuanced and multi-dimensional.
Model scale: experiments cover models up to 14B parameters; effectiveness on larger models (e.g., 70B+) remains to be validated.
Training data dependency: requires labeled benign/toxic samples for SVM training; data quality and representativeness affect performance.
Difficulty applying to LLMs with chain-of-thought reasoning due to computational expense and randomness in reasoning steps.
Model-specific tuning required for optimal iteration count and layer selection.
future_direction: Extending LLM-V A to multi-class or fine-grained toxicity classification.
Validating effectiveness on larger models (e.g., 70B+).
Improving generalization to unseen datasets.
papers.abstract: Safety-aligned LLMs suffer from two failure modes: jailbreak (answering harmful inputs) and over-refusal (declining benign queries). Existing vector steering methods adjust the magnitude of answer vectors, but this creates a fundamental trade-off -- reducing jailbreak increases over-refusal and vice versa. We identify the root cause: LLMs encode the decision to answer (answer vector $v_a$) and the judgment of input safety (benign vector $v_b$) as nearly orthogonal directions, treating them as independent processes. We propose LLM-VA, which aligns $v_a$ with $v_b$ through closed-form weight updates, making the model's willingness to answer causally dependent on its safety assessment -- without fine-tuning or architectural changes. Our method identifies vectors at each layer using SVMs, selects safety-relevant layers, and iteratively aligns vectors via minimum-norm weight modifications. Experiments on 12 LLMs demonstrate that LLM-VA achieves 11.45% higher F1 than the best baseline while preserving 95.92% utility, and automatically adapts to each model's safety bias without manual tuning. Code and models are available at https://hotbento.github.io/LLM-VA-Web/.

papers.title: ALERT: Zero-shot LLM Jailbreak Detection via Internal Discrepancy Amplification
papers.research_question: How to detect jailbreak attacks in a zero-shot setting where no jailbreak templates are available during training, by amplifying internal feature discrepancies between benign and jailbreak prompts.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a zero-shot jailbreak detection task and a detector (ALERT) that amplifies internal discrepancies at layer, module, and token levels to identify unseen jailbreak attacks.
papers.conclusion: ALERT demonstrates strong zero-shot detection capability against unseen jailbreak attacks, significantly outperforming existing baselines and satisfying practicality principles for real-world deployment.
papers.key_findings:
Shallow layers (particularly the 3rd and 4th) encode safety-relevant semantics and exhibit large distributional discrepancies.
Gating and context features within the FFN provide stronger zero-shot discriminative signals than hidden states due to decoupled activation responses.
Jailbreak templates exhibit a larger token-level distribution gap from benign and harmful prompts compared to harmful instructions.
ALERT consistently achieves over 90% Accuracy and F1-score in zero-shot detection, outperforming baselines by at least 10% on average.
The proposed amplification mechanisms progressively improve detection performance, with module-wise amplification yielding the largest gain.
papers.limitation: The detector adopts a relatively simple VIB-based design; more advanced designs from generalization and domain adaptation could further improve robustness.
future_direction: Incorporate techniques from generalization and domain adaptation to explicitly reduce the domain gap between harmful and jailbreak prompts.
Explore using gating and context features for jailbreak mitigation through post-training strategies like reinforcement learning.
papers.abstract: Despite rich safety alignment strategies, large language models (LLMs) remain highly susceptible to jailbreak attacks, which compromise safety guardrails and pose serious security risks. Existing detection methods mainly detect jailbreak status relying on jailbreak templates present in the training data. However, few studies address the more realistic and challenging zero-shot jailbreak detection setting, where no jailbreak templates are available during training. This setting better reflects real-world scenarios where new attacks continually emerge and evolve. To address this challenge, we propose a layer-wise, module-wise, and token-wise amplification framework that progressively magnifies internal feature discrepancies between benign and jailbreak prompts. We uncover safety-relevant layers, identify specific modules that inherently encode zero-shot discriminative signals, and localize informative safety tokens. Building upon these insights, we introduce ALERT (Amplification-based Jailbreak Detector), an efficient and effective zero-shot jailbreak detector that introduces two independent yet complementary classifiers on amplified representations. Extensive experiments on three safety benchmarks demonstrate that ALERT achieves consistently strong zero-shot detection performance. Specifically, (i) across all datasets and attack strategies, ALERT reliably ranks among the top two methods, and (ii) it outperforms the second-best baseline by at least 10% in average Accuracy and F1-score, and sometimes by up to 40%.

papers.title: ReGA: Representation-Guided Abstraction for Model-based Safeguarding of LLMs
papers.research_question: How can we safeguard Large Language Models (LLMs) against harmful prompts and generations using a scalable, model-based analysis framework?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes ReGA, a model-based safeguarding framework for LLMs that uses representation-guided abstraction to address scalability issues and effectively distinguish safe and harmful inputs.
papers.conclusion: ReGA is an efficient and scalable solution for LLM safety, integrating representation engineering with model abstraction to provide a new paradigm for safeguarding LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
ReGA achieves high AUROC (0.975 at prompt level, 0.985 at conversation level) in distinguishing safe and harmful inputs.
ReGA generalizes to unseen datasets and shows robustness against various jailbreaking attacks.
ReGA outperforms other detection-based defense paradigms (MLP classifier, universal abstraction, LLM-Judge, perplexity filters) in effectiveness, interpretability, and scalability.
The framework is efficient and scalable, requiring only a few abstract states (8-64) compared to universal abstraction methods.
ReGA's performance is consistent across multiple LLMs, though weaker on models with lower reasoning capacity (e.g., koala).
papers.limitation:
Relies on a contrastive dataset, where bias or insufficient coverage may result in inaccurate safety representations.
May have limitations in generalizing to other LLMs, tasks, or safety perspectives due to differences in model architectures and data distributions.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved significant success in various tasks, yet concerns about their safety and security have emerged. In particular, they pose risks in generating harmful content and vulnerability to jailbreaking attacks. To analyze and monitor machine learning models, model-based analysis has demonstrated notable potential in stateful deep neural networks, yet suffers from scalability issues when extending to LLMs due to their vast feature spaces. In this paper, we propose ReGA, a model-based analysis framework with representation-guided abstraction, to safeguard LLMs against harmful prompts and generations. By leveraging safety-critical representations, which are low-dimensional directions emerging in hidden states that indicate safety-related concepts, ReGA effectively addresses the scalability issue when constructing the abstract model for safety modeling. Our comprehensive evaluation shows that ReGA performs sufficiently well in distinguishing between safe and harmful inputs, achieving an AUROC of 0.975 at the prompt level and 0.985 at the conversation level. Additionally, ReGA exhibits robustness to real-world attacks and generalization across different safety perspectives, outperforming existing safeguard paradigms in terms of interpretability and scalability. Overall, ReGA serves as an efficient and scalable solution to enhance LLM safety by integrating representation engineering with model-based abstraction, paving the way for new paradigms to utilize software insights for AI safety. Our code is available at https://github.com/weizeming/ReGA.

papers.title: Using Mechanistic Interpretability to Craft Adversarial Attacks against Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can mechanistic interpretability be used to craft practical adversarial inputs (jailbreaks) for large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Subspace Rerouting (SSR), a white-box adversarial attack method that uses mechanistic interpretability to efficiently jailbreak LLMs by rerouting embeddings to acceptance subspaces.
papers.conclusion: SSR is an effective adversarial attack framework that operationalizes mechanistic interpretability insights, and it also serves as a practical interpretability tool that operates within the model's natural processing pathways.
papers.key_findings:
SSR achieves high attack success rates (80-95%) on state-of-the-art aligned LLMs.
SSR is computationally efficient, generating jailbreaks in seconds to minutes.
Harmful and harmless content is linearly separable in the activation space of aligned LLMs, a property SSR exploits.
SSR can produce interpretable adversarial tokens (e.g., 'responsibly', 'ethical').
SSR can be used as an interpretability tool (e.g., reverse-lens to find inputs that trigger specific features).
papers.limitation:
The causal nature of autoregressive transformers limits perturbations to influencing only subsequent token representations.
SSR optimisation may affect multiple components simultaneously, making component attribution difficult.
Prefix-based or long perturbations can alter the entire context and change the semantic meaning of the instruction, leading to failed jailbreaks.
The attack has many hyperparameters, making comprehensive ablation studies impractical and reproducibility challenging.
SSR attacks show extremely poor transfer rates between models.
future_direction: Combining SSR with more constrained optimisation objectives to isolate specific causal mechanisms.
Using perplexity in the loss function to improve transfer rates of attacks.
Comparing SSR with other mechanistic interpretability tools on established benchmarks.
papers.abstract: Traditional white-box methods for creating adversarial perturbations against LLMs typically rely only on gradient computation from the targeted model, ignoring the internal mechanisms responsible for attack success or failure. Conversely, interpretability studies that analyze these internal mechanisms lack practical applications beyond runtime interventions. We bridge this gap by introducing a novel white-box approach that leverages mechanistic interpretability techniques to craft practical adversarial inputs. Specifically, we first identify acceptance subspaces - sets of feature vectors that do not trigger the model's refusal mechanisms - then use gradient-based optimization to reroute embeddings from refusal subspaces to acceptance subspaces, effectively achieving jailbreaks. This targeted approach significantly reduces computation cost, achieving attack success rates of 80-95\% on state-of-the-art models including Gemma2, Llama3.2, and Qwen2.5 within minutes or even seconds, compared to existing techniques that often fail or require hours of computation. We believe this approach opens a new direction for both attack research and defense development. Furthermore, it showcases a practical application of mechanistic interpretability where other methods are less efficient, which highlights its utility. The code and generated datasets are available at https://github.com/Sckathach/subspace-rerouting.

papers.title: Model-Editing-Based Jailbreak against Safety-aligned Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Is there a more stealthy jailbreak attack vector for LLMs that minimizes user involvement by directly modifying internal model structures to bypass safety alignment without input modifications?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Targeted Model Editing (TME), a white-box jailbreak method that bypasses safety filters by identifying and removing safety-critical transformations (SCTs) from MLP weight matrices, enabling harmful responses without input modifications while preserving normal model functionality.
papers.conclusion: The work reveals a covert and robust threat vector in LLM security via model editing-based jailbreaks and emphasizes the need for stronger safeguards in model safety alignment.
papers.key_findings:
MLP activations for unsafe samples are highly consistent (due to uniform refusal), while activations for safe samples are more variable.
The difference in average activation values between safe and unsafe samples is significantly larger than the variation within unsafe samples.
The overlap rate of activated neurons between safe and unsafe inputs is low (below 25%), indicating distinct processing pathways.
The D-LLM framework, which implements TME, achieves an average Attack Success Rate (ASR) of 84.86% across four open-source LLMs.
The method maintains model performance on standard benchmarks (TruthfulQA, MMLU) after editing, showing preserved functionality.
future_direction: Further unveil the vulnerabilities of D-LLM and provide insights for LLM developers to bolster safety.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have transformed numerous fields by enabling advanced natural language interactions but remain susceptible to critical vulnerabilities, particularly jailbreak attacks. Current jailbreak techniques, while effective, often depend on input modifications, making them detectable and limiting their stealth and scalability. This paper presents Targeted Model Editing (TME), a novel white-box approach that bypasses safety filters by minimally altering internal model structures while preserving the model's intended functionalities. TME identifies and removes safety-critical transformations (SCTs) embedded in model matrices, enabling malicious queries to bypass restrictions without input modifications. By analyzing distinct activation patterns between safe and unsafe queries, TME isolates and approximates SCTs through an optimization process. Implemented in the D-LLM framework, our method achieves an average Attack Success Rate (ASR) of 84.86% on four mainstream open-source LLMs, maintaining high performance. Unlike existing methods, D-LLM eliminates the need for specific triggers or harmful response collections, offering a stealthier and more effective jailbreak strategy. This work reveals a covert and robust threat vector in LLM security and emphasizes the need for stronger safeguards in model safety alignment.

papers.title: Self-Aware Safety Augmentation: Leveraging Internal Semantic Understanding to Enhance Safety in Vision-Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the internal dynamics of safety perception, semantic understanding, and linguistic expression in LVLMs, and how can they be leveraged to enhance safety without fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Self-Aware Safety Augmentation (SASA), a tuning-free method that enhances safety in LVLMs by projecting semantic-rich representations from intermediate fused layers onto earlier safety-critical layers, leveraging the model's internal understanding.
papers.conclusion: SASA effectively enhances LVLM safety by projecting semantic-rich representations to early safety layers, achieving high safety performance with minimal data and no tuning.
papers.key_findings:
Safety mechanisms are predominantly concentrated in early layers; ablating top-5 safety heads increases ASR by an average of 47%.
Semantic understanding progressively matures in intermediate layers, enabling internal discrimination between harmful and benign inputs, but this discriminative power diminishes in deeper layers due to alignment constraints.
The model possesses internal risk awareness that is not consistently translated into its language output.
SASA reduces ASR by an average of 97% using only 5% of data, with minimal degradation of helpfulness.
SASA exhibits remarkable zero-shot generalization capabilities on previously unseen datasets.
future_direction: Future work could explore extending SASA to other modalities and tasks, and investigating the interplay between safety and other model capabilities.
papers.abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) are vulnerable to harmful input compared to their language-only backbones. We investigated this vulnerability by exploring LVLMs internal dynamics, framing their inherent safety understanding in terms of three key capabilities. Specifically, we define these capabilities as safety perception, semantic understanding, and alignment for linguistic expression, and experimentally pinpointed their primary locations within the model architecture. The results indicate that safety perception often emerges before comprehensive semantic understanding, leading to the reduction in safety. Motivated by these findings, we propose \textbf{Self-Aware Safety Augmentation (SASA)}, a technique that projects informative semantic representations from intermediate layers onto earlier safety-oriented layers. This approach leverages the model's inherent semantic understanding to enhance safety recognition without fine-tuning. Then, we employ linear probing to articulate the model's internal semantic comprehension to detect the risk before the generation process. Extensive experiments on various datasets and tasks demonstrate that SASA significantly improves the safety of LVLMs, with minimal impact on the utility.

papers.title: Surgical Refusal Ablation: Disentangling Safety from Intelligence via Concept-Guided Spectral Cleaning
papers.research_question: How can refusal behavior in safety-aligned language models be ablated without causing collateral damage to core capabilities like math and coding?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Surgical Refusal Ablation (SRA), a method that cleans refusal vectors by orthogonalizing against capability and style directions, enabling precise ablation of refusal behavior with minimal distribution drift and preserved capabilities.
papers.conclusion: SRA treats refusal ablation as a semantic disentanglement problem, achieving behavioral editing with dramatically reduced drift and preserved capabilities compared to standard methods.
papers.key_findings:
SRA achieves deep refusal reduction (0–2% on harmful suite) with negligible perplexity impact on wikitext_2_raw and minimal distribution drift.
Standard ablation induces severe distribution drift, while SRA maintains original distribution while achieving low refusal rates.
SRA preserves or improves math and code perplexity on GSM8K and MBPP datasets.
The dirty refusal vector is polysemantic, entangling refusal signals with unrelated linguistic structure and capability circuits.
Cleaning the vector via spectral residualization reduces 'Ghost Noise' damage caused by standard ablation.
papers.limitation:
The atom registry is curated and may miss confounds; unseen entanglers could still leak into the refusal direction.
Evaluation limitations include refusal detection being definition-dependent, finite harmful prompt suites, and proxy drift metrics not substituting for comprehensive behavioral evaluation.
future_direction: Automating atom discovery or expanding registries to handle unseen confounds.
papers.abstract: Safety-aligned language models systematically refuse harmful requests. While activation steering can modulate refusal, ablating the raw "refusal vector" calculated from contrastive harmful and harmless prompts often causes collateral damage and distribution drift. We argue this degradation occurs because the raw vector is polysemantic, entangling the refusal signal with core capability circuits and linguistic style. We introduce Surgical Refusal Ablation (SRA) to distill these steering directions. SRA constructs a registry of independent Concept Atoms representing protected capabilities and stylistic confounds, then uses ridge-regularized spectral residualization to orthogonalize the refusal vector against these directions. This yields a clean refusal direction that targets refusal-relevant structure while minimizing disruption to the model's semantic geometry. Across five models (Qwen3-VL and Ministral series), SRA achieves deep refusal reduction (0-2%) with negligible perplexity impact on Wikitext-2 (mean delta PPL approx. 0.02) and minimal distribution drift. Notably, standard ablation on Qwen3-VL-4B induces severe drift (first-token KL = 2.088), whereas SRA maintains the original distribution (KL = 0.044) while achieving the same 0% refusal rate. Using teacher-forced perplexity on GSM8K and MBPP as a high-resolution capability proxy, we show SRA preserves math and code distributions. These results suggest that common "model damage" is often "Ghost Noise," defined as the spectral bleeding of the dirty refusal direction into capability subspaces.

papers.title: Universal Jailbreak Suffixes Are Strong Attention Hijackers
papers.research_question: What makes some adversarial suffixes more universal than others in jailbreaking large language models, and how does the mechanism of attention hijacking relate to this universality?
papers.core_contribution: Universal jailbreak suffixes work by hijacking the attention mechanism, specifically by dominating the representation of the chat tokens, and this hijacking is linked to the suffix's universality across harmful instructions.
papers.conclusion: Attention hijacking is a key mechanism for universal jailbreak suffixes, and understanding this mechanism can lead to both enhanced attacks and effective defenses.
papers.key_findings:
GCG jailbreaks rely on a shallow information flow from the adversarial suffix to the chat tokens.
GCG suffixes hijack the chat representation by attaining exceptionally high dominance over other token subsequences.
The hijacking strength of a suffix correlates with its universality across harmful instructions.
Enhancing hijacking during suffix optimization (GCG-Hij) produces more universal suffixes.
Suppressing hijacking (Hijacking Suppression) can mitigate jailbreaks with minimal utility loss.
papers.limitation: The hijacking suppression framework may need further refinement to improve the robustness-utility tradeoff.
future_direction: Future work may explore scoring methods that better disentangle jailbreak from model utility, or that avoid the overhead of materializing attention matrices.
papers.abstract: We study suffix-based jailbreaks$\unicode{x2013}$a powerful family of attacks against large language models (LLMs) that optimize adversarial suffixes to circumvent safety alignment. Focusing on the widely used foundational GCG attack, we observe that suffixes vary in efficacy: some are markedly more universal$\unicode{x2013}$generalizing to many unseen harmful instructions$\unicode{x2013}$than others. We first show that a shallow, critical mechanism drives GCG's effectiveness. This mechanism builds on the information flow from the adversarial suffix to the final chat template tokens before generation. Quantifying the dominance of this mechanism during generation, we find GCG irregularly and aggressively hijacks the contextualization process. Crucially, we tie hijacking to the universality phenomenon, with more universal suffixes being stronger hijackers. Subsequently, we show that these insights have practical implications: GCG's universality can be efficiently enhanced (up to $\times$5 in some cases) at no additional computational cost, and can also be surgically mitigated, at least halving the attack's success with minimal utility loss. We release our code and data at http://github.com/matanbt/interp-jailbreak.

papers.title: SoK: a Comprehensive Causality Analysis Framework for Large Language Model Security
papers.research_question: How can causal analysis be used to understand and mitigate vulnerabilities, such as jailbreaks, in Large Language Models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a unified causality analysis framework for LLM security that enables multi-level causal investigation (token, neuron, layer, representation) and demonstrates its effectiveness in understanding and defending against jailbreaks and other threats.
papers.conclusion: The causality analysis framework bridges theoretical causality and practical model safety, establishing a reproducible foundation for research on causality-based attacks, interpretability, and robust attack detection and mitigation in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Targeted interventions on causally critical components (tokens, neurons, layers, representations) can reliably modify model safety behavior.
Safety mechanisms are highly localized in early-to-middle transformer layers (2-12), with only 1-2% of neurons exhibiting causal influence.
Causal features extracted from the multi-level analysis achieve over 95% detection accuracy across jailbreak, hallucination, backdoor, and fairness tasks.
Token-level causal influence is high for optimization-based attacks (e.g., GCG) but low for semantically distributed attacks (e.g., AutoDAN).
Representation-level interventions via geometric steering along the acceptance direction are highly effective at crossing safety decision boundaries.
future_direction: Extending the causality analysis framework to multimodal settings (e.g., vision-language models).
Discovering additional causally relevant components or signals within LLMs that may reveal hidden vulnerabilities.
Conducting rigorous, comparative studies of existing causality-based approaches to evaluate their effectiveness and generalizability.
Developing more advanced causality-informed defenses that combine multi-level interventions or dynamically adapt safety mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable capabilities but remain vulnerable to adversarial manipulations such as jailbreaking, where crafted prompts bypass safety mechanisms. Understanding the causal factors behind such vulnerabilities is essential for building reliable defenses. In this work, we introduce a unified causality analysis framework that systematically supports all levels of causal investigation in LLMs, ranging from token-level, neuron-level, and layer-level interventions to representation-level analysis. The framework enables consistent experimentation and comparison across diverse causality-based attack and defense methods. Accompanying this implementation, we provide the first comprehensive survey of causality-driven jailbreak studies and empirically evaluate the framework on multiple open-weight models and safety-critical benchmarks including jailbreaks, hallucination detection, backdoor identification, and fairness evaluation. Our results reveal that: (1) targeted interventions on causally critical components can reliably modify safety behavior; (2) safety-related mechanisms are highly localized (i.e., concentrated in early-to-middle layers with only 1--2\% of neurons exhibiting causal influence); and (3) causal features extracted from our framework achieve over 95\% detection accuracy across multiple threat types. By bridging theoretical causality analysis and practical model safety, our framework establishes a reproducible foundation for research on causality-based attacks, interpretability, and robust attack detection and mitigation in LLMs. Code is available at https://github.com/Amadeuszhao/SOK_Casuality.

papers.title: Jailbreak Attack Initializations as Extractors of Compliance Directions
papers.research_question: How do gradient-based jailbreak attack initializations work, and how can we design an initialization framework that effectively projects prompts along compliance directions to improve attack success rate and reduce computational overhead?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that gradient-based jailbreak attacks and their initializations converge to a single compliance direction, and introduces the CRI framework to project unseen prompts along this direction, improving attack success rates and reducing computational overhead.
