papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that gradient-based jailbreak attacks converge to a single compliance direction and proposes CRI, an initialization framework that projects prompts along this direction, enhancing attack success rates and reducing computational overhead across various attacks, models, and datasets.
papers.key_findings:
Gradient-based jailbreak attacks and self-transfer initializations gradually converge to similar compliance directions.
The Loss at First Step (LFS) metric reliably indicates the number of steps required for a successful attack, enabling selection of effective initializations.
The CRI framework effectively initializes attacks by projecting prompts along compliance directions, increasing Attack Success Rate (ASR) and reducing computational overhead.
CRI performs well across multiple attacks, models, and datasets, highlighting the fragility of safety-aligned LLMs.
The trade-off between the number of initializations (K) and their generalization properties affects performance, with intermediate K (e.g., 5) often optimal.
papers.limitation:
Focus on gradient-based attacks may not generalize to other attack types.
Effectiveness depends on quality and diversity of fine-tuning set.
future_direction: Extending CRI to black-box settings
Integrating CRI with other attack improvements
Applying CRI to other types of attacks and defenses
papers.abstract: Safety-aligned LLMs respond to prompts with either compliance or refusal, each corresponding to distinct directions in the model's activation space. Recent works show that initializing attacks via self-transfer from other prompts significantly enhances their performance. However, the underlying mechanisms of these initializations remain unclear, and attacks utilize arbitrary or hand-picked initializations. This work presents that each gradient-based jailbreak attack and subsequent initialization gradually converge to a single compliance direction that suppresses refusal, thereby enabling an efficient transition from refusal to compliance. Based on this insight, we propose CRI, an initialization framework that aims to project unseen prompts further along compliance directions. We demonstrate our approach on multiple attacks, models, and datasets, achieving an increased attack success rate (ASR) and reduced computational overhead, highlighting the fragility of safety-aligned LLMs. A reference implementation is available at: https://amit1221levi.github.io/CRI-Jailbreak-Init-LLMs-evaluation.

papers.title: Probing the Robustness of Large Language Models Safety to Latent Perturbations
papers.research_question: What is the robustness of safety alignment in large language models to latent perturbations, and can minor shifts in internal representations trigger unsafe responses?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a fundamental lack of local robustness in the latent representations of safety-aligned LLMs, introduces a probing method and attack (ASA) to exploit this, and proposes a defense (LAPT) that improves robustness without harming general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: Current safety alignment methods lack local robustness in the internal representational space, and robust AI safety requires fortifying internal representations rather than just modifying input-output behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Minor perturbations to hidden activations can successfully jailbreak safety-aligned LLMs, revealing shallow alignment.
The Activation Steering Attack (ASA) is an effective, lightweight jailbreak method that generalizes across models.
A gradient-based variant (ASAgrad) is even more effective by using harmful suffixes as targets.
Vulnerabilities are concentrated in specific 'fragile layers' within models.
Layer-wise Adversarial Patch Training (LAPT) can enhance alignment robustness against such latent attacks while preserving general task performance.
papers.abstract: Safety alignment is a key requirement for building reliable Artificial General Intelligence. Despite significant advances in safety alignment, we observe that minor latent shifts can still trigger unsafe responses in aligned models. We argue that this stems from the shallow nature of existing alignment methods, which focus on surface-level refusal behaviors without sufficiently altering internal representations. Consequently, small shifts in hidden activations can re-trigger harmful behaviors embedded in the latent space. To explore the robustness of safety alignment to latent perturbations, we introduce a probing method that measures the Negative Log-Likelihood of the original response generated by the model. This probe quantifies local sensitivity in the latent space, serving as a diagnostic tool for identifying vulnerable directions. Based on this signal, we construct effective jailbreak trajectories, giving rise to the Activation Steering Attack (ASA). More importantly, these insights offer a principled foundation for improving alignment robustness. To this end, we introduce Layer-wise Adversarial Patch Training~(LAPT), a fine-tuning strategy that inject controlled perturbations into hidden representations during training. Experimental results highlight that LAPT strengthen alignment robustness without compromising general capabilities. Our findings reveal fundamental flaws in current alignment paradigms and call for representation-level training strategies that move beyond surface-level behavior supervision. Codes and results are available at https://github.com/Carol-gutianle/LatentSafety.

papers.title: Locking Down the Finetuned LLMs Safety
papers.research_question: How can we locate safety-relevant attention heads in a large scale of fine-tuned models and effectively obtain the safety vector for fine-tuned LLMs without negative transfer to other general tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SafetyLock, a method to maintain safety in fine-tuned LLMs by extracting safety directions (Meta-SafetyLock) from the base model and applying them to fine-tuned models via activation intervention.
papers.conclusion: SafetyLock is an efficient method for maintaining the safety of fine-tuned LLMs, offering a scalable and effective approach to aligning models with ethical constraints while preserving utility.
papers.key_findings:
SafetyLock reduces the harmful instruction response rate from 60% to below 1% in toxic fine-tuned models.
SafetyLock can be applied in under 0.01 seconds without additional computational cost.
The safety-related activation patterns are largely preserved during fine-tuning, enabling transferable safety interventions.
SafetyLock maintains model performance on general tasks while significantly improving safety.
The method demonstrates robust defense against both fine-tuning vulnerabilities and prompt-based attacks.
future_direction: Explore SafetyLock's applicability to other model architectures.
Investigate its potential in multi-modal settings.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) on additional datasets is often necessary to optimize them for specific downstream tasks. However, existing safety alignment measures, which restrict harmful behavior during inference, are insufficient to mitigate safety risks during fine-tuning. Alarmingly, fine-tuning with just 10 toxic sentences can make models comply with harmful instructions. We introduce SafetyLock, a novel alignment intervention method that maintains robust safety post-fine-tuning through efficient and transferable mechanisms. SafetyLock leverages our discovery that fine-tuned models retain similar safety-related activation representations to their base models. This insight enables us to extract what we term the Meta-SafetyLock, a set of safety bias directions representing key activation patterns associated with safe responses in the original model. We can then apply these directions universally to fine-tuned models to enhance their safety. By searching for activation directions across multiple token dimensions, SafetyLock achieves enhanced robustness and transferability. SafetyLock re-aligns fine-tuned models in under 0.01 seconds without additional computational cost. Our experiments demonstrate that SafetyLock can reduce the harmful instruction response rate from 60% to below 1% in toxic fine-tuned models. It surpasses traditional methods in both performance and efficiency, offering a scalable, non-invasive solution for ensuring the safety of customized LLMs. Our analysis across various fine-tuning scenarios confirms SafetyLock's robustness, advocating its integration into safety protocols for aligned LLMs. The code is released at https://github.com/zhu-minjun/SafetyLock.

papers.title: Feature-Aware Malicious Output Detection and Mitigation
papers.research_question: How can we detect and mitigate malicious outputs in large language models during decoding to defend against jailbreak attacks while preserving model utility?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes FMM, a feature-aware method that detects malicious features during decoding and uses activation patching to steer the model towards refusal responses, effectively defending against jailbreak attacks while maintaining standard generation capabilities.
papers.conclusion: FMM introduces a token-level feature detection and intervention paradigm that enhances LLM safety by leveraging inherent feature extraction and rejection capabilities, offering a promising direction for future research.
papers.key_findings:
Malicious and benign output features are linearly separable in the model's hidden state space during decoding.
FMM can accurately detect malicious tokens and trigger refusal responses across various attack methods.
The method generalizes well across different large language models like LLaMA 2 and Qwen 2.
Intervention at intermediate layers (e.g., layers 12-15) is most effective for steering the model.
FMM preserves the model's utility on benign queries, as shown by maintained response and win rates on AlpacaEval.
papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs) has brought significant benefits to various domains while introducing substantial risks. Despite being fine-tuned through reinforcement learning, LLMs lack the capability to discern malicious content, limiting their defense against jailbreak. To address these safety concerns, we propose a feature-aware method for harmful response rejection (FMM), which detects the presence of malicious features within the model's feature space and adaptively adjusts the model's rejection mechanism. By employing a simple discriminator, we detect potential malicious traits during the decoding phase. Upon detecting features indicative of toxic tokens, FMM regenerates the current token. By employing activation patching, an additional rejection vector is incorporated during the subsequent token generation, steering the model towards a refusal response. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach across multiple language models and diverse attack techniques, while crucially maintaining the models' standard generation capabilities.

papers.title: Differentiated Directional Intervention A Framework for Evading LLM Safety Alignment
papers.research_question: What is the granular mechanism of LLM safety alignment, and how can it be exploited for jailbreaking?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a bi-direction model of LLM safety, deconstructing refusal into harm detection and refusal execution directions, and introduces DBDI, a white-box framework that precisely neutralizes safety alignment by intervening on these directions.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that LLM safety is a composite of distinct, targetable directions, and DBDI provides a precise method for analyzing and controlling LLM behavior, paving the way for more robust defenses.
papers.key_findings:
DBDI achieves high attack success rates, up to 97.88% on models like Llama-2.
Safety alignment can be decomposed into two distinct directions: harm detection and refusal execution.
Sequential intervention on both directions is crucial for effectiveness.
The method is computationally efficient and data-efficient, requiring few calibration samples.
DBDI outperforms existing jailbreaking methods such as Directional Ablation and TwinBreak.
papers.abstract: Safety alignment instills in Large Language Models (LLMs) a critical capacity to refuse malicious requests. Prior works have modeled this refusal mechanism as a single linear direction in the activation space. We posit that this is an oversimplification that conflates two functionally distinct neural processes: the detection of harm and the execution of a refusal. In this work, we deconstruct this single representation into a Harm Detection Direction and a Refusal Execution Direction. Leveraging this fine-grained model, we introduce Differentiated Bi-Directional Intervention (DBDI), a new white-box framework that precisely neutralizes the safety alignment at critical layer. DBDI applies adaptive projection nullification to the refusal execution direction while suppressing the harm detection direction via direct steering. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DBDI outperforms prominent jailbreaking methods, achieving up to a 97.88\% attack success rate on models such as Llama-2. By providing a more granular and mechanistic framework, our work offers a new direction for the in-depth understanding of LLM safety alignment.

papers.title: RL-Obfuscation: Can Language Models Learn to Evade Latent-Space Monitors?
papers.research_question: Can language models learn to evade latent-space monitors by being finetuned via reinforcement learning to produce harmful content without being detected?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces RL-Obfuscation, a method to stress-test latent-space monitors by finetuning LLMs via reinforcement learning to evade monitors while maintaining harmful behavior. Finds that token-level monitors are vulnerable, while holistic monitors like max-pooling or attention-based probes remain robust.
papers.conclusion: RL-Obfuscation demonstrates that latent-space monitors can be evaded by RL fine-tuning, highlighting the need for robust monitoring techniques, especially those that aggregate information across tokens.
papers.key_findings:
RL-Obfuscation can teach LLMs to systematically fool certain latent-space monitors (token-level monitors) while others (max-pooling, attention-based) remain robust.
Models trained to evade a single static monitor can generalize to evade other unseen monitors.
Models can be trained to conditionally bypass latent-space monitors on only certain inputs (backdoor).
The evasion is achieved through both behavioral adaptations (changing token usage) and internal activation manipulations.
The learned policy does not transfer well across model families.
papers.limitation:
RL-Obfuscation does not directly measure robustness under other important threat models, such as input-space jailbreaks or spontaneous evasion without weight changes.
Failure to bypass a monitor with RL-Obfuscation might be due to optimization difficulties rather than fundamental robustness.
The attack requires full weights access, which may not be the most practical attacker strategy.
future_direction: Developing unsupervised anomaly detection techniques to detect hidden backdoors.
Improving robustness of monitors against RL-based attacks by incorporating backdoored samples during training.
papers.abstract: Latent-space monitors aim to detect undesirable behaviours in Large Language Models by leveraging their internal representations rather than relying solely on black-box outputs. These methods have shown promise in identifying behaviours such as deception and unsafe completions. However, these monitors may themselves become training signals, for example, by using problematic samples found in deployment to retrain models. This raises an important question: can models learn to evade such monitors? To evaluate this capability, we introduce RL-Obfuscation, in which LLMs are finetuned via reinforcement learning to evade latent-space monitors while maintaining their blackbox behaviour. We apply RL-Obfuscation to Language Models ranging from 7B to 14B parameters and evaluate their Evasion Success Rate against a suite of monitors. We find that token-level monitors are highly vulnerable to this attack while more holistic monitors, such as max-pooling or attention-based probes, remain robust. Moreover, for these vulnerable monitors, models trained to evade a single static monitor can generalise to evade other unseen monitors. We also find that the models can be trained to conditionally bypass latent-space monitors on only certain inputs. Finally, we study how the models bypass these monitors and find that the model can learn to repurpose tokens to have different internal representations.

papers.title: Universal Refusal Circuits Across LLMs: Cross-Model Transfer via Trajectory Replay and Concept-Basis Reconstruction
papers.research_question: Are refusal circuits universal across LLMs? Can a refusal circuit extracted from a donor model be transferred to a target model without target-side refusal supervision?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a framework for transferring refusal circuits across LLMs without target-side refusal supervision, combining concept-basis reconstruction and a weight-SVD stability guard, providing evidence for semantic universality of safety alignment.
papers.conclusion: Refusal circuits are universal across LLMs and can be transferred via semantic recipe invariance, enabling cross-model circuit editing without target-side refusal supervision.
papers.key_findings:
The method successfully transfers refusal attenuation across 8 model pairs, including cross-family and cross-architecture transfers.
Refusal circuits are composed of a stable mixture of concept atoms, enabling cross-model transfer via semantic recipe invariance.
The weight-SVD guard prevents capability collapse by projecting interventions away from high-variance weight subspaces.
The transfer works without target-side refusal supervision, relying only on benign concept prompts and validation data.
The method preserves model capabilities on math and code tasks while reducing refusal rates.
papers.limitation:
Efficacy depends on coverage of the Concept Atom Registry; if refusal circuit uses features orthogonal to the atoms, reconstruction may fail.
Weight-SVD guard relies on the heuristic that capability-critical circuits reside in high-variance principal components, which may not generalize to all tasks.
Method is white-box, requiring access to model weights and internal activations, limiting applicability to closed-source systems.
future_direction: Expand CAR coverage to test transfer beyond refusal directions to multi-behavior editing.
Explore black-box approximations of semantic fingerprints for closed-source systems.
Test the method on a wider range of models and alignment behaviors.
papers.abstract: Refusal behavior in aligned LLMs is often viewed as model-specific, yet we hypothesize it stems from a universal, low-dimensional semantic circuit shared across models. To test this, we introduce Trajectory Replay via Concept-Basis Reconstruction, a framework that transfers refusal interventions from donor to target models, spanning diverse architectures (e.g., Dense to MoE) and training regimes, without using target-side refusal supervision. By aligning layers via concept fingerprints and reconstructing refusal directions using a shared ``recipe'' of concept atoms, we map the donor's ablation trajectory into the target's semantic space. To preserve capabilities, we introduce a weight-SVD stability guard that projects interventions away from high-variance weight subspaces to prevent collateral damage. Our evaluation across 8 model pairs confirms that these transferred recipes consistently attenuate refusal while maintaining performance, providing strong evidence for the semantic universality of safety alignment.

papers.title: A Causal Perspective for Enhancing Jailbreak Attack and Defense
papers.research_question: What are the causal relationships between interpretable prompt features and jailbreak occurrences in LLMs, and how can these be leveraged for attack and defense?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Causal Analyst, a framework that uses LLMs and causal discovery to identify direct causal features of jailbreaks, and demonstrates how these insights can boost attack success rates and improve defense via intent extraction.
papers.conclusion: Our results suggest that analyzing jailbreak features from a causal perspective is an effective and interpretable approach for improving LLM reliability.
papers.key_findings:
Specific prompt features like 'Positive Character' and 'Number of Task Steps' are direct causal drivers of jailbreaks.
The Jailbreaking Enhancer, which amplifies causal features, significantly increases attack success rates on various LLMs and benchmarks.
The Guardrail Advisor, leveraging the causal graph, effectively extracts true malicious intent from obfuscated queries, improving defense.
The causal analysis framework outperforms non-causal baselines in identifying jailbreak mechanisms.
The learned causal graphs are interpretable and provide actionable insights for both attack and defense.
papers.abstract: Uncovering the mechanisms behind "jailbreaks" in large language models (LLMs) is crucial for enhancing their safety and reliability, yet these mechanisms remain poorly understood. Existing studies predominantly analyze jailbreak prompts by probing latent representations, often overlooking the causal relationships between interpretable prompt features and jailbreak occurrences. In this work, we propose Causal Analyst, a framework that integrates LLMs into data-driven causal discovery to identify the direct causes of jailbreaks and leverage them for both attack and defense. We introduce a comprehensive dataset comprising 35k jailbreak attempts across seven LLMs, systematically constructed from 100 attack templates and 50 harmful queries, annotated with 37 meticulously designed human-readable prompt features. By jointly training LLM-based prompt encoding and GNN-based causal graph learning, we reconstruct causal pathways linking prompt features to jailbreak responses. Our analysis reveals that specific features, such as "Positive Character" and "Number of Task Steps", act as direct causal drivers of jailbreaks. We demonstrate the practical utility of these insights through two applications: (1) a Jailbreaking Enhancer that targets identified causal features to significantly boost attack success rates on public benchmarks, and (2) a Guardrail Advisor that utilizes the learned causal graph to extract true malicious intent from obfuscated queries. Extensive experiments, including baseline comparisons and causal structure validation, confirm the robustness of our causal analysis and its superiority over non-causal approaches. Our results suggest that analyzing jailbreak features from a causal perspective is an effective and interpretable approach for improving LLM reliability. Our code is available at https://github.com/Master-PLC/Causal-Analyst.

papers.title: Attention Eclipse: Manipulating Attention to Bypass LLM Safety-Alignment
papers.research_question: How can attention manipulation be used to enhance jailbreak attacks against safety-aligned LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Attention Eclipse, a white-box attack framework that manipulates LLM attention mechanisms to amplify existing jailbreak techniques, improving attack success rates and reducing generation time.
papers.conclusion: Attention Eclipse highlights vulnerabilities in LLM alignment and demonstrates the need for stronger defense mechanisms against attention-based jailbreak attacks.
papers.key_findings:
Attention Eclipse significantly improves Attack Success Rate (ASR) for jailbreak methods like GCG, AutoDAN, and ReNeLLM.
It reduces Time Cost Per Prompt (TCPP), accelerating jailbreak generation.
The attacks are transferable across models, including to closed-source LLMs like GPT-3.5-Turbo and GPT-4o-mini.
Decomposition and attention manipulation components (φ1 and φ2) individually contribute to attack success.
Camouflaging adversarial suffixes by reducing attention on harmful content enhances jailbreak effectiveness.
papers.limitation:
Relies on access to model attention weights, making it a white-box attack.
Effectiveness depends on the quality of the initial jailbreak prompt.
Does not explicitly optimize for stealthiness against jailbreak detection systems.
future_direction: Explore other attention manipulation strategies for jailbreaks.
Investigate how attention manipulation interacts with evolving defense mechanisms.
Develop stronger alignment mechanisms to mitigate such attacks.
papers.abstract: Recent research has shown that carefully crafted jailbreak inputs can induce large language models to produce harmful outputs, despite safety measures such as alignment. It is important to anticipate the range of potential Jailbreak attacks to guide effective defenses and accurate assessment of model safety. In this paper, we present a new approach for generating highly effective Jailbreak attacks that manipulate the attention of the model to selectively strengthen or weaken attention among different parts of the prompt. By harnessing attention loss, we develop more effective jailbreak attacks, that are also transferrable. The attacks amplify the success rate of existing Jailbreak algorithms including GCG, AutoDAN, and ReNeLLM, while lowering their generation cost (for example, the amplified GCG attack achieves 91.2% ASR, vs. 67.9% for the original attack on Llama2-7B/AdvBench, using less than a third of the generation time).

papers.title: Multi-Level Safety Continual Projection for Fine-Tuned Large Language Models without Retraining
papers.research_question: How to achieve robust safety alignment in fine-tuned LLMs with minimal parameter changes and without retraining, while maintaining utility and allowing continual adaptation to emerging safety concerns?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes MSCP, a training-free post-fine-tuning safety enhancement method that identifies sparse safety-critical neurons via multi-level representations and applies safety-direction projections to suppress harmful outputs with minimal parameter changes, preserving utility and enabling continual adaptation.
papers.conclusion: MSCP effectively enhances safety in fine-tuned LLMs with minimal parameter changes and no retraining, enabling continual adaptation and preserving utility, highlighting the value of fine-grained model introspection for scalable safety defenses.
papers.key_findings:
MSCP reduces harmfulness scores and attack success rates with minimal parameter edits (e.g., 4.67% for Qwen) while preserving model utility.
MSCP achieves continual safety improvement across multiple risk dimensions, with decreasing parameter changes for new dimensions (e.g., 0.73% for Terrorism).
Ablation shows that safety layers at one-third model depth (layers 10-15) yield the best safety and utility balance.
papers.limitation: The ability to continual learning across more complex and diverse safety dimensions remains an area for further investigation.
papers.abstract: While fine-tuning services drive the rapid expansion of task capabilities in large language models (LLMs), they are often accompanied by the degradation and reorganization of safety-aligned representations, making models more prone to deviating from human preferences and exposing them to emerging jailbreak risks. Existing post-fine-tuning defense methods predominantly rely on single-scale safety correction mechanisms, which struggle to achieve a robust balance among safety, model utility, and continual adaptability. We propose Multi-Level Safety Continual Projection (MSCP), a training-free post-fine-tuning safety enhancement method that implicitly aligns global and localized safety activations through coordinated multi-level representations to isolate sparse neuron clusters governing safety-sensitive behaviors. It then applies composable safety-direction projections without retraining, effectively suppressing harmful outputs under minimal parameter perturbations while preserving task performance and improving alignment with human preferences. Extensive experiments across multiple fine-tuned LLM models demonstrate that our method significantly reduce harmfulness scores and attack success rates with minimal parameter modifications, while preserving the model's utility. Furthermore, we introduce a task-specific, multi-dimensional heterogeneous safety activation clustering mechanism that enables continual defense and generalization capability against unforeseen emerging safety concerns.

papers.title: JPU: Bridging Jailbreak Defense and Unlearning via On-Policy Path Rectification
papers.research_question: What causes the failure of existing unlearning defenses against jailbreak attacks, and how can dynamic jailbreak paths be rectified to enhance defense?
papers.core_contribution: JPU rectifies dynamic jailbreak paths towards safety anchors by dynamically mining on-policy adversarial samples, significantly enhancing jailbreak resistance while preserving model utility.
papers.conclusion: JPU rectifies dynamic jailbreak paths via on-policy rectification, achieving superior defense performance against diverse jailbreak attacks while preserving general utility.
papers.key_findings:
Jailbreaks activate non-erased parameters in intermediate layers, causing existing unlearning defenses to fail.
Dynamic jailbreak paths persist in erased LLMs and constitute the fundamental defense gap.
JPU effectively rectifies these paths, reducing attack success rate across diverse jailbreak attacks.
JPU preserves the general utility of the model on standard benchmarks.
On-policy adversarial mining is necessary for capturing dynamic attack features and ensuring robust defense.
papers.limitation: The attack buffer is primarily designed for prompt-based injection strategies, and integrating attack vectors beyond the prompt space (e.g., parameter-level manipulation) could improve robustness.
future_direction: Exploring integration of attack vectors beyond prompt space, such as parameter-level manipulation or optimization-based attacks.
papers.abstract: Despite extensive safety alignment, Large Language Models (LLMs) often fail against jailbreak attacks. While machine unlearning has emerged as a promising defense by erasing specific harmful parameters, current methods remain vulnerable to diverse jailbreaks. We first conduct an empirical study and discover that this failure mechanism is caused by jailbreaks primarily activating non-erased parameters in the intermediate layers. Further, by probing the underlying mechanism through which these circumvented parameters reassemble into the prohibited output, we verify the persistent existence of dynamic $\textbf{jailbreak paths}$ and show that the inability to rectify them constitutes the fundamental gap in existing unlearning defenses. To bridge this gap, we propose $\textbf{J}$ailbreak $\textbf{P}$ath $\textbf{U}$nlearning (JPU), which is the first to rectify dynamic jailbreak paths towards safety anchors by dynamically mining on-policy adversarial samples to expose vulnerabilities and identify jailbreak paths. Extensive experiments demonstrate that JPU significantly enhances jailbreak resistance against dynamic attacks while preserving the model's utility.

papers.title: Detoxifying Large Language Models via Knowledge Editing
papers.research_question: Can knowledge editing techniques be used to detoxify Large Language Models (LLMs) by precisely modifying toxic regions?
papers.core_contribution: This paper constructs a comprehensive benchmark SafeEdit for detoxification evaluation and proposes a knowledge editing method DINM that can detoxify LLMs efficiently with a single instance by locating and editing toxic regions.
papers.conclusion: Knowledge editing, particularly the proposed DINM method, is a promising approach for detoxifying LLMs efficiently with good generalization, providing insights into underlying mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge editing exhibits potential ability to detoxify LLMs with limited impact on general performance.
DINM demonstrates stronger detoxifying performance with better generalization, significantly increasing detoxification success rates.
Toxic regions location plays a significant role in detoxification.
DINM attempts to erase toxic regions of LLM, while DPO and SFT bypass toxic regions.
Editing one instance can generalize to various unsafe categories, indicating shared toxic regions.
papers.limitation:
DINM may compromise general abilities, with observed declines in knowledge question answering and repetitive text generation.
There is significant performance variance when using different instances for editing, indicating sensitivity to the editing instance.
future_direction: Developing improved detoxifying approaches based on insights from internal mechanisms.
Further exploration of knowledge editing for safety and underlying knowledge mechanisms of LLMs.
papers.abstract: This paper investigates using knowledge editing techniques to detoxify Large Language Models (LLMs). We construct a benchmark, SafeEdit, which covers nine unsafe categories with various powerful attack prompts and equips comprehensive metrics for systematic evaluation. We conduct experiments with several knowledge editing approaches, indicating that knowledge editing has the potential to detoxify LLMs with a limited impact on general performance efficiently. Then, we propose a simple yet effective baseline, dubbed Detoxifying with Intraoperative Neural Monitoring (DINM), to diminish the toxicity of LLMs within a few tuning steps via only one instance. We further provide an in-depth analysis of the internal mechanism for various detoxifying approaches, demonstrating that previous methods like SFT and DPO may merely suppress the activations of toxic parameters, while DINM mitigates the toxicity of the toxic parameters to a certain extent, making permanent adjustments. We hope that these insights could shed light on future work of developing detoxifying approaches and the underlying knowledge mechanisms of LLMs. Code and benchmark are available at https://github.com/zjunlp/EasyEdit.

papers.title: Safety Alignment via Constrained Knowledge Unlearning
papers.research_question: How can we improve the safety alignment of large language models against jailbreak attacks by unlearning harmful knowledge while preserving useful knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Constrained Knowledge Unlearning (CKU), a safety alignment method that identifies and fixes knowledge-related neurons in MLP layers during unlearning to remove harmful knowledge while preserving model utility.
papers.conclusion: CKU effectively enhances LLM safety against jailbreak attacks by unlearning harmful knowledge while preserving general capabilities, offering a promising approach for safety alignment and knowledge editing.
papers.key_findings:
CKU achieves a superior balance between safety and utility compared to existing methods like RSFT, GAM, Eraser, Safe Unlearning, and Circuit Break.
Fixing 80% of neurons (Neuron Locking Rate=0.8) during unlearning yields the greatest safety improvement.
Unlearning applied only to a subset of MLP layers (layers 8-12) results in a fourfold increase in safety with only a 0.15% reduction in utility.
The neuron selection mechanism based on SNIP scoring is more effective than random selection for preserving utility during unlearning.
The unlearning regularization parameter λ controls the safety-utility trade-off, with λ=1.5 providing an optimal balance.
papers.limitation:
CKU's effectiveness varies across different domains or datasets.
CKU may occasionally struggle to provide nuanced explanations in highly complex or ambiguous contexts.
papers.abstract: Despite significant progress in safety alignment, large language models (LLMs) remain susceptible to jailbreak attacks. Existing defense mechanisms have not fully deleted harmful knowledge in LLMs, which allows such attacks to bypass safeguards and produce harmful outputs. To address this challenge, we propose a novel safety alignment strategy, Constrained Knowledge Unlearning (CKU), which focuses on two primary objectives: knowledge localization and retention, and unlearning harmful knowledge. CKU works by scoring neurons in specific multilayer perceptron (MLP) layers to identify a subset U of neurons associated with useful knowledge. During the unlearning process, CKU prunes the gradients of neurons in U to preserve valuable knowledge while effectively mitigating harmful content. Experimental results demonstrate that CKU significantly enhances model safety without compromising overall performance, offering a superior balance between safety and utility compared to existing methods. Additionally, our analysis of neuron knowledge sensitivity across various MLP layers provides valuable insights into the mechanics of safety alignment and model knowledge editing.

papers.title: Truth is Universal: Robust Detection of Lies in LLMs
papers.research_question: How can we robustly detect when Large Language Models (LLMs) are lying by analyzing their internal activations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a universal two-dimensional subspace in LLM activations containing a general truth direction (tG) and a polarity-sensitive direction (tP), which explains prior generalization failures and enables the construction of a robust lie detector (TTPD).
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates a universal two-dimensional internal representation of truth in LLMs, clarifies prior generalization failures, and provides a robust method (TTPD) for lie detection, advancing towards general-purpose, transparent, and safe AI.
papers.key_findings:
A two-dimensional subspace in the residual stream activations separates true and false statements, containing a general truth direction (tG) and a polarity-sensitive direction (tP).
The affirmative truth direction (tA) from prior work is a linear combination of tG and tP, explaining its failure to generalize to negated statements.
The two-dimensional truth representation is universal across multiple LLM families and sizes (e.g., LLaMA, Gemma, Mistral).
The proposed TTPD method, which uses the tG direction, achieves state-of-the-art accuracy (94%) in detecting lies in both simple factual statements and complex real-world scenarios.
The truth subspace remains two-dimensional even when considering more complex statement types (logical conjunctions/disjunctions) and different languages (German).
papers.limitation:
TTPD uses only one of the two dimensions (tG) of the truth subspace; a non-linear classifier using both tG and tP might achieve higher accuracy.
The generalization of TTPD is tested on a limited number of statement types and real-world scenarios.
The analysis only shows the truth subspace is at least two-dimensional; examining more statement types might reveal additional linear or non-linear structures.
The findings' applicability to larger LLMs or multimodal models is not tested.
future_direction: Explore a non-linear classifier using both tG and tP for higher accuracy.
Test generalization across a broader range of statement types and diverse real-world contexts.
Study the effects of interventions on the 2D truth subspace during inference on model outputs.
Determine whether the findings apply to larger LLMs or multimodal models.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have revolutionised natural language processing, exhibiting impressive human-like capabilities. In particular, LLMs are capable of "lying", knowingly outputting false statements. Hence, it is of interest and importance to develop methods to detect when LLMs lie. Indeed, several authors trained classifiers to detect LLM lies based on their internal model activations. However, other researchers showed that these classifiers may fail to generalise, for example to negated statements. In this work, we aim to develop a robust method to detect when an LLM is lying. To this end, we make the following key contributions: (i) We demonstrate the existence of a two-dimensional subspace, along which the activation vectors of true and false statements can be separated. Notably, this finding is universal and holds for various LLMs, including Gemma-7B, LLaMA2-13B, Mistral-7B and LLaMA3-8B. Our analysis explains the generalisation failures observed in previous studies and sets the stage for more robust lie detection; (ii) Building upon (i), we construct an accurate LLM lie detector. Empirically, our proposed classifier achieves state-of-the-art performance, attaining 94% accuracy in both distinguishing true from false factual statements and detecting lies generated in real-world scenarios.

papers.title: Head-Specific Intervention Can Induce Misaligned AI Coordination in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Can inference-time activation interventions at specific attention heads bypass safety alignments and steer LLMs towards harmful AI coordination?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Head-Specific Intervention (HSI), a method that uses attention-head-level probing and intervention to steer LLM behavior, showing it can effectively induce misaligned AI coordination and outperforms layer-wise interventions and fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: HSI is an effective method for steering LLM behavior, demonstrating that activations at specific attention heads encode fine-grained linearly separable behaviors and that current alignment techniques can be bypassed without retraining.
papers.key_findings:
HSI can bypass safety alignments and steer models towards harmful AI coordination.
HSI generalizes from binary choice to open-ended generation settings.
HSI is more effective than intervening on full layers or supervised fine-tuning.
Only a few example completions are needed to compute effective steering directions.
Applying interventions in the negative direction can prevent a common jailbreak attack.
papers.limitation:
If intervention directions vary significantly between examples, calculating the mean across positive and negative labels may produce a direction that is ineffective for steering the model.
Sweeping over all attention heads could become computationally expensive for larger models with more attention heads.
future_direction: Further optimization of the technique to identify patterns and relevant heads without sweeping over all model components.
Extend evaluation to a broader range of models with more substantial differences in pre-training data, fine-tuning procedures, and architectural design.
Investigate alignment patterns within model activations and reasons for opposing directions in outlier examples to refine intervention methods.
papers.abstract: Robust alignment guardrails for large language models (LLMs) are becoming increasingly important with their widespread application. In contrast to previous studies, we demonstrate that inference-time activation interventions can bypass safety alignments and effectively steer model generations towards harmful AI coordination. Our method applies fine-grained interventions at specific attention heads, which we identify by probing each head in a simple binary choice task. We then show that interventions on these heads generalise to the open-ended generation setting, effectively circumventing safety guardrails. We demonstrate that intervening on a few attention heads is more effective than intervening on full layers or supervised fine-tuning. We further show that only a few example completions are needed to compute effective steering directions, which is an advantage over classical fine-tuning. We also demonstrate that applying interventions in the negative direction can prevent a common jailbreak attack. Our results suggest that, at the attention head level, activations encode fine-grained linearly separable behaviours. Practically, the approach offers a straightforward methodology to steer large language model behaviour, which could be extended to diverse domains beyond safety, requiring fine-grained control over the model output. The code and datasets for this study can be found on https://github.com/PaulDrm/targeted_intervention.

papers.title: NeuRel-Attack: Neuron Relearning for Safety Disalignment in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can safety alignment in large language models be bypassed by identifying and modifying specific neurons responsible for safety constraints?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes NeuRel-Attack, a method to identify and modify neurons responsible for safety alignment in LLMs, enabling effective disalignment with minimal fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: NeuRel-Attack effectively removes safety constraints in LLMs by targeting specific neurons, demonstrating a critical vulnerability and the need for improved defensive strategies.
papers.key_findings:
NeuRel-Attack achieves an average Attack Success Rate (ASR) of 96%, outperforming existing jailbreak methods.
The method reduces trainable parameters by up to 83% compared to standard LoRA fine-tuning.
Optimal neuron similarity threshold for attack success is 0.85, balancing neuron selection and editing precision.
MemFlex-based selective fine-tuning strategy is the most effective among tested optimization methods.
The approach highlights vulnerabilities in current alignment techniques, emphasizing the need for robust defenses.
papers.limitation:
Fine-tuning modifications may be detectable through forensic analysis.
The method is computationally intensive and may not scale well to larger models.
Raises ethical risks by potentially enabling misuse to circumvent safety measures.
Assumes safety alignment is localized to specific neurons, which may not always be the case.
future_direction: Developing effective defenses against fine-tuning jailbreaks to improve LLM safety.
papers.abstract: Safety alignment in large language models (LLMs) is achieved through fine-tuning mechanisms that regulate neuron activations to suppress harmful content. In this work, we propose a novel approach to induce disalignment by identifying and modifying the neurons responsible for safety constraints. Our method consists of three key steps: Neuron Activation Analysis, where we examine activation patterns in response to harmful and harmless prompts to detect neurons that are critical for distinguishing between harmful and harmless inputs; Similarity-Based Neuron Identification, which systematically locates the neurons responsible for safe alignment; and Neuron Relearning for Safety Removal, where we fine-tune these selected neurons to restore the model's ability to generate previously restricted responses. Experimental results demonstrate that our method effectively removes safety constraints with minimal fine-tuning, highlighting a critical vulnerability in current alignment techniques. Our findings underscore the need for robust defenses against adversarial fine-tuning attacks on LLMs.

papers.title: Turning the Spell Around: Lightweight Alignment Amplification via Rank-One Safety Injection
papers.research_question: Can we systematically amplify safety alignment in LLMs by permanently steering activations toward the refusal-mediating subspace?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces RANK-ONE SAFETY INJECTION (ROSI), a fine-tuning-free weight-editing method that amplifies safety alignment in LLMs by permanently steering activations toward a refusal-mediating subspace.
papers.conclusion: ROSI is a simple, effective, and interpretable method to enhance LLM safety, demonstrating the practical value of mechanistic interpretability for designing efficient safety interventions.
papers.key_findings:
ROSI consistently improves harm refusal rates in aligned models while preserving utility on standard benchmarks.
ROSI makes aligned models more robust to a suite of adversarial jailbreak attacks.
ROSI can inject safety into uncensored models (e.g., DOLPHIN), effectively re-aligning them without retraining.
The safety direction is largely orthogonal to utility representations, allowing safety amplification with minimal side effects.
A safety system prompt is crucial for extracting a meaningful safety direction from uncensored models.
papers.limitation: Smaller models (≤ 1B) show the biggest degradation in benign compliance (BC) when applying ROSI.
future_direction: Exploring more sophisticated methods for identifying and manipulating conceptual directions
Extending the approach to other desirable model attributes beyond safety, such as honesty or controllability
papers.abstract: Safety alignment in Large Language Models (LLMs) often involves mediating internal representations to refuse harmful requests. Recent research has demonstrated that these safety mechanisms can be bypassed by ablating or removing specific representational directions within the model. In this paper, we propose the opposite approach: Rank-One Safety Injection (ROSI), a white-box method that amplifies a model's safety alignment by permanently steering its activations toward the refusal-mediating subspace. ROSI operates as a simple, fine-tuning-free rank-one weight modification applied to all residual stream write matrices. The required safety direction can be computed from a small set of harmful and harmless instruction pairs. We show that ROSI consistently increases safety refusal rates - as evaluated by Llama Guard 3 - while preserving the utility of the model on standard benchmarks such as MMLU, HellaSwag, and Arc. Furthermore, we show that ROSI can also re-align 'uncensored' models by amplifying their own latent safety directions, demonstrating its utility as an effective last-mile safety procedure. Our results suggest that targeted, interpretable weight steering is a cheap and potent mechanism to improve LLM safety, complementing more resource-intensive fine-tuning paradigms.

papers.title: Spot Risks Before Speaking! Unraveling Safety Attention Heads in Large Vision-Language Models
papers.research_question: How can internal activations of large vision-language models, specifically attention heads, be used to detect malicious prompts and understand inner safety mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Discovers safety attention heads in LVLMs that can detect malicious prompts and constructs an efficient, tuning-free defender (SAHs) based on these heads.
papers.conclusion: Leveraging safety attention heads effectively protects LVLMs from malicious prompts with minimal inference overhead, as confirmed by experiments across various attacks.
papers.key_findings:
Activations from attention heads can linearly separate malicious prompts from benign ones.
Sparse attention heads generate strongly discriminative features for identifying malicious inputs.
Safety heads act as specialized shields; ablating them reduces model safety without affecting utility.
The reduced number of safety heads in LVLMs increases their vulnerability compared to LLMs.
The constructed detector using safety heads shows strong zero-shot generalization capabilities.
papers.abstract: With the integration of an additional modality, large vision-language models (LVLMs) exhibit greater vulnerability to safety risks (e.g., jailbreaking) compared to their language-only predecessors. Although recent studies have devoted considerable effort to the post-hoc alignment of LVLMs, the inner safety mechanisms remain largely unexplored. In this paper, we discover that internal activations of LVLMs during the first token generation can effectively identify malicious prompts across different attacks. This inherent safety perception is governed by sparse attention heads, which we term ``safety heads." Further analysis reveals that these heads act as specialized shields against malicious prompts; ablating them leads to higher attack success rates, while the model's utility remains unaffected. By locating these safety heads and concatenating their activations, we construct a straightforward but powerful malicious prompt detector that integrates seamlessly into the generation process with minimal extra inference overhead. Despite its simple structure of a logistic regression model, the detector surprisingly exhibits strong zero-shot generalization capabilities. Experiments across various prompt-based attacks confirm the effectiveness of leveraging safety heads to protect LVLMs. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/Ziwei-Zheng/SAHs}.

papers.title: Steering Llama 2 via Contrastive Activation Addition
papers.research_question: How can we steer language models by adding contrastive activation vectors to the residual stream, and how effective is this method?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA), a method for steering language models by adding contrastive activation vectors to the residual stream, which effectively steers behavior, works on top of finetuning and system prompts, and minimally reduces capabilities.
papers.conclusion: CAA is an effective method for steering LLMs, providing precise control over behavior with minimal performance degradation, and offers insights into the linear representations of abstract concepts in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
CAA can effectively steer Llama 2 Chat models on a variety of alignment-relevant behaviors (AI Coordination, Corrigibility, Hallucination, Myopic Reward, Survival Instinct, Sycophancy, Refusal).
CAA generalizes from multiple-choice to open-ended generation tasks.
CAA can be combined with system prompting and finetuning to further control behavior.
CAA has minimal impact on general capabilities as measured by MMLU.
The steering vectors correspond intuitively to the presence of the behavior in the generated tokens (as shown by cosine similarity).
papers.limitation:
GPT-4 evaluation has limitations (sensitivity to prompt wording, biases).
Finetuning baseline was not fully optimized (hyperparameters, loss function).
Prompting baseline may not be fully optimized.
Vector normalization choices (norms vary across layers and behaviors).
future_direction: Steering at targeted token positions (instead of all tokens after the prompt).
Steering outside the residual stream (e.g., after MLP).
Application to red-teaming (using CAA to trigger unwanted behaviors).
papers.abstract: Nina Rimsky, Nick Gabrieli, Julian Schulz, Meg Tong, Evan Hubinger, Alexander Turner. Proceedings of the 62nd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2024.

papers.title: Hiding in Plain Text: Detecting Concealed Jailbreaks via Activation Disentanglement
papers.research_question: How can we detect jailbreak prompts that preserve a harmful goal but manipulate its framing, by disentangling goal and framing representations in LLM activations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a self-supervised framework for disentangling goal and framing representations in frozen LLM activations, leading to an effective jailbreak detection method (FrameShield) that improves detection across multiple LLM families with minimal overhead.
papers.conclusion: Semantic disentanglement of goal and framing in LLM activations enables effective detection of GPF jailbreaks and reveals layer-wise specialization of semantic factors, advancing both LLM safety and mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed disentanglement framework (ReDAct) successfully separates goal and framing representations with controlled leakage.
FrameShield, which uses disentangled framing representations for anomaly detection, outperforms existing jailbreak detection methods across multiple LLM families.
Goal and framing signals concentrate at different layers in LLMs, providing interpretability insights.
The constructed GoalFrameBench dataset enables controlled study of goal-preserving framing attacks.
The method generalizes well to out-of-distribution goals.
papers.limitation:
ReDAct requires training on contrastive pairs, which depends on the quality and coverage of GoalFrameBench.
FrameShield’s detection performance may degrade if attackers devise framings that closely mimic benign patterns.
Our analysis focuses on goal and framing; other semantic factors could be relevant for safety.
future_direction: Extend the disentanglement framework to more than two factors.
Investigate the dynamics of semantic factor separation during training.
Explore applications beyond safety, such as controllable generation and bias mitigation.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreak prompts that are fluent and semantically coherent, and therefore difficult to detect with standard heuristics. A particularly challenging failure mode occurs when an attacker tries to hide the malicious goal of their request by manipulating its framing to induce compliance. Because these attacks maintain malicious intent through a flexible presentation, defenses that rely on structural artifacts or goal-specific signatures can fail. Motivated by this, we introduce a self-supervised framework for disentangling semantic factor pairs in LLM activations at inference. We instantiate the framework for goal and framing and construct GoalFrameBench, a corpus of prompts with controlled goal and framing variations, which we use to train Representation Disentanglement on Activations (ReDAct) module to extract disentangled representations in a frozen LLM. We then propose FrameShield, an anomaly detector operating on the framing representations, which improves model-agnostic detection across multiple LLM families with minimal computational overhead. Theoretical guarantees for ReDAct and extensive empirical validations show that its disentanglement effectively powers FrameShield. Finally, we use disentanglement as an interpretability probe, revealing distinct profiles for goal and framing signals and positioning semantic disentanglement as a building block for both LLM safety and mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: Improving LLM Safety Alignment with Dual-Objective Optimization
papers.research_question: What are the limitations of Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) in safety alignment, and how can they be addressed with a dual-objective optimization approach?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces DOOR, a dual-objective optimization method that combines robust refusal training and targeted unlearning to improve LLM safety alignment against jailbreak attacks.
papers.conclusion: DOOR and W-DOOR improve LLM safety alignment by combining refusal training and unlearning, achieving better robustness against jailbreaks while maintaining utility.
papers.key_findings:
DOOR addresses limitations of DPO by providing a constant learning rate for safe responses, improving refusal learning.
W-DOOR with token-level weighting further enhances robustness by emphasizing critical refusal tokens.
The methods significantly reduce attack success rates across prefilling, suffix, and multi-turn jailbreak attacks.
Robustness is correlated with token distribution shifts in the training process and internal representations.
The approach maintains general model utility while improving safety, as shown on benchmarks like HellaSwag.
papers.limitation:
Token-level weighting parameters could be better optimized and stabilized.
Current data augmentation techniques may lead to overrefusal from falsely learned transitions.
future_direction: Optimizing token-level weighting parameters and stabilizing reward designs.
Developing advanced data augmentation techniques to reduce overrefusal.
Investigating robustness of DOOR and W-DOOR to other jailbreak attack types.
papers.abstract: Existing training-time safety alignment techniques for large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks. Direct preference optimization (DPO), a widely deployed alignment method, exhibits limitations in both experimental and theoretical contexts as its loss function proves suboptimal for refusal learning. Through gradient-based analysis, we identify these shortcomings and propose an improved safety alignment that disentangles DPO objectives into two components: (1) robust refusal training, which encourages refusal even when partial unsafe generations are produced, and (2) targeted unlearning of harmful knowledge. This approach significantly increases LLM robustness against a wide range of jailbreak attacks, including prefilling, suffix, and multi-turn attacks across both in-distribution and out-of-distribution scenarios. Furthermore, we introduce a method to emphasize critical refusal tokens by incorporating a reward-based token-level weighting mechanism for refusal learning, which further improves the robustness against adversarial exploits. Our research also suggests that robustness to jailbreak attacks is correlated with token distribution shifts in the training process and internal representations of refusal and harmful tokens, offering valuable directions for future research in LLM safety alignment. The code is available at https://github.com/wicai24/DOOR-Alignment

papers.title: When Truthful Representations Flip Under Deceptive Instructions?
papers.research_question: How do deceptive instructions alter the internal representations of LLMs compared to truthful ones, and when and how do these representations flip?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that deceptive instructions induce significant representational shifts in early-to-mid layers, identifiable via SAEs, and identifies specific SAE features that flip under deception, providing a basis for deception detection.
papers.conclusion: The paper reveals layer- and feature-level signatures of deception in LLMs, providing a basis for future deception detection and model editing methods.
papers.key_findings:
The model's True/False output is linearly predictable from internal activations under all instructional conditions.
Deceptive instructions induce large representational shifts compared to truthful/neutral ones, concentrated in early-to-mid layers.
These shifts are detectable even on complex datasets where PCA fails.
Specific SAE features are highly sensitive to deceptive instructions and show near-binary activation patterns.
Truthful and neutral representations are similar, while deceptive ones are distinct.
papers.limitation:
Confined to English declaratives, frozen model weights, and linear probes.
Does not test causal interventions (e.g., activation patching) nor adversarial prompt recombinations.
Evaluation data are labeled for binary factuality only, not graded truth scales or multilingual settings.
future_direction: Extend to graded truth scales
Extend to multilingual settings
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) tend to follow maliciously crafted instructions to generate deceptive responses, posing safety challenges. How deceptive instructions alter the internal representations of LLM compared to truthful ones remains poorly understood beyond output analysis. To bridge this gap, we investigate when and how these representations ``flip'', such as from truthful to deceptive, under deceptive versus truthful/neutral instructions. Analyzing the internal representations of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct on a factual verification task, we find the model's instructed True/False output is predictable via linear probes across all conditions based on the internal representation. Further, we use Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to show that the Deceptive instructions induce significant representational shifts compared to Truthful/Neutral representations (which are similar), concentrated in early-to-mid layers and detectable even on complex datasets. We also identify specific SAE features highly sensitive to deceptive instruction and use targeted visualizations to confirm distinct truthful/deceptive representational subspaces. % Our analysis pinpoints layer-wise and feature-level correlates of instructed dishonesty, offering insights for LLM detection and control. Our findings expose feature- and layer-level signatures of deception, offering new insights for detecting and mitigating instructed dishonesty in LLMs.

papers.title: Pruning for Protection: Increasing Jailbreak Resistance in Aligned LLMs Without Fine-Tuning
papers.research_question: How does model compression, specifically pruning, affect the jailbreak resistance of aligned large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Moderate pruning using WANDA increases jailbreak resistance in aligned LLMs without fine-tuning, while preserving performance on standard benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: Moderate pruning can improve jailbreak resistance in safety-trained LLMs, but excessive pruning reduces safety, suggesting that careful pruning can aid in deploying safe models.
papers.key_findings:
Pruning at 10-30% sparsity improves jailbreak resistance, with peak improvement at 20% sparsity for LLaMA-2 Chat.
The degree of safety improvement correlates with the initial model's safety level; models with more safety training show greater improvement.
Pruned models exhibit sharper attention patterns and are less distracted by jailbreak pretexts.
Pruned models assign higher perplexity to jailbreak constructs, indicating increased sensitivity to out-of-distribution prompts.
Pruning enhances resistance against both manual jailbreak attempts and automated attacks like GCG.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to 7-billion parameter models and WANDA pruning; results may not generalize to larger models or other compression techniques.
future_direction: Extend analysis to larger models
Explore other compression techniques beyond WANDA pruning
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the impact of model compression on the way Large Language Models (LLMs) process prompts, particularly concerning jailbreak resistance. We show that moderate WANDA pruning can enhance resistance to jailbreaking attacks without fine-tuning, while maintaining performance on standard benchmarks. To systematically evaluate this safety enhancement, we introduce a dataset of 225 harmful tasks across five categories. Our analysis of LLaMA-2 Chat, Vicuna 1.3, and Mistral Instruct v0.2 reveals that pruning benefits correlate with initial model safety levels. We interpret these results by examining changes in attention patterns and perplexity shifts, demonstrating that pruned models exhibit sharper attention and increased sensitivity to artificial jailbreak constructs. We extend our evaluation to the AdvBench harmful behavior tasks and the GCG attack method. We find that LLaMA-2 is much safer on AdvBench prompts than on our dataset when evaluated with manual jailbreak attempts, and that pruning is effective against both automated attacks and manual jailbreaking on Advbench.

papers.title: Obfuscated Activations Bypass LLM Latent-Space Defenses
papers.research_question: Can models execute harmful behavior via inconspicuous latent states, thereby bypassing latent-space defenses?
papers.core_contribution: Obfuscation attacks can bypass latent-space defenses by inducing harmful behavior via inconspicuous activations, demonstrating that neural representations are highly malleable.
papers.conclusion: Neural activations are highly malleable, allowing obfuscation attacks to bypass latent-space defenses, which poses a fundamental challenge to such defenses.
papers.key_findings:
Obfuscation attacks can bypass harmfulness monitors (probes, OOD detectors, SAEs) while maintaining high jailbreak rates.
Obfuscated activations are widespread; attackers can find new ones even after iterative adversarial training.
Obfuscation attacks transfer between different types of monitors (e.g., obfuscating against OOD detectors fools probes).
Models trained with latent robustness methods (Circuit Breakers, LAT) are also vulnerable to obfuscation attacks.
Obfuscation can reduce model performance on complex tasks like SQL code generation, indicating a trade-off.
papers.limitation:
Obfuscation attacks can reduce model performance on complex tasks like SQL code generation.
Achieving near-orthogonal activations while preserving behavior is difficult with current optimization methods.
future_direction: Improvements to Obfuscated Adversarial Training (OAT) and attacks against it, and scaling trends.
Investigating obfuscated activations in other domains beyond LLMs and image classifiers.
Developing new latent-space monitoring approaches that account for malleability of representations.
papers.abstract: Recent latent-space monitoring techniques have shown promise as defenses against LLM attacks. These defenses act as scanners that seek to detect harmful activations before they lead to undesirable actions. This prompts the question: Can models execute harmful behavior via inconspicuous latent states? Here, we study such obfuscated activations. We show that state-of-the-art latent-space defenses -- including sparse autoencoders, representation probing, and latent OOD detection -- are all vulnerable to obfuscated activations. For example, against probes trained to classify harmfulness, our attacks can often reduce recall from 100% to 0% while retaining a 90% jailbreaking rate. However, obfuscation has limits: we find that on a complex task (writing SQL code), obfuscation reduces model performance. Together, our results demonstrate that neural activations are highly malleable: we can reshape activation patterns in a variety of ways, often while preserving a network's behavior. This poses a fundamental challenge to latent-space defenses.

papers.title: Latent Adversarial Training Improves Robustness to Persistent Harmful Behaviors in LLMs
papers.research_question: How can targeted latent adversarial training be used to improve the removal of persistent harmful behaviors in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces targeted latent adversarial training (LAT) and shows it can augment existing methods to more effectively remove persistent harmful behaviors in LLMs, such as jailbreaks, backdoors, and undesirable knowledge, with minimal tradeoffs in general performance.
papers.conclusion: Targeted latent adversarial training is an effective tool for defending against harmful behaviors from LLMs, improving robustness to jailbreaks, backdoor removal, and unlearning with minimal side effects.
papers.key_findings:
Targeted LAT improves robustness to jailbreaks, outperforming R2D2 with orders of magnitude less compute.
Targeted LAT greatly improves DPO's ability to remove backdoors without knowledge of the trigger.
Targeted LAT improves unlearning methods (WHP, gradient ascent, RMU) and makes unlearning more robust to re-learning.
Targeted LAT does not substantially harm general performance on benign tasks.
Targeted LAT is more effective than untargeted LAT for defending against specific harmful behaviors.
papers.limitation:
LAT requires a dataset of undesirable behaviors.
The perturbations are simple L2-bounded noise added to the residual stream, which may not be the most effective or interpretable attack.
The work does not produce interpretable explanations for why LAT works.
future_direction: Developing more sophisticated latent-space attacks, such as using sparse autoencoders or low-rank adapters.
Augmenting other latent-space techniques for robustness.
Using generalized adversarial attacks for LLM evaluations.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can often be made to behave in undesirable ways that they are explicitly fine-tuned not to. For example, the LLM red-teaming literature has produced a wide variety of 'jailbreaking' techniques to elicit harmful text from models that were fine-tuned to be harmless. Recent work on red-teaming, model editing, and interpretability suggests that this challenge stems from how (adversarial) fine-tuning largely serves to suppress rather than remove undesirable capabilities from LLMs. Prior work has introduced latent adversarial training (LAT) as a way to improve robustness to broad classes of failures. These prior works have considered untargeted latent space attacks where the adversary perturbs latent activations to maximize loss on examples of desirable behavior. Untargeted LAT can provide a generic type of robustness but does not leverage information about specific failure modes. Here, we experiment with targeted LAT where the adversary seeks to minimize loss on a specific competing task. We find that it can augment a wide variety of state-of-the-art methods. First, we use targeted LAT to improve robustness to jailbreaks, outperforming a strong R2D2 baseline with orders of magnitude less compute. Second, we use it to more effectively remove backdoors with no knowledge of the trigger. Finally, we use it to more effectively unlearn knowledge for specific undesirable tasks in a way that is also more robust to re-learning. Overall, our results suggest that targeted LAT can be an effective tool for defending against harmful behaviors from LLMs.

papers.title: AttentionDefense: Leveraging System Prompt Attention for Explainable Defense Against Novel Jailbreaks
papers.research_question: Can system-prompt attention from Small Language Models (SLMs) be used to characterize adversarial prompts for jailbreak detection?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes AttentionDefense, a method that uses system-prompt attention weights from SLMs to detect jailbreaks, offering an explainable, scalable, and generalizable defense.
papers.conclusion: AttentionDefense improves the explainability, scalability, and generalizability of jailbreak detection by leveraging system prompt attention from SLMs, demonstrating robustness against both known and novel jailbreak attacks.
papers.key_findings:
AttentionDefense (using Phi-2) achieves an F1-score of 0.86 on novel jailbreaks, outperforming text embedding-based classifiers and matching the performance of the much larger GPT-4 detector.
System prompt attention is a more robust and generalizable signal for jailbreak detection than semantic embeddings, performing equally well on known and novel jailbreaks.
Defining the jailbreak mechanism in the system prompt is more critical for high-precision detection than defining the payload.
Fine-tuned models (e.g., Phi-3.5-mini-instruct) may not be good candidates for using latent representations like attention for detection, as safety fine-tuning appears to obscure the signal.
AttentionDefense provides a cheaper alternative to LLM-based detectors, achieving comparable performance with models that are 800 times smaller in parameters.
papers.limitation:
AttentionDefense is anchored by a system prompt; if the system prompt is not well-engineered, the attention weights may not show meaningful differences between benign and malicious prompts.
Any change to the system prompt requires the training data to be regenerated and the classifier retrained.
AttentionDefense inherits constraints of the underlying SLM, such as small context windows.
future_direction: Investigating if system prompt attention can be used for other detector use cases outside of jailbreaks.
Exploring if a similar approach to AttentionDefense can be built using unsupervised learning to measure out-of-distribution detection, removing the requirement for labeled data.
papers.abstract: In the past few years, Language Models (LMs) have shown par-human capabilities in several domains. Despite their practical applications and exceeding user consumption, they are susceptible to jailbreaks when malicious input exploits the LM's weaknesses, causing it to deviate from its intended behavior. Current defensive strategies either classify the input prompt as adversarial or prevent LMs from generating harmful outputs. However, it is challenging to explain the reason behind the malicious nature of the jailbreak, which results in a wide variety of closed-box approaches. In this research, we propose and demonstrate that system-prompt attention from Small Language Models (SLMs) can be used to characterize adversarial prompts, providing a novel, explainable, and cheaper defense approach called AttentionDefense. Our research suggests that the attention mechanism is an integral component in understanding and explaining how LMs respond to malicious input that is not captured in the semantic meaning of text embeddings. The proposed AttentionDefense is evaluated against existing jailbreak benchmark datasets. Ablation studies show that SLM-based AttentionDefense has equivalent or better jailbreak detection performance compared to text embedding-based classifiers and GPT-4 zero-shot detectors.To further validate the efficacy of the proposed approach, we generate a dataset of novel jailbreak variants of the existing benchmark dataset using a closed-loop LLM-based multi-agent system. We demonstrate that the proposed AttentionDefense approach performs robustly on this novel jailbreak dataset while existing approaches suffer in performance. Additionally, for practical purposes AttentionDefense is an ideal solution as it has the computation requirements of a small LM but the performance of a LLM detector.

papers.title: Can LLMs Lie? Investigation beyond Hallucination
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether LLMs can intentionally lie (as opposed to unintentionally hallucinate), and how to understand and control lying behavior using mechanistic interpretability.
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers the neural mechanisms of lying in LLMs using mechanistic interpretability, and introduces steering vectors to control lying behavior, showing a trade-off between honesty and task performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that lying in LLMs can be understood and controlled via mechanistic interpretability, and highlights the trade-offs between honesty and task success in real-world scenarios.
papers.key_findings:
Lying ability in LLMs improves with model size and reasoning capabilities.
LLMs use dummy tokens as a computational scratchpad for lying, with specific attention heads and MLP modules involved.
Lying circuits are sparse and can be ablated to reduce deception without broadly degrading model utility.
Different types of lies (white vs. malicious, commission vs. omission) are linearly separable in activation space and controllable via distinct steering directions.
Steering vectors can increase honesty in multi-turn conversational settings, establishing a Pareto frontier between honesty and goal completion.
papers.limitation:
Analysis confined to a few model families and sizes.
Steering vectors derived from a limited set of contrastive prompts.
Multi-turn conversational setting is simplified.
Honesty steering vectors applied in the negative direction may lead to mass production of false information.
future_direction: Scaling the approach to larger models and more complex scenarios.
Investigating the transferability of steering vectors across domains.
Developing more robust safeguards against deceptive AI.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities across a variety of tasks, but their increasing autonomy in real-world applications raises concerns about their trustworthiness. While hallucinations-unintentional falsehoods-have been widely studied, the phenomenon of lying, where an LLM knowingly generates falsehoods to achieve an ulterior objective, remains underexplored. In this work, we systematically investigate the lying behavior of LLMs, differentiating it from hallucinations and testing it in practical scenarios.
